ResponsesInList.Text:
I have a moodle installation (2.7.9) that used to work fine. When we deployed an IDM-sso solution ( Oracle Access Manager) that included a load balancer, our problems started. 1) First, a user that was authenticated correctly (using a custom built auth plugin) 2) When the user tries to post a forum message everything is ok 3) When a user starts writing the forum message and spends more than 120 seconds on that page and the clicks the post button he/she gets the message " Sorry, guests are not allowed to post." 4) When he/she clicks continue they are shown as logged in. I immediately started searching for session time out, and using a script, i figured out that moodle was throwing him out after ~120 seconds (session timeout is set in 2 hours). Sessions are handled in the DB ( MySQL ). When i printed the $SESSION var i got 
```text
object(stdClass)#69 (1) {
  ["has_timed_out"]=>
  bool(true)
}
```
 Any clues on what might be happening?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle session timeout not being respected
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Christos, what is the logic/algo behind that load balancer? You should inspect the HTTP Request&Response to look for the clues about why the Moodle session will be considered as expired: everything is based on cookies on Moodle side and it could be possible that something is mangling those cookies after that period. HTH , Matteo

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle session timeout not being respected
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Matteo, We are using Zenloadbalancer ( http://www.zenloadbalancer.com/ ) as part of an Oracle IAM and SSO solution we recently added to our infrastructure. You are probably right, that something is mangling those cookies, but i bypassed that by activating the ldap auth as a second auth solution, so i guess that after failing the first auth (IAM0 it moves to the next Ldap that actually works. I know that it is not the best solution, but it works. I will look more into this to figure out what is going on. Thank you for responding. Best regards, Christos

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle session timeout not being respected
ResponsesInList.Text: Are you sure that you're actually storing the sessions in the database ($CFG->dbsessions is true, and you're using a database which supports session locking)?  Records being present in the database doesn't necessarily mean that the sessions themselves are there - sessions are tracked in the database for other session storage methods too. I ask this as it sounds as though you may have your sessions stored on (local) disk, with the load balancer sending the later request to a different node which doesn't have the session file available.  You may be able to identify this situation by tracking which node serves each request.  If this does turn out to be the problem, switching to either database or memcache/memcached (assuming a single memcached instance is shared by all nodes for this purpose) session handling ought to do the trick; if that's not an option for whatever reason, perhaps you can configure the load balancing to use "sticky" sessions (pinning the user to a single node for the duration of their session) so that all of the requests within a given user's session are served by the same node and thus have the session file available.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: moodle clonepermissions
ResponsesInList.Text: The different types of risk associated with capabilities are explained here: https://docs.moodle.org/en/Risks The valid values are a combination of the RISK_* defined values (your IDE should be able to autocomplete them when you type them). clonepermissionsfrom is used during the creation of a new capability - it is allocated automatically to all the roles that already have the given capability. e.g. if 'clonepermissionsfrom' is set to 'moodle/course:view', then your new capability will be given to every existing role that already has the 'moodle/course:view' capability (after installation, site admins are free to reallocate the capability).

But - if you have a javascript error earlier in the page, than the requirejs calls it could be affected. Also - the above error does look more like you have some faulty AMD code somewhere so you should double check you haven't left any files in and "amd" folders. You could disable "cachejs" to see the non-minified version of the JS in your browser, and you will probably get a better error message.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What is RequireJS doing?
ResponsesInList.Text: It is very hard to debug these things in my experience.  First make sure you purge your cache so that the error is not something already fixed. In fact it helps to turn off all javascript caching. Do that at: Site Administration - > appearance -> Ajax and Javascript 500 errors are errors occurring in PHP. There might be something in your server error logs with more information about where that is occurring. The error about the missing init function, likely relates to whatever it was to be init'ed not being created in the first place. So you need to find out what that was. In your own code are any of your JS functions called "init"? Do you have any Generico templates that might be failing? Try disabling Generico and see if that makes any difference.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What is RequireJS doing?
ResponsesInList.Text: The call to first.js is actually the call that will load all of the AMD modules on your moodle site in a single request. I don't know why it is returning a 500 error - but I would start by checking the permissions on all the files in any amd/ folder under moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Bug that is reproducible only with a new change
ResponsesInList.Text: Doing work on MDL-25740 we encounter a slight (but nasty) bug in Javascript confirmation dialog. The bug is seen under very specifical conditions that didn't existed in several previous Moodle versions: using confirmation dialog from secure quiz attempt window with actual form with user-entered data in it. The standard Moodle practice is that bug should be backported, but improvment should not. However in this case the bug is reproducible only with improvment. It is not possible to write test instructions for that bug for previous Moodle versions without something like "alter Moodle code like this ..." and there is no possibility the bug will harm anyone using older versions. So what policy Moodle should have on this issue? Can be bundle the bug fix and improvment together in one issue (but with different commits of course)? Or should they be filed separately on the tracker? Should the bug fix be backported to the issues where it is unreproducible? How should testing instructions be written to such bug if it is filed separately and not reproducible by itself?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Bug that is reproducible only with a new change
ResponsesInList.Text: If you have added an "improvement", and it causes a bug, you would not need to backport the bug fix, as the bug only exists in the newer versions with the improvement. Bug fixes are only backported when the bugs exist in earlier, supported versions. mike

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Bug that is reproducible only with a new change
ResponsesInList.Text: It's not improvment that causes the bug. It's about improvment which uses standard library function in a way that it was not used before and library function has a bug that is visible under these circumstances only.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Bug that is reproducible only with a new change
ResponsesInList.Text: Okay. So the standard answer would be if the bug exists in supported versions, then the fix would be backported to those supported versions. Right now, that would include 3.0, 2.9 and 2.7 (LTS). I'm not sure about 2.8. But, if the bug truly doesn't impact anything but the latest version, backporting may be skipped since it would offer no useful improvement. mike

Memory limit problems: High resolution images vs thumbnails generation
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi everyone, We happen to have recurrent memory exhaustion problems in production when users try to upload high resolution images in many different areas in Moodle that generate a thumbnail using the GD library (Mostly through the file manager). For example, a jpeg image like this one -> https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B0H8CbGn160eMHg3cGZrSmtzRTA/view with dimensions of 16,313 x 3,621 would take 236,277,492 bytes of image data to generate the thumbnail (4 bytes per pixel) because GD has to decompress the data to be able to use it. Note: The problem apply to servers using the GD library bundled with PHP
(Recommended) and not the one from the OS. See the following issue I
created in the PHP bug tracker for more details: https://bugs.php.net/bug.php?id=71093 Actually the only way I see to resolve this problem without modifying the Moodle core code is to increase the PHP memory limit in the php.ini config which is overkill and leave the server more vulnerable. The other way would be to modify the functions that generate the thumbnails in "lib/gdlib.php" to raise the memory limit -> raise_memory_limit(MEMORY_EXTRA) Is there anyone having the same problems in their Moodle instance? Do you think the idea of modifying the core to raise memory limit would be acceptable? Is there any other suggestions or recommandations? Thanks for your feedbacks!

ResponsesInList.Title: HEADS UP: Changing build process for bootstrapbase in core
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Everyone, Up to now, we've been using recess as the official tool to compile less in bootstrapbase. From memory the decision to use recess as the official tool was more or less just because its what bootstrap 2 upstream used. It has actually always been particularly poor at debug output and so on and twitter have now stopped maintenance of recess ( MDL-51582 ) so it makes sense to finally switch away from it. Now that we have grunt - it seems natural to use that for building less, it makes it simpler and more standard for newcomers, basing on grunt means we can start to make use of other clever plugins without impacting developer workflow (like community developed themes are doing already ), there is great tool support for grunt, it uses the same less.js as lessc etc etc. So thats what i've done in MDL-51582 . I think this is all fairly non controversial - the main reason for posting this is because I want to propose that we make this change on all supported branches (master, 30, 29). My rationale is: Consistent - less complicated for developers Making the change has no impact on third parties - only people changing core (in fact, people are already using lessc with out bootstrap in third party themes). We already require grunt for JS on these branches The grunt way is just easier than the manual commands we currently have (once grunt is installed) This means once this is integrated, you'd have to use grunt instead of recess to compile less (to get consistent output). I welcome you feedback! cheers, Dan

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: I've done that before, but it wasn't pretty.  We did it by keeping the username and the email address matching rather than trying to change the core login code. To do this we used a custom auth plug-in to handle creating new users, and profile edits so that every time the email address was changed it would change the username at the same time. And we had our own login screen, though I don't think that's essential. If any-one has better ideas for how to do this, I'd love to hear them!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: +1 I've had to do this before (we were integrating with another system that used the email address as the login) and we did exactly the same as you. Force usernames to be the same as email addresses. Having said that, as long as you are prepared to write a custom plugin (in Moodle 2 it's fairly easy to sub-class an existing plugin and just change the bits that matter) the actual bit of code that says YES/NO to the login is fairly simple. You only need to change that to make an additional check for the email address matching. My only remaining concern is that (last time I looked) Moodle does not actively enforce unique emails. So you might want to modify the field to make it a unique index.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: Howard, would it not be a trivial matter to make the email field in the User table a unique to ensure no duplicates allowed? What would that do to the data entry times in Moodles with a larger User base?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: It's trivial to run the command to do it. Obviously, if there are existing duplicates they will need to to be found and fixed first. In theory any additional index will increase the write times to the table, but even on very large sites the user table isn't that big in the great scheme of things. The remaining issue is that some operations might fail unpleasantly due to the lack of checks for duplicate emails. A small price to pay I suspect.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes you could easily do that at the database layer and I doubt it would have a significant performance implication (though I am not a performance expert, so you may wish to test). You might get some unhelpful error messages if people edited/created user records so that they broke the database uniqueness restriction though unless you also go through the forms to add validation for that. I'm not sure if you can do that without customising core Moodle though.  So far everything Howard and I suggested could be done with a plug-in, which will be much easier for you to maintain through future Moodle upgrades.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: Then it would seem that Moodle devs relied upon the idea that all emails must, of necessity, be unique. However, what then prevents users from sharing a single email address? mmm A properly ordered database and a single function would then provide a workaround for that issue? Should this be a Moodle Tracker item? A potential security issue perhaps?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: No. If you go through the UI then it's very difficult to create duplicate emails. You've probably noticed the recurrant question from people *wanting* to share a single email (mad though it may appear). However, it's not rigorously enforced and it is possible to do (e.g. I don't think authentication plugins that create users check at all). It's a small point - in the vast majority of cases email uniqueness is a side-issue.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello! Thanks for your replies. I was able to implement the logging in using email or username already. Yey! Of course, I made both the email and username unique first. I altered the edit_form.php's validation function to make them unique. And then, I hacked the function authenticate_user_login in moodlelib.php I added something like: check username and pw if existing and correct if match, log in. if no match, check email and pw if existing and correct... if match, log in. if no match, log in failure Basically, I only added a little tweak in moodlelib.php the others are just functions to make sure that the email is always unique.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: Forcing the email field to be unique shouldn't require much database overhead at all, at least in MySQL . All you'd need is a UNIQUE HASH index on the 'email' field. You'd need to catch the insert failure at the front-end, but that's simple too. It's probably worth noting that, in the mdl_course table, shortname isn't required to be unique. It's enforced at the front-end, but there's nothing at the database level to prevent duplicated. Should you end up with duplicate shortnames (and you use the shortname to apply enrolments), all hell can break loose. It's an amateur mistake, but it's one I've made before.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: I wrote the attached mod to the authenticate_user_login function in  lib/moodlelib.php.  If the supplied $username matches an email address in the mdl_user table, it makes a log entry and switches the $username variable to the value of the username field in the matched user record.  It is very simple, and I've already thought of a couple problems others may have with it. 1.  If e-mail addresses are not unique on your system, the wrong user may be selected and login will fail (unless the users also have the same password, in which case the user will log in to the wrong account). 2.  If you authenticate against an external database or LDAP or similar method and rely on Moodle to create the account when the user logs in the first time, this mod will not help you for that initial login as the user is not yet in the mdl_user table.  I run the sync_users.php program every time my external database changes, so this is not an issue for me. 3.  I don't use mnet and have no idea how it works.  This probably won't work for mnet users. Patch was written with version 2.5.1+ (Build: 20130802).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: Two comments; 1. Why change core code when you can create an authentication plugin? http://docs.moodle.org/dev/Authentication_plugins 2. AFAIK Moodle needs the user email address to be unique already. Anne.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: 1.  From the page you linked: a lot of interesting stuff happens in authenticate_user_login() . 2.  It looks up the username in the mdl_user table to see if they are allowed to log in, and which authentication plugin handles their login requests. (This will be the plugin that handled their first-ever login request.) I want my users to be able to use either their username or their e-mail address when they log in.  An authentication plugin won't help with this because the logic that needs "fixed" is in the core code. 2.  While it's true that the program won't allow you to use an e-mail address that is already in use, that doesn't mean it can't be changed in the database.  The e-mail field is not a unique field in my My SQL database.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi David, In the default situation people can log in using their username. So 50% of your requirement is already covered. The other 50% is that if they do no use their username, but their email instead, they still should be able to log in. So if it doesn't exists yet, you'd need to write a auth plugin that accepts the email address of a user and based on that checks against the password. Because the auth plugins work via a failover/waterfall method; as long as one auth plugin does not authenticate the user the next auth plugin in line will be called, this will result in users begin able to either use their username or email to log in. If there is a chance of email duplication (I seem to recall Moodle code really doesn't like that), you could make sure that in that case people or the admin get a warning. Anne.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Login Using Email or Username
ResponsesInList.Text: I spent this afternoon trying to write the plugin you suggest. When Moodle successfully authenticates a user during the failover/waterfall portion of authenticate_user_login() after not finding the username in the user table, it attempts to create a new account.  The user already has an account, so it will likely fail because of duplicate users (or worse...it will actually create a new account and the user now has two!). If you enable $CFG->authpreventaccountcreation to try to stop this behavior, it never gets to the failover/waterfall routine. Dave

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Auto quiz creation
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Alexis, The classification of the questions is key here, and your contract-giver needs to consider that extremely carefully.  To have any sort of meaningful automation of the quiz question selection, you are going to need a lot of categories. To give an example from language teaching: To create quizzes for practising the past simple, I have categories for positive sentences, negative sentences, open and closed questions.  There are sub categories for each of those for the different question types - cloze, essay, short answer, multiple-choice, drag and drop and so on.  In each of these sub categories, there are basic, intermediate and advanced categories.  All of that is repeated for general English, Business English, and technical English.  (Not forgetting labels categories to provide structure to the quiz.) And the same is repeated for more than a dozen other subject areas. In short, there are a hell of a lot of categories, but because all the date is is the right place, it's now quite easy to put together either very specific or more complex quizzes. The structure of your question bank is vital because any incongruence there will make any accurate automation of the process nigh on impossible. It might well be possible to use tags to reduce some of the levels of categories, but either way the questions will still have to be tagged which may turn out to be more work than a good categorisation. All the best Andy (who saw the light at the end of the tunnel, but then found out it was a person with a torch bringing me more work!)

ResponsesInList.Title: mform callback custom messages
ResponsesInList.Text: I have a form element in which I want to provide various feedback strings based on its content. I can use a callback rule and supply the function which performs the validation, but how should I modify the value of the error message to render if the condition returns false; the following doesn't work. $err = ""; $checkit = function ($val) { if (empty($val)) { $err = "can't be empty"; } else if (strrpos( $val , "bob-", -strlen($val)) !== FALSE) { $err = "can't start with bob"; } else if (someComplicatedRegex($val)) { $err = "got the format wrong"; }; return empty($err); // empty == true, not empty == false } $mform->addElement('text', 'myfield', get_string('myfield', 'auth_mything'), 'maxlength="12"'); $mform->setType(' myfield ', PARAM_NOTAGS); $mform->addRule(' myfield ', $err, 'callback', $checkit, ' server ');

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: mform callback custom messages
ResponsesInList.Text: If you don't want the simple built-in validation rules (e.g. 'required', 'maxlength', etc), then your best bet is to add server-side validation with the 'validation' function in your form class. Within your 'validation($data, $files)' function, do all the checks you require, then return an array of 'elementname' => 'error message'. If the array is empty, then Moodle accepts the form and processes it. if the array is non-empty, then each of the error messages is displayed with its associated form element.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is there any code checker for JavaScript plugins?
ResponsesInList.Text: There is JavaScript checking on Travis CI, if you have a public plugin repository on GitHub. Whenever you push an update to GitHub, Travis kicks in and automatically checks both the PHP and JavaScript code. It works a treat for me - the results are shown online on the corresponding Travis website, e.g. https://travis-ci.org/ecampbell/moodle-atto_wordimport/jobs/92241555 for my particular plugin. Instructions on how to configure this are at https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=323384 The main downside is that you must first publish your changes to Github in order for the checks to run, so you then have to update the files again to fix the problems. Another issue is that the versions of the code-checking programs that run on the local Moodle CodeChecker are older than the versions on the Travis CI site, so you may get different results. For example, the directive "@codingStandardsIgnoreLine" generates a warning locally, but is accepted by Travis CI.

ResponsesInList.Title: Adhoc scheduled task?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello, is there a way to schedule a task to run once in future? What I am trying to achieve with this is the following: * Let's say the user has to do something at least N minutes, so when the user starts to do something, I would like to schedule a task to now + N minutes that will check if it's done and take the necessary actions (of course it will take care of user's logouts and session timeouts and so, but there is no reason to test if it's done before the minimum amount of time and I think this approach is better than call a query each minute (even if it is only one query for all users)). In classic unix cron I could set all the "time variables", that includes the year (moodle does not have year on it's syntax), and it would be executed only once in the expected date/time. But then that task would be there forever and would accumulate with others of the same kind and it's not really a good side effect. Does anyone have any ideas? Kind regards, Daniel

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Adhoc scheduled task?
ResponsesInList.Text: When the user does the thing, you could kick off another process to monitor his or her progress. I have had success with Gearman for similar stuff and it has a nice PHP client . The Gearman job could just sleep for N minutes and then check back with Moodle through it's web services to see if the user has completed the task. Or better, the job could be a Moodle CLI script, so it can communicate with Moodle directly. Honestly, it's a lot to set up though. The more conventional approach is probably better, especially if many people are engaged in this workflow. If you run a query for users who have begun, but not completed, a task every single time cron runs, it is a waste only if no users are returned.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Adhoc scheduled task?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello, Brendan this Gearman seems to be a nice tool, but really also seems to much work. When you say "The Gearman job could just sleep for N minutes and then check", well, that is not really that elegant too, and could be done with Moodle's ad-hoc tasks that are non-blockable by default and run in background. Kind regards, Daniel

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Adhoc scheduled task?
ResponsesInList.Text: I don't think that's possible at the moment. It would be a useful feature, though, so it might be worth raising in the Moodle Tracker. It's possible it was implemented the way it is deliberately to prevent some other problem, though, so it's maybe not that simple.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: When will core use renderers?
ResponsesInList.Text: Some general comments - Moodle is a very large project with a mix of old and new code maintained by many different people over the years. When we are limited by the existing APIs - we need to find a way to improve them without breaking backwards compatibility (big lesson from the 1.9 -> 2.0 transition). We also only have limited resources - so when we add a new API (like templates) - we will use this API for new developments (Competency Based Education) - but we won't go back and refactor all the existing things in Moodle because we don't have the resources. Moodle prioritises its work as Students > Teachers > Admins > Developers - so if we spend an entire release refactoring code so that it is nice for developers - then there are no new features or improvements for admins, teachers and students. When we do prioritise refreshing an existing module - then we will obviously convert it to use the newest APIs - so things will get updated over time. Anyone from the community is encouraged to contribute - and if developers want to improve things for other developers - please send patches. Nothing is black and white though - and often time spend improving APIs and old code will save us time later in reduced bugs, less maintenance etc. Back to the original topic - converting code to use renderers - the integrators have been rejecting code that does not use renderers for many many years now (as long as I have worked on Moodle). It is not simple or quick to convert old modules to renderers - most people do not even understand the difference between a well designed renderer and a bad one (DB queries etc). Anyone is encouraged to contribute though - and the more of Moodle that is updated to use renderers the better.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: When will core use renderers?
ResponsesInList.Text: 'often time spend improving APIs and old code will save us time later in reduced bugs, less maintenance etc' And there you have the other view point put in your own words Damyon Taking time out to refactor Moodle may well result in a (relatively) short period of time where there is a hiatus on new features, but the benefits once it is done would mean that was very quickly caught back up and could draw additional developer support into the community in the long run - those people who want to get involved, take one look, do what they have to and back off again. Also a consideration of whether the mix of multiple half-employed APIs, and adding a new one to that mix, actually creates a benefit (through the newer, better api) or itself creates additional HQ developer workload going forward (because of the length of time that multiple methodologies are having to be considered in parallel). Student>Teacher>Admin>Developer is fine as a general priority, and I have had similar discussions in other workplaces (the student always comes first in school for example - but when that is used as an excuse for decisions that are actively to the detriment of the staff, does it really benefit the students? or does it create an environment that fails to foster the best learning atmosphere?). I am not saying developers should always come first, not at all, the end user and the user experience should be our priority - but sometimes the best for the end user is to give the best scaffolding and support to the people who create the user experience (widest sense rather than web page UX). General priorities are (should be) there as a guide - when they become fixed in stone they begin to cause problems. As one example - Bootstrap - no apparent movement on the (developer/forum/moot/tracker?) requests to implement BS3 in core for Moodle3.0, yet we then have to pick up requests from forum users (and other discussions) telling front end users that no, that bootstrap code you are trying to put into your content area (as a teacher) wont work, because you need to use BS2 not BS3 - yes I know its old and... yes I know it says supports bootstrap... No, core isn't moving to the current standards at the moment.  A backend decision that significantly affects the front end users. Again, please don't misunderstand my comments - I fully understand the resource implications as well as the priorities - the comments are for debate and to spark the discussion as I really feel that it is important for that discussion to happen and to bring alternative views to HQ and Martin (and to the community). That doesn't mean I (or anyone else) expect them to happen, but it does (I hope) mean that alternative views get listened to and, if there is sufficient weight behind them from the community, taken into consideration. Having the open discussion is not intended to imply anything other than 100% support for HQ/Moodle/Martin, just a desire to see Moodle get even better, both as a product in its own right and as a community/ecostructure to be part of I don't believe my comments are just 'argument for argument's sake' though. I do believe those concerns are there among the people in the community (as well as potential community members) - they are small and they are minor, but they are there. Most of us do understand HQ's position and while we may like to see things done differently in a particular instance, fully appreciate that is not always possible. Could someone in my original position (a class teacher with little/no development experience) now get so far interested in,  hooked on and involved in Moodle as to become a forum moderator in one of the areas that do require development skills (rather than the pedagogy of the 'Teaching with Moodle' or other equally valuable forums) or is the current setup a barrier? - we get a lot of 'newbie' posts, but how many of them stick around and come back and start providing support after they get their questions answered (rather than - or as well as, I still do both! - coming back with more questions) as they learn more about moodle background and how it works? How many posts do we see from people who do already have development experience who just say they need significant help to understand Moodle when looking at the code base as it is now? That community and those fresh faces are (alongside the experienced, long service members) the life blood of Moodle that keeps it moving forward at the pace it does, supporting HQ and allowing the HQ developers to focus on the improvements and developments they make.

ResponsesInList.Title: Warning: 2.9.3 non-backwards-compatibility
ResponsesInList.Text: Since we upgraded to Moodle 2.9.3, a bunch of our behat tests are failing because of MDL-51756 , which is outputting a lot of developer debug warnings on some pages. There was nothing aobut this in the release notes until I added an unhelpful warning just now. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Warning: 2.9.3 non-backwards-compatibility
ResponsesInList.Text: (I haven't refamiliarised with myself with it properly, just replying quickly from memory). The debug warning is to tell you that you've specified a function parameter as ' VALUE_OPTIONAL ' but provided a default value. If you want it to fall back to a default value you should declare your function parameters as VALUE_DEFAULT.  See fixes in core: https://github.com/moodle/moodle/commit/4d9edf1b152f24a770c93b4debddad52d91c6557 We made this throw a debug warning because if you enabled that function in a webservice called with xmlrpc (and potentially other protocols) it would throw an exception and break the entire service including unrelated functions. It was extremely obtuse and difficult to spot where the problem was coming from and would be silent until you added that function to a service. Note its a mischaracterisation to say this is non-backwards compatible, its a DEBUG_DEVELOPER warning and does not affect production environments. On the other hand, if one day you added one of those 'broken' services to an existing web-service it would break the entire web-service and not be at all obvious where the problem came from. I'm sorry that this got missed from the release notes and the debug warning was not explanatory enough.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New completion status
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Stephan Something to check is whether a "timecompleted" datestamp (in course_completions) exists; this gets stamped when a successful Completion is achieved (after the cron cycles and updates everything).  If you have a record of an attempt, but no timecompleted datestamp, then it's a failed/incomplete attempt (unless you have set up your Course Completion incorrectly) A side thing to note is that this "timecompleted" is a one-off; it never updates with any subsequent completions.  If it's a course that the user will re-do in the future, you have to come up with clever jiggery to nullify this datestamp, clear the grades, wipe quiz attempts, etc., etc... because, you know, there's never ever any reason for someone to re-do the same course again in the Real World...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Git workflow
ResponsesInList.Text: Our preferred method for managing client codebases uses submodules, Gerrit, and client specific branches. The steps we go through: Checkout MOODLE_29_STABLE Fork a client branch, eg. git checkout -b clientname-version-sitetype. Push to Gerrit. Add plugins using submodules. Submodules repos are also on Gerrit. If a plugin requires customisation, fork a new branch from the submodule, and push it to the Gerrit repo. To manage code changes, we use Gerrit for code reviews, and controlling what patches are merged. Gerrit also handles submodules nicely - if a patch is merged in a submodule branch, and a project tracks that submodule branch, the parent project will automatically be updated. This removes the overhead of managing submodule changes in the parent project. It probably wouldn't be too hard to script this if you weren't using Gerrit. Merging upstream releases of core or plugins is pretty simple. Just merge the latest parent branch, push, and test. The biggest advantage of using submodules like this is keeping all the plugin code separate. Tracking upstream plugin changes if plugins are part of the main repo can be a serious pain. Deployments are a separate issue, and there are many ways to do it. I've used capistrano, debian packages, git checkouts, CI tools... Currently one project I manage uses GoCD and Jenkins. This can be overkill for some projects though. Another uses custom bash scripts with git-archive-all to create a tarball of the full codebase, which is then extracted on the servers. That works well enough.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Git workflow
ResponsesInList.Text: I've found this thread very interesting and am grateful for all of the suggestions shared. I will be looking into Capistrano , Ansible , Chef , Composer , Docker , Gerrit, GoCD , Puppet and Tasc . It's been a few years since I last looked into these types of tools so there may now be something to suit my needs. My situation is a little more complicated than yours because I need to support multiple version of Moodle and multiple versions of plugins in several cases. One of the things you keep in mind is that the GitHub repositories for 3rd party plugins rarely contain the same code as the released code on moodle.org/plugins. In some cases the code is behind while in other cases it is ahead (i.e. new version in development/testing). Be aware and be careful of this as you can end up breaking plugins and your Moodle site. With very few exceptions, the only git repo that I typically clone is Moodle itself. What I've done is to setup a directory tree structure and have a bash script that assembles/updates a Moodle site with plugins, as needed. Here is an example of my directory structure which matches where plugins would be placed if in the Moodle directory tree (minus the plugins directory). Moodle moodle/ Unlike the rest of the directories below, this is a clone of my Moodle fork repository on GitHub which includes all versions of Moodle so it can easily be switched from one version to another when creating a new site. I can also simply merge recent updates into the code. If I need to create a pull request, I will create separate branche (with tracking enabled!) and push it to my GitHub fork. If the core code gets updated before my modifications are merged into the core code, I can rebase my patch branches to merge changes. If you never plan on submitting fixes for Moodle core code, you can skip having a fork on GitHub to make things a little simpler. When I create a new Moodle site, I simply copy the files to a new location on my webserver and git checkout the desired MOODLE_XX_STABLE branch. If you do a lot of core patches, you may also want to have your own branch which integrates all of your fixes so that you don't have to wait for fixes to be integrated into the core code. Plugins I put all of my 3rd party plugins under a folder called plugins. They are organized in the same structure as if they were in the directory tree of Moodle making it easy to keep track of the types and locations of plugins. For example: plugins/auth/ plugins/availability/conditions plugins/blocks/ plugins/course/format plugins/enrol/ plugins/filter/ plugins/lib/editor/atto/plugins/ plugins/lib/editor/tinymce/plugins/ plugins/local/ plugins/mod/ plugins/report/ plugins/theme/ Inside each of the above directories, I have a directory for each plugin of each version of Moodle. Unlike with Moodle, this is necessary because there is no standard organization of branches in plugins. The main branch in some plugins might be "master" while others, like Configurable Reports, might be CR_23_STABLE. For example: plugins/mod/attendance24 plugins/mod/attendance25 plugins/mod/attendance26 plugins/mod/attendance27 plugins/mod/attendance28 plugins/mod/attendance29 In this case, there is a release for each version of Moodle the Attendance activity module. However, in cases where a version of the plugin is the same across several versions of Moodle, subsequent directories would actually be symlinks so that I only need to make changes in one place when making modifications: plugins/mod/groupchoice22 plugins/mod/groupchoice23 (symlink to groupchoice22) plugins/mod/groupchoice24 (symlink to groupchoice22) plugins/mod/groupchoice25 (symlink to groupchoice22) plugins/mod/groupchoice26 (symlink to groupchoice22) plugins/mod/groupchoice27 plugins/mod/groupchoice27 (symlink to groupchoice27) plugins/mod/groupchoice28 (symlink to groupchoice27) plugins/mod/groupchoice29 (symlink to groupchoice27) My script removes the version number at the end of the plugin's directory name. Custom/Customized Plugins (optional) Although not required, I also maintain a separate "cplugins" directory tree at the same level as "plugins" where I put plugins that I've ether developed myself or 3rd party plugins that I've customized. It makes my build script a little more complicated but makes it easier for me to easily see what I need to maintain. Managing plugin source code As I previously mentioned, git repos are not consistently reflective of the current stable release on Moodle.org/plugins. What you can do is to setup each of these plugin directories as it's own local repo. Then, each time you download a new version of the plugin, replace the existing code (but not the .git directory) with the new version you downloaded and create a new commit for it. This will enable you to move forward and backwards in versions of the code as needed. I've tried using git subtrees (not submodules) and run into directory structure issues that I was unable to resolve in an automated way. The advantage of having your plugins separate from your Moodle code is that you can then have a system whereby you can pick and choose which plugins to include into the instance of a particular Moodle site. If designed right, this same system can double as a way to add new plugins into existing instances of Moodle and update existing plugins in a given site. Even if you maintain only one Moodle site, the ability to create multiple sites can be a real benefit. For example you might want to test a new plugin, a new version of a plugin or a new version of Moodle without impacting your production site. Save even more time/effort/money the Open Source way Whenever you customize a 3rd party plugin, depending on the nature of the customization, I encourage you to contribute your modifications back to the original author through a pull request. Some managers will see this as giving away the results of your time and effort but, since you feel are doing the work anyway, little additional effort is required to share the changes back to the author. Explain to him/her the true long term benefit of participating in Open Source. Think about it. Each time you download a plugin, you are receiving hundreds or even thousands of hours of time and effort that one or more people put into this for free. Why return the favour by sharing your customizations with the author? If the author also thinks this would be a great addition, he/she will integrate the changes into the core plugins code. The best part is that, once integrated into the plugin, your modifications will be perpetually maintained and supported by the author of the plugin and possibly even enhanced over time. The same can be said for Moodle core. This means that, when comes the time for you to upgrade to a newer release of Moodle, the modifications will already be upgraded for you and you won't have to spend any time, money or effort re-applying your changes. It's a win-win situation. You get free maintenance enhancements for the life of the plugin and the Moodle world benefits from your genius and may even raise your awareness of issues you didn't think of before it impacts your users. In general, I've found many Moodle plugin developers to be very responsive and appreciative and open to most contributions. I've submitted issues, fixes and enhancements to 3rd party plugin developers and seen them integrate the changes into their core code not within years, months or weeks, but often literally days or even hours and occasionally even within minutes of sharing changes with them depending on the complexity of the change. You will only see this in the open source community. Microsoft, Apple and other large companies? They might require you to pay for a subscription or at the very least charge your credit card just so that you can report an issue to them. In my experience, unless you are a MAJOR client, the response in the end is often something like "This issue may be addressed in a future release". Will it? Think of it from a business perspective. Why fix an issue if you are making money from it being broken? They have shareholders to keep happy. Imagine if that was the way things went in the Open Source community. Progress would be slowed down to a snails pace. Even if the author of a Moodle plugin has abandoned their project or is too busy to respond, you've got the support of the whole Moodle community to help you out. If you don't like the direction in which a plugin is going, you can fork it yourself and customize it to your hearts content however you loose the benefits and handing off future maintenance and upgrades of your plugin. I've digressed a little here but the point is that sharing back to the community should also be part of your git workflow. Additional development tools On a side note, you might also find the Moodle MDK command line tool to be useful in addition to Moosh previously mentioned in this thread. As part of your QA testing, the Moodle Code Checker plugin can help you get 98% of the way to meeting Moodle coding style guidelines . Hope you find something useful in all of this. Best regards, Michael Milette

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Filepicker issue within local plugin setting page
ResponsesInList.Text: Files on a form are stored in a draft file area, so that they can be updated as much as you like and the 'real' files are not changed until you click on the 'save' button. As the files are not in the 'real' location, they must be served from the draft area - hence the use of the 'draftfile.php' script (which will, as far as I know, only serve the files to the user who owns them AND will only serve them for a few days, until the draft file area is automatically cleaned). To serve files from a 'real' location you need to serve them via pluginfile.php. To do this, your plugin needs to have a _pluginfile function, in order to authenticate the request and make sure the user has permission to view them. If writing a _pluginfile function is too difficult for you (and there are numerous examples in the Moodle code that you could use as examples), then you either need to find/hire a developer who is capable of doing so or do without the feature - serving files from within Moodle does not work without it.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Need Help with some Development Questions and Evaluation
ResponsesInList.Text: Most of these things can be don on top of Moodle, just my writing add-ons of different types. You have a lot of requirements, so I may miss some, but here are some typical examples: "I would like the student to select the provider when signing up" Look at custom user profile fields https://docs.moodle.org/30/en/User_profile_fields "at physical locations and happen on specific days" Have a look at the Scheduler or Face-to-face plugins . "transcripts that must include courses that employees/students have taken" - to get exactly what you want, you probably need to make a custom gradebook report plugin. However, the standard Overview report sort-of does this, and might give you some clues how to start your own report. ( https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Grades#Report_plugins ). Alternatively, look at the Course completion system. I can't remember if that gives any reports as standard. ( https://docs.moodle.org/30/en/Course_completion ). https://docs.moodle.org/30/en/Badges May also be worth a look. "send reminder emails at different intervals to remind employee/students of upcoming classes" The basic idea would be any sort of plugin (local?) with a Scheduled task ( https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Task_API ) that runs once per day. It should do a database query to find all the courses that start in X days time, then use the Message system ( https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Message_API ) to send all the users in those courses a message. "When registering the activation email goes to the provider" sort-of similar, only use the Event system ( https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Events_API ) to find when a user has registered, in order to send the message. I am going to stop there. The point is almost everything you want can be done as a fairly simple add-on. You can develop them one at a time (so you can start with the ones that give the biggest benefit for effort trade-off). Meanwhile, you still get all the features of Moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: FULL Site-wide Course Totals Report
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello everyone. I've been trying to come up with a query similar to this one: https://docs.moodle.org/23/en/ad-hoc_contributed_reports#Site-Wide_Grade_Report_with_Just_Course_Totals But I also need it to return the rows where the course total isn't found for a student, kind of like the Export Grades to TXT function does as shown in the following image: So far my query looks like this: SELECT c.shortname, u.firstname, u.lastname, u.idnumber, u.institution, u.department, u.email, CASE WHEN gg.itemid NOT IN (SELECT `itemid` FROM `mdl_grade_grades` WHERE `userid` = u.id) THEN '-' ELSE ROUND(gg.finalgrade,2) END AS 'Course Total' But it's still not working as it should. Any suggestions?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: FULL Site-wide Course Totals Report
ResponsesInList.Text:
Your query needs to be reworked like this: 
```text
SELECT


  c.shortname,


  u.firstname,


  u.lastname,


  u.idnumber,


  u.institution,


  u.department,


  u.email,


  CASE


    WHEN gg.itemid IS NULL THEN '-'


    ELSE ROUND(gg.finalgrade,2)


  END AS 'Course Total'  


FROM       mdl_course c


INNER JOIN mdl_context          ctx ON c.id = ctx.instanceid AND ctx.contextlevel = 50


INNER JOIN mdl_role_assignments ra  ON ra.contextid = ctx.id AND ra.roleid = 5


INNER JOIN mdl_user             u   ON u.id = ra.userid      AND u.deleted = 0


LEFT JOIN  mdl_grade_items      gi  ON gi.courseid = c.id    AND gi.itemtype = 'course'


LEFT JOIN  mdl_grade_grades     gg  ON gg.userid = u.id      AND gi.id = gg.itemid


ORDER BY c.shortname ASC
```

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: FULL Site-wide Course Totals Report
ResponsesInList.Text: Wow...works wonderfully. Thank you very much . I always get confused on what kind of JOIN to use for such things. Oh and btw ...I forgot to mention that I needed the course totals only from the courses that contain Quiz Modules so I tried adding this to the query: INNER JOIN unip_course_modules cm ON c.id = cm.course AND cm.module = 12 But it's still bringing back data from courses that don't have quizzes. Is there anything else I should add to the query? Once again thanks for your support.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: FULL Site-wide Course Totals Report
ResponsesInList.Text:
```text
SELECT


  c.shortname,


  u.firstname,


  u.lastname,


  u.idnumber,


  u.institution,


  u.department,


  u.email,


  CASE


    WHEN gg.itemid IS NULL THEN '-'


    ELSE ROUND(gg.finalgrade,2)


  END AS 'Course Total'  


FROM       mdl_course c


INNER JOIN mdl_context          ctx ON c.id = ctx.instanceid AND ctx.contextlevel = 50


INNER JOIN mdl_role_assignments ra  ON ra.contextid = ctx.id AND ra.roleid = 5


INNER JOIN mdl_user             u   ON u.id = ra.userid      AND u.deleted = 0


LEFT  JOIN mdl_grade_items      gi  ON gi.courseid = c.id    AND gi.itemtype = 'course'


LEFT  JOIN mdl_grade_grades     gg  ON gg.userid = u.id      AND gi.id = gg.itemid


WHERE EXISTS (


   SELECT      cc.id 


   FROM        mdl_course_modules cc


   LEFT  JOIN  mdl_grade_items    gi1 ON gi1.itemmodule = 'quiz'


   WHERE       


               gi1.courseid = c.id 


)


ORDER BY c.shortname ASC
```

ResponsesInList.Title: MUC and localcache
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm again beginning to look at performance issues of clusters and determine where gains can be made.  It's good that string cache ( MDL-41019 ) have been included.  However having a central store for that means that I am seeing 100-700 calls to MUC during a page load just for strings.  With network overhead of shared storage, that can add up to 700ms to a page load time. The creation of localcachedir was a great step in the direction of speeding up accesses.  There is then the wiki page https://docs.moodle.org/25/en/Caching#Cache_definition_configuration which describes the different core caches and whether they need to be local or shared.  I have spent quite some time reading and working on the MUC code and the idea of having to understand which caches could be configured locally or not it's still very much out of my league of understanding. With the above in mind and Petr's original proposal to add the ability to use localcache for revision based systems, I'd like to discuss options for progressing that forward.  Particularly for some caches like string and database metadata . Things I've thought about so far; 1. Add a revision tag to the loader class in MUC as well as a definition item for revisions.  If those are set by the developer, you don't get to configure the cache in MUC, it's automatically a localcache but the API for MUC users is the basically the same.  Just a requirement to set a revision before get/set. 2. Do the items in 1, but also add the data to a shared storage as a backup cache if local doesn't have it.  If it's expensive to build the cache then this addition may be helpful to warm a cache in a new node without too much user impact. 3. Upgrade the file cachestore to be the backend for all the local caches, so it uses all the same mechansims as other caches and is well tested.  This would just require detection that it's a localcache to ensure the directory is created in the correct location. With those in place, any cache with a revision flag, either at the cache or key level would be able to move to local.  I believe this would have a performance improvement on networked clusters without any impact on single server installations.  Immediate candidates appear to be stringcache, langcache, database-meta and course_modinfo. I would appreciate any feedback and further ideas before I push any further ahead with development in this area. Thanks Russell

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: MUC and localcache
ResponsesInList.Text: As for which cache would be fastest for every setup - there is no right answer - that is why things should be configurable. Localcache is generally fast because it is a) local - ie - not shared storage - 0 network accesses. It is possible to speed localcache up even more by e.g. mounting on a ram disk. MUC can be faster or slower than localcache e.g. for a single server accessing memcache through a socket - extremely fast - faster than local storage, for a memcache on the network - probably slower than localcache because of the network access. Instead of mandating things like "all strings should go to localcache" I would rather see a localcache MUC plugin which incorporates the jsrev in the keys. This would only be safe to use for certain types of cached info (static things that only change on upgrade etc). This allows the admin to configure whatever is fastest for their environment.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: MUC and localcache
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for the input Damyon it has sparked other thoughts. In part, I'm then confused about the reason localcachedir was created at all and why it wasn't implemented in MUC initially.  My current guess is that there are things like minified JS and HTML that are better served from a filesystem.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: MUC and localcache
ResponsesInList.Text: Yup - if you look into jsrev / themerev they are incremented when caches are purged ( js_reset_all_caches() ) - this is the only way to effectively "purge" localcache folders (the old data is still there but will never be looked at again).

ResponsesInList.Title: [Solved] Problem with Cron.
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello, I'm a new here and a brazilian developer. I have a work with moodle on FIAP (Brazilian University on Tecnology). I had one problem on the cron tasks. The local plugin tasks performed one time in a day. Looking the problem, i seen the code off cron and understood that the schedule task that run the local plugins is named the "legacy_plugin_cron_task" and  with the failed the moodle increments a delay execution time in 60 seconds on the column on the database named "faildelay" on the table "task_scheduled". My cron had a problem in the one local plugin and break the execution off the cron. With the last 10 or 20 executions, the "falidelay" had 8400 seconds and the cron run one time in day. I fixed the ploblem with my plugin and put the 0 on the table "task_schedule", and the run working normaly. So for document. Thanks a lot.

ResponsesInList.Text: I'm not 100% convinced you should be directly building URLs to the theme directory; generally speaking, there should be a Moodle function to build the reference to a resource for you. For example, if you take a look at theme/base/layout/frontpage.php, then you'll see $OUTPUT->pix_url('favicon', 'theme') is used to build the url to favicon in the current theme. There's a built-in fallback mechanism to search parent themes for missing resources when you use functions like this. It's probably worth reading through https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Creating_a_theme and then the subtopics under https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Themes Phil

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to insert multi select records?
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi Mian The form data is return as an object: 
```text
object
(
stdClass
)[
1204
]
  
public
 'courseid' => 
    
array
 
(size=2)

      0 =>  '3' 
(length=1)

      1 =>  '2' 
(length=1)

  
public

(length=1)

  
public
 'username' =>  'admin' 
(length=5)

  
public

(length=6)
```
 The selected courses are in an array, which can't be directly inserted into the database . You need to process this data first. This is often done with an explicitly created object for insertion into the database. For example: 
```text
$todb = new stdClass();


$todb->courses = implode(',', $formdata->courseid);


$todb->username = $formdata->username;


$DB->insert_record('table', $todb);
```
 There are examples of this throughout core Moodle code, which you should examine to figure out ways to improve your code.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle logs and Fluentd
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello, yes, the idea is a write-only log store. The main purpose is to visualize logs using Kibana ( https://www.elastic.co/products/kibana ), that fetches data from an Elasticsearch ( https://www.elastic.co/products/elasticsearch ) index, that is feeded by the Fluentd. The main reason to use Fluentd instead of using Elasticsearch directly is because Fluentd formats the data sent in a "logstash" format, creating one index for each day, with name conventions and so. Kind regards, Daniel

ResponsesInList.Title: Efficient ancestor context lookups
ResponsesInList.Text: For a couple of recent projects, I've found myself needing to write database queries including fragments similar to "... { context }.path like '%/30/%' and {context}.path not like '%/30/52214/%'". Whilst these work, using LIKE in a query never performs as well as direct comparison. It would be useful to have a new table with one row per contextid/contextlevel/instanceid combination. In principle this could be done by adding a flag column to {context} and tweaking context lookup functions to check the flag value to indicate the closest context, however this would probably break a reasonable chunk of code that, for various reasons, needs to check tables directly. There should be performance gains in context-checking functions if this was implemented, but with a performance penalty when contexts get moved - category-parent and course-category changes are the ones that spring to mind, but there may be others. I'd expect these to be relatively infrequent events compared to context lookups. I'm happy to write the code for this, I'm just looking for feedback on whether or not this is desirable, and whether or not it would be accepted by core. Phil

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Efficient ancestor context lookups
ResponsesInList.Text: What exactly are you trying to do? If you want to find all the contexts that are ancestor of path /1/5/30/ 52214 then the answer is WHERE context.id IN ( 1, 5, 30 ) - which is lightening fast.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Efficient ancestor context lookups
ResponsesInList.Text: My original example was perhaps oversimplified, as I didn't want to get bogged down in implementation details of my use case when promising an architectural enhancement. The problem with using WHERE context.id IN (<list-of-values>) is that I'd need to do a lookup on the course to get the context path, split the context path into an array, then use that array in a DB query. There are two basic scenarios, from projects for different clients. Scenario 1: For a given category, identify all the users with a given role on all sub-categories, courses, and activities . This involves cross-referencing user capability assignments with context paths for any {category,course,activity} context at or below a known context. Example: all teachers in SMD; all students taking Physics 101. Scenario 2: For a given course, check if it is in category A and not in category B. This matches A/C, A/D, A/D/E, but not A/B/F or A/B. This particular client has a category structure of Modules/<Academic Year>, and it's necessary to filter the list of enrolled courses into groups of 'current' and 'previous'. Anything from a category other than 'Modules' also needs to be grouping into 'current'. This leads to a LIKE... NOT LIKE... query on the path, which is much less efficient than being able to compare numeric values. Context paths are used rather than category paths because I can already use context_course::instance(<courseid>)->path and take advantage of any caching, rather than assuming I need to issue a database query to look up the category path from the course id. IMHO , it's much better to: 1) Offload the heavy processing to the DB (which, in a good implementation, performs much better than any interpreted language). 2) Design the application to allow the DB to perform well. This means simple comparisons (integers, fixed-length strings) rather than complex operations (regex, substring, etc.) Phil

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Efficient ancestor context lookups
ResponsesInList.Text: OK, so you have specific reporting requirements, which are pretty specific to your institution. This is not a reason to re-write the whole of accesslib.php, which is absolutely critical to Moodle's performance. At the OU, It is quite easy to find current modules, because $course->shortname looks like 'DD102-15J', and the -15 there says it is a 2015 course. For your example 1) you don't actually need people with a role " on all sub-categories, courses, and activities" because the student role will only be assigned at the course level. Anyway, if I needed to to support ad-hoc reporting requirements like this, and the SQL that just uses standard Moodle tables was too slow in practice, when I tried it, I would probably just make an extra table to store e.g. course metadata (e.g. a table with columns (courseid, academic_year) with a local plugin with a scheduled task to keep it up to date.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Efficient ancestor context lookups
ResponsesInList.Text: Tim, It's a been a long day for me, so apologies if this comes across a bit short, but... Not sure where 'reporting requirements' came from here; this isn't for generating periodic reports, nor 'specific to your institution' since I'd given two separate use cases for two different clients (institutions). It simply isn't realistic to expect an institution to change to use a specific format for short name (or the more logical choice of idnumber) on a production site with existing integrations that have already used these fields. At no point have I suggested " re-write the whole of accesslib.php" either, which wouldn't be necessary with the enhancement I've outlined - additional functions could make use of the proposed new table, and legacy code would function unchanged. Updating the library to take advantage of the faster lookups this would make possible is not a pre-requisite. Example 1 you refer to was " Example: all teachers in SMD; all students taking Physics 101." - how does the fact that student enrolments are at a course level have any bearing on identifing all the teachers in a given category (in this example, the SMD faculty)? This type of behaviour is useful for customising blocks to display audience-specific (but not as fine-grained as user-specific) content regardless of the context of the page they're on. And of course, the biggest reason to prefer contributing a core enhancement over local changes is simply that enhanced functionality becomes available to the whole Moodle developer community - once upon a time this was very much the spirit of open source, which sadly seems to have largely given way to forking with limited distribution of enhancements.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Efficient ancestor context lookups
ResponsesInList.Text: Well, you had not given any requirements until now, so I had to guess, based on the low-leve code examples you gave, what you were actually trying to do, and I guessed wrongly. Sorry. I am still not sure exactly what you are trying to do (why wouldn't a block/whatever:view capability cover it?) It is my experience that it really helps to know the real requirement before you try to advise on how to implement it. (The inappropriate advice I gave you is a good example of that.) Anyway, I hope someone else can work out what you are asking and help you.

ResponsesInList.Title: New forms library
ResponsesInList.Text: We are going to create a new forms library for Moodle. I have created a devpad page for general discussion and ideas as to how to proceed with this project. All information and discussion will happen on devpad (the link mentioned below) for one week before we start work on a specification. If you would like to have some input as to how the new forms lib will be implemented then please go to https://devpad.moodle.org/p/new_forms_lib and join the conversation.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New forms library
ResponsesInList.Text: Not that Moodle does not just use QuickForms. We already have our own form API class moodleform. Internally uses HTMLQuickForm for some stuff, but for other Moodle code, the QuickForms API is only partially exposed. We should definitely get rid of QuickForms internally. We should not change the API that existing Moodle code uses to create forms if at all possible. That would create huge amounts of work for many people. (Has anyone tried to count how many forms are defined in Moodle core, and in all the plugins in the plugins DB? That would be useful data that might inform this the design decisions we need to make. Might also be interesting to count how often each element type is used in Moodle code. Also, how often features like repeat_elements, groups of fields, defintion_after_data, hard_freeze, etc. are used. Can anyone conjure up the necessary regular-expression magic to do this?) So, what should we do. When this has been discussed at hack-fests in the past (which has happened several times over many years) the discussion has normally suggested a plan something like this: Change the moodleform internals, so that when a form is displayed, that is done entirely with Moodle rendering code (that is, templates) not QuickForms. Change the moodleform internals, so that when the form is submitted, and we need to validate then get the values out, that is done without any remaining QuickForms stuff. (I think quite a lot of this skips QuickForms already.) Change how the moodleform class represents the structure of the form internally, so that the objects for each element are no longer based on the QuickForms classes. At this point, QuickForms is gone. Work out a JSON format for the form data, so that the structure of a form can be sent to JavaScript , and make code to export a form in that structure. Write the JS code that takes that JSON and displays the form. (2. & 3. might need to be combined. It could well be possible to work on 5. & 6. in parallel to 1. to 3.) This approach is incremental, and is the best chance of preserving most backwards-compatibility. We will probably be forced to break a few complex and rare things, e.g. people who have defined their own element types. I also recommend that you look at some of the more complex forms in Moodle. Places I know complexity lies: The edit question forms The course settings form Activity settings forms for the more complex activities (forum, assignment, workshop, quiz, ...)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New forms library
ResponsesInList.Text: We should not change the API that existing Moodle code uses to create forms if at all possible. That would create huge amounts of work for many people. I would refine that to be - we should have a backwards compatibility layer which continues to work indefinitely with the existing API. I don't think you should be constrained for the new ways of creating/improving forms having to follow this (relatively horrible) api. Previous discussions: I can remember which should be re-read (i'm sure there are more, this is a hot potato of Moodle development for as long as I can remember): https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Perth_Hackfest_October_2012/Forms_API https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=200124 https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=211454 Offtopic rant: Why do people prefer etherpads, or wiki talk pages for discussions? They are terrible for threaded asycronous discussion.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New forms library
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks everyone for joining in on this conversation. Your input has been most valuable. We have created an epic for this issue ( MDL-52143 ). Feel free to continue to make comments there. We will now start writing up the specification . Once a specification has been complete, I will create another post in the new features forum.

ResponsesInList.Text: Who did join in the conversation? How much discussion was there? Let's at least copy-and-paste the summary of the Etherpad document here: Summation of this document Backwards compatibility is an important thing and we shouldn't try to replace mforms. Most people agree that just a simple update to mforms to make it php7 compliant is the way to proceed. Mforms are used extensively throughout Moodle. ResponsesInList.Text: Hi David, no that sort of thing isn't possible in SQL. It sounds like you could probably get the data you're looking for using get_fast_modinfo(), though - have you tried that? You may well get the data from the cache, so it wouldn't hit the database at all.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SQL: Dynamic table names for course modules in a sql query
ResponsesInList.Text: More generically, and assuming direct DB access is needed, you could build one query in a loop (whether hitting the DB directly is better or worse than using the caching functions will depend on whether or not you mostly hit or miss cache). For example (pseudo-code!): $config = array('<tablename>' => '<fieldname>', ...); $sql = array(); foreach ($config as $table => $field) { $sql[] = "SELECT {$table}.$field  AS <commonname> FROM {$table} WHERE ...."; } $sql = implode($sql, " UNION "); $DB->get_XXX($sql, ...); I've used this approach when needing to get counts of activities with a given deadline, as the deadline field is a per-activity-type one not per-activity, and the relevant field name changes between types. Phil

ResponsesInList.Title: Announcement - re-usable UI components prototype
ResponsesInList.Text: A quick heads-up; I've created a repo at https://github.com/dunlop-lello/moodle-local_ui with some in-progress work on a re-usable widget framework, and would like some general feedback on the architecture. The intention is that widgets are more general than per-plugin components, so should be re-usable across plugins, and should be over-ridable in a renderer. Although I'd like to see the included widget and model plugin types migrate into core at some point, I'd like this to be usable without patching core, hence the slightly odd syntax for the helper functions for building widgets as generic HTML, quickform elements, and admin settings. Feedback and suggestions are welcome at this point; I'd probably recommend holding fire on using the plugin for real at the moment, as I'm reasonably likely to want to change the API in incompatible ways.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Different dashboards for student and teacher
ResponsesInList.Text: What is a 'teacher'? What is a 'student'? As far as Moodle is concerned, these are roles that only really apply within an individual course - at the site level, where the dashboards are concerned, they are only 'users'. But to give a (hopefully) slightly more helpful answer, Moodle does not give the option of specifying a different default dashboard layout for different users. However, users are free to customise their own dashboard, once they have logged in. This is, of course, something that could be developed for an individual Moodle site, which is why I assume you've posted it in the developer forum, but it would probably require a reasonable amount of changes to the core Moodle code (always a bad idea from a maintenance perspective).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Different dashboards for student and teacher
ResponsesInList.Text: The simplest way, without custom development, is to change the'View Block' permissions for certain roles, for the blocks you want to display or hide. In other words, this with the Teacher role would see some blocks but not others, and those with the Student role would see some blocks but not others. See https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=318747#p1278630 for more information. You can do this with any block in Moodle, but from v2.8 onwards, it appears that the 'Assign Roles' link has gone for blocks on the Dashboard page - but if you have access to the backend database , you can trick Moodle if you know the contextid number of the block. See https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=318747#p1294163 for more information and instructions.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to build a main menu using the navigation block
ResponsesInList.Text: I have just discovered how to do this and I figured I'd post it incase someone else is looking for help. In initialise(), lines 1114-1123 of / lib / navigationlib.php, Moodle searches /local for plugins that extend the navigation menu.  If it finds one, it passes a $global_navigation object.  So here's what you do: 1) Create the directory / wwwroot /local/myplugin 2) Create a new file called "lib.php" in the directory. 3) Moodle looks for a function name that matches "myplugin" + "_extends_navigation".  In our case, add the following function to your file: function myplugin_extends_navigation(global_navigation $navigation) { $nodeFoo = $navigation->add('Foo'); $nodeBar = $nodeFoo->add('Bar'); } Reload the main page and you should now see this:

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Creating a Page Activity/Resource directly in Database
ResponsesInList.Text: Firstly, if you're inserting records into the database directly, you should be using $DB->insert() rather than building and executing an SQL statement directly: https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Data_manipulation_API#Inserting_Records Not only will it return the ID of the inserted record, but it internally uses query parameters to handle the data safely.  If you're writing other queries, which also need to include user-specified or dynamic values, always use query parameters (either named or positional - see https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Data_manipulation_API#Main_info ) in order to protect against SQL injection attacks.  Your code above currently performs no sanitisation whatsoever on the GET parameter you're using in the $DB->get_records_sql calls - so SQL can readily be injected via the TargetCourseID and LoadIntoSection GET parameters, without even having to work around the use of addslashes() (which also fails to completely protect against injection). That said, directly inserting into the database is probably not the best approach.  If you're able to provide us with a bit more context about what you're trying to achieve and why, I'm sure somebody will be able to help you figure out a better approach.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: HTML5 + JavaScript + CSS presentations made easy - Anyone want to integrate it with Moodle?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Stuart, I think 3rd party services like Prezi, Slideshare, etc. are good for prototyping and/or quick 'n' dirty, ad hoc shows. But for resources that we intend to use over longer periods of time, where we want to ensure consistency and stability, I think using 3rd party services leaves too much out of our control. What if they change the ways they do business? What if they introduce intrusive or inappropriate advertising? Or what if we want to share or distribute resources for use in other Moodles or CMS' or LMS', as in OER, for example? I think it's nice to be able to zip up a bunch of directories with collated resources that you can upload to your Moodle and display on a course in a couple of minutes. Plus, some people have problems with setting up authentication to access 3rd party services. And what if a teacher leaves or changes the resources in her/his 3rd party service accounts? Reveal.js actually does less than the Book resource module but it's quick and slick for slideshows and if it's used with pre-collated presentation packages, it could offer some advantages in terms of ease of use and cross platform portability. It would allow resource designers and developers to use the authoring tools and IDEs that they're familiar with: create packages on their local machines then send them to Moodle. It's easy to swap out CSS files to instantly change the styling of the slideshow, which is less prone to the kinds of bad layout designs we see with typical PPT slides: "car boot sale poster" style mixed fonts and text colours, dark text on dark backgrounds, jarring differences from one slide to the next for no apparent reason, etc. I've tried it with various "exotic" media: HTML video and audio, SVG (inline and external files), animated SMIL SVG, iframes, etc. and it all seems to work well.
