ResponsesInList.Title: Re: HTML5 + JavaScript + CSS presentations made easy - Anyone want to integrate it with Moodle?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Gareth, Thanks! The very cool part is by this guy who came up with reveal.js: https://github.com/hakimel - Credit where it's due Tests? Not sure what you mean. Presentations, perhaps? The moodledata workaround is to get away from Moodle file manager's rather difficult to manage path naming. Here's the rationale: In order to create a presentation, you write an HTML fragment. Each page/slide is contained within section tags, and nesting sections is possible for sub-pages. Each of those sections may contain one or more media files and each media file requires a valid URL . Content creators can use any text editor or IDE they like to create presentations and they can run and test them in a local mirror of moodledata/repository/revealjscontent/ which should include a copy of reveal.js with the same local directory structure. This means that they can use Notepad++, Netbeans, Dreamweaver, or whatever their personal preference is for content authoring, check that it works in their browsers and then simply upload the directories and files with their favourite FTP client. Likewise for editing/updating. Considering that one presentation alone may contain dozens or even a hundred or so media files, using Moodle's file manager and copying and pasting the links across to the HTML fragment would be a time-consuming and laborious task, to say the least. Having the moodle/mod/revealjs/mod_form.php + locallib.php, moodle/mod/revealjs/view.php and moodle/mod/revealjs/content.php files use straightforward, consistent, and predictable URLs, based on the directory structure of Moodle and moodledata, means that the URLs in the HTML fragments can be kept consistent, and the presentations themselves are " context independent" and "context sensitive." Therefore, presentations can simply be uploaded to any Moodle and "just work." i.e. the module provides consistent base URLs instead of the learning content files providing context specific ones that would break on another Moodle. I envisage that moodledata/repository/revealjsconent/... will contain accumulated libraries of presentations that all editing users of that installation will be able to deploy from a dropdown list. I've incorporated "namespace" directories in moodledata so that users can identify who and/or where the presentations came from. Having FTP as the only way to upload content encourages Moodle admins to delegate the curation of presentations and content to a capable person or persons and so keep it logical and manageable for everyone. Hopefully, it'll also discourage the accumulation of ad-hoc presentations that only ever get used once or not at all - Those can be deployed by other means via Moodle's file manager and Book module, for example. Having local versions of presentations in mirrored directories means editing and updating specific files in a presentation is possible and that those changes will be reflected across all instances on that Moodle (Particularly useful for swapping out media files, providing alternative media files for cross-platform compatibility, changing logos, and correcting typos). Backup and restore is relatively easy: zip up and download moodledata/repository/revealjsconent/ or subdirectories of it as necessary, and use Moodle's backup and restore for the Presentation module instances. If Hakim (reveal.js developer) or anyone else creates plugins for Wordpress and/or other CMS', presentations could be shared across those platforms too. Just using some of the principles of MVC and portability (IMS and SCORM)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: HTML5 + JavaScript + CSS presentations made easy - Anyone want to integrate it with Moodle?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Nadav, Yes, content authors can use any 3rd party editor or service to create slideshows on editey, slid.es, etc. - whatever they prefer, although desktop editors and IDEs tend to be less buggy, more powerful, have more options available (e.g. search and replace), and there's fewer issues with converting presentations into something portable, i.e. on USB as I described earlier. Also, there's nothing to stop authors from hot-linking to media files anywhere on the web. The str_replace() function to build the paths to the File System directories ignores any absolute URLs. A case in point for the portability issue, I've just come back from a Ph.D proposal presentation in a meeting room at the University of Toronto where there was no internet access available to the presenter (They didn't have the WiFi password for that building and the user account on the PC didn't allow internet access). Another case, at a SIG in the University of Guelph a week ago, the same thing happened at the meeting room there - no internet access. I think it's really important for presentations to be able to run on minimal equipment with minimal resources, e.g. on a laptop screen with no internet for a small group of people sitting around a table, without having to resort to PowerPoint (which is what currently happens in most cases). A standalone version of reveal.js looks perfect for this and making the presentations portable between that and Moodle seems like a good solution to me. This is why I want to make it as open to 3rd party editors, including WYSIWYG , to make it less daunting.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Uploaded images not display in Moodle 2.9 version
ResponsesInList.Text: Draftfile links are temporary links used whilst a Moodle editor is being displayed. When you click on 'Save', the files will be transferred into a permanent file area and the links to them will be updated to reflect this. The reason for this is so that the files in the permanent file area are not affected until you press 'save' (and are not touched at all if you press 'cancel'). If you copy the link to a file whilst you are using the editor and paste it somewhere else, then at some point (usually a week or two later), that link will no longer work, as the draft file area will be automatically cleared out.

ResponsesInList.Title: Time to prepare your plugins for 3.0
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello all, Moodle 3.0 beta is now available for download . It is a good time to start testing and upgrading your plugins.  After you make sure that your plugin works fine on 3.0, please edit the latest version of it in the plugins directory and add Moodle 3.0 to the "Supported Moodle" field. It is very important to check that all information in version.php is correct. Plugin installation in 3.0 has become easier for administrators ( MDL-49329 ) but it also means that plugins must be very accurate with the information they have in version.php. Always make sure that required Moodle version is correct, dependencies are listed, your plugin version numbers always increment between releases, you specify $plugin->component ( MDL-48494 ) and you never use $module ( MDL-43896 ). Please read lib/upgrade.txt and make sure you don't use any of deprecated functions. Don't forget to check out upgrade.txt file in your plugin directory, for example mod/upgrade.txt for modules, auth/upgrade.txt for authentication plugins, and so on. Theme developers take a look at theme/upgrade.txt and theme/bootstrapbase/upgrade.txt , plugins implementing web services might be interested in webservice/upgrade.txt , why not just run git grep "=== 3.0 ===" to see the list of all upgrade.txt files. Logs now can be backed up and restored. Your plugin may need to define additional mapping for 'objectid' and 'other' fields in the events, see MDL-46455 . There are also some new features for plugin developers such as new autocomplete field ( MDL-51247 ) and ability to hook into user preference page ( MDL-50125 ). See the list of issues affecting developers for more details. Happy moodling and see you in 3.0!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tracker - too many commits
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Josh, Check out the Moodle docs about rewriting commits . I like to use rebase and it's a good command to get to know if you are contributing to Moodle often. This accomplish what you were trying to do with the merge commit that CiBot is complaining about, which is to keep your branch up-to-date with the most recent changes upstream. It will also let you fix your commit message, which is the other thing CiBot was complaining about. Another way to make CiBot happy would be to create a new branch based on the most recent version of the upstream branch and cherry-pick your single commit onto it, though it would require you to update the ticket's branch fields.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tracker - too many commits
ResponsesInList.Text: Well, it now complaining that you have a merge commit. You should alwasy rebase (instead of merge) to get your changes on top of latest master before submitting them for integration.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tracker - too many commits
ResponsesInList.Text:
I use rebase -i (interactive) https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Rewriting-History If you use the command 
```text
git rebase -i HEAD~2
```
 then you will see the instructions for squashing the last two commits into one.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New comer, how to modify the look of plugins!
ResponsesInList.Text: Plugins can include a css file, but that would mean having to monitor and amend every plugin individually at any upgrade. It is far more common to use the theme to override the plugin css and create the overall look and feel of the site as a whole, including the plugins being used. If you have access to the code files (which you would need to amend the plugin css) then you don't necessarily have to use the customcss theme setting, you could create a plugins.css file (or one for each plugin), add it to the styles folder of your theme and reference the files in the theme config.php - OR use the additional customcss setting Richard

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New comer, how to modify the look of plugins!
ResponsesInList.Text: And just to add to this - all the CSS on the site (from the current theme, all the plugins, etc.) gets merged together into one big file and sent to the user. So, despite where it originates from, there is not a set of CSS that is only applied to a certain plugin - all of it applies to all pages (but, mostly, plugins will target specific 'classes' or 'ids' in the HTML, so that only the elements within that plugin will be styled). Note that theme CSS is included after the plugin-specific CSS, so that the theme CSS has a chance to override the plugin CSS (as later rules take precedence over earlier rules, assuming they are both as specific as each other).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New comer, how to modify the look of plugins!
ResponsesInList.Text: If you are creating the plugin then surely you know what elements you are adding that you want to style, while common elements that go across all plugins are given a generic style by core code and you don't normally need to do anything with that - bear in mind that people use themes to control the look and feel of a whole site, they really dont want to have to add customcss for every specific third party plugin simply because the developer of that plugin overrode all the core styles. If you need to style anything taht comes from core, then use firebug or chrome developer tools - but when adding the css, make sure you use a selector that makes it specific enough to your plugin so that other elements across the site as a whole are not affected. So wrap your plugin in a div with a 'myplugin' class name and any css you do add, make sure it uses that selector to specify the css as being for your plugin and not across the entire site - just in case that class is used elsewhere.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Customising the log in page
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Angela. When you talk about your "small login form" what do you mean? Are you using the login page of Moodle? Are you using an alternative one? I think you should let us know more about your Moodle setup. I guess the answer you are looking for is not as easy as it appears to be. It all depends on your authentication method for Moodle. If you have e-mail authentication method, a person is able to create its own user and password through an e-mail confirmation mechanism. If you choose no authentication method, anyone can sign up. If you select any other method, then an external system must exists to grant access for an user and a person can not choose the one of its preference. In the other hand, if you choose manual accounts only method, only accounts created by the admin (manually created or loaded up from text files) can login. Anyway, you EVER can setup an alternative URL to accomplish authentication tasks for all of the authentication methods in Moodle. Hope this helps. Good luck.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Hide audio url
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Noor, Yes, there are several ways of hiding/obfuscating links and paths to media files. However, for every way of doing this, there's a way of getting around it. If you have a look at plugins for Firefox and Chrome, you'll see that downloading media files or retrieving them from the browser cache is high on the list of the most popular ones. In short, everything you try may make it a little more difficult but anyone who really wants to can get around any measures that you implement. On the other hand, some measures may also make it more difficult for your users to listen to the files as intended, e.g. web browser or internet connection/firewall incompatibilities or the need for plugins.

ResponsesInList.Title: CSS files in a theme create a hierarchy?
ResponsesInList.Text: In the document named " Themes Overview " in the developer docs, it is written, " New theme developers should note that the order in which CSS files are found and included creates a hierarchy. This order ensures that the rules, within a theme's style sheets, take precedence over identical rules in other files that may have been introduced before. " It is not clear where are the CSS files being included which creates the hierarchy. Is this about the way the stylesheets are listed/included in the config.php of the theme by the following statement? $THEME->sheets = array( 'core' , 'base' , 'course' ) ;

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: CSS files in a theme create a hierarchy?
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, and also by the way parent themes are listed (if more than one) in the config.php E.g. in Formal White (version   = 2013110500) `$THEME->parents = array('canvas', 'base');` So, any css in core moodle is overwritten by anything in base theme, which is overwritten by anything in canvas theme, which is overwritten by the css in formal white which would go in the order listed in the formal white config.php. `$THEME->sheets = array('frame' , 'menu', 'course', 'pagelayout', 'core', 'calendar', 'tabs', 'quiz', 'forum', 'block' , 'formal_white');` ie. any rules for the same css selector in frame.css would be overwritten by those in menu.css, then by those in course.css etc.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: CSS files in a theme create a hierarchy?
ResponsesInList.Text:
```text
$THEME->parents = array('canvas', 'base');


So, any css in core moodle is overwritten by anything in base theme, which is overwritten by anything in canvas theme, which is overwritten by the css in formal white
```
 So you mean in the array $THEME->parents, the CSS in the theme whose name occurs first (i.e. on the left) overwrites the CSS in the theme whose name occurs after (i.e. to the right of) the first element. Right? 
```text
$THEME->sheets = array('frame' , 'menu', ...);


ie. any rules for the same css selector in frame.css would be overwritten by those in menu.css, then by those in course.css etc.
```
 Here you are saying that the CSS in the stylesheet whose name occurs first (i.e. on the left) is overwritten by any CSS in the stylesheet whose name follows (i.e. occurs to the right of the first element of the array). Are you sure you didn't make a mistake in describing the sequence in which the overriding takes place?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: CSS files in a theme create a hierarchy?
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes and Yes And yes - I'm sure I didn't make a mistake in describing the way it works Whether that is a logical implementation is another matter! ;) Listing of any parent themes goes parent -> grandparent -> great grandparent -> ... { -> core (not explicitly listed) } Listing of the css sheets follows standard ways to implement multiple css sheets in any html files which means that the first sheet is implemented, then the next sheet overrides that, the subsequent sheet overrides that, etc so that the latest defined css rules override those defined previously. While it may have been better originally to have defined the parent themes to follow along the same lines as the stylesheets, that isn't the way it was done, so the way I described is the working situation. Richard

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: restrict activity drag&drop on new course format
ResponsesInList.Text: Ordinarily, the ability to move course sections is restricted to Teacher, Managers and Admins, or whomever writes courses. If you want to restrict this capability site wide, you do not need to do anything fancy. Go to Site Admin > Users > Permissions > Define Roles > Teacher and click on the "Settings" icon to the right of the page. Look for the capability "Move Sections" and set that to "Prevent". This means only Managers and Admins can move courses site wide. You can also restrict Managers using the same technique in the Manager's Role. If you want to restrict this capability in a course, then  in the Course Admin > Users > Permissions you can make the same restriction, or you can prevent anyone other than an Admin from moving sections. Site wide restrictions, start at Site Admin, for course only restrictions, start at Course Admin. You don't need to do anything with code, it is all controlled by Permissions and Capabilities.

It seems like I can use composer installers like this topic is discussing: https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=275466 But contributed plugins most likely don't have the correct "type" in their composer.json file (actually, they probably won't have a composer.json file at all). Even if I got that method working for plugins, I feel like I am stuck keeping moodle core code in my own vcs.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How are you deploying moodle?
ResponsesInList.Text: Make a git repository, with your own branch off MOODLE_2X_STABLE, containing the core Moodle code, and any addons you want added (ideally added using a sub-directory merge). Then, installing Moodle on your server is just a git clone or checkout. The advantages of doing it this way: git status on the server verifies that none of the files have become corrupted. easy to upgrade to future versions (either core or plugins or both). (You can also just cherry-pick specific fixes if you ever need to.) you get a full history of everything ever deployed to your servers. On the server, you can use command-line install/upgrade.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How are you deploying moodle?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Brendan, Went through this myself over the last few months. With the exception of Moodle, I've noticed that many Git repositories for 3rd party plugins are often either not up to date or a work in progress. Some plugins don't even have a corresponding git repo because they use some other kind of version system. In some cases, the Github repo didn't contain branches for the version I needed and, when they did, they didn't use standard naming conventions for the branch names. This lack of standardization makes it near impossible to use Git repositories to correctly automate the installation of plugins using regular Git methods. What I ended up doing is downloading plugins from their download link on the Moodle plugins site into a parallel directory structure (e.g. moodle-plugins) that mirrors their location if they were in Moodle. To manage the version issue you noted, I added the moodle version number to the folder. For example, I have a moodle-plugins/theme/essentials27 and a moodle-plugins/theme/essentials28. my script copies the folder, parsing out the number from the folder name during the installation. This allows me to have a version of the plugin for each version of Moodle. When a plugin applies to multiple versions of Moodle, I simply create a symbolic link to the original folder so that I only have to maintain one version of the source code. As for Moodle itself, I use Git to simply clone/fork moodle. Finally, when I need a new site, I use a script I wrote that copies Moodle into it's destination and also copies any required plugins into their correct location from my moodle-plugins folder. This approach enables me to easily use "git pull" to update each of my Moodle sites when a new release becomes available. As for the plugins, unfortunately they still need to be manually updated. It's a semi automated process but, once I had the script written, it saves me hours of work. I can now create a new site in about 3.5 minutes. My script actually prompts me for basic site specific information, performs the full installation, configures file and folder permissions, installs language packs, and then customizes 300+ core and plugin settings. If you figure out a better way to manage updating of the 3rd party plugins, I would appreciate it very much if you would please share. Best regards, Michael Milette

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How are you deploying moodle?
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for sharing Brendan. However our plugins don't all come from the public repository. Sometimes they are custom plugins I've developed while other times they are fixed and/or enhanced forked versions of the publicly available plugins. I've also written a script that presents me with a form listing of only the plugins we use most off the time. I can then just check the boxes next to the plugins I want to install and they all get installed in one shot. Using my script, it takes me about 3.5 minutes (depending on the server load at the time) to create an installation customized to most of our client's requirements. It installs any version of Moodle (2.5 to 2.9) I need, pulls any recent Moodle updates from Moodle.org, installs and configures themes and plugins and then customizes about 300 settings. About the only things it can't do yet that I wish it did was to create repositories and batch restore courses. Without this automation, it would take me hours, if not days to create and configure just one site and the process would be prone to mistakes. This way I get a perfect almost totally configured Moodle site each time. It is so convenient that I create test Moodle sites just to try stuff out and then delete them just as easily. Once setup, I have a script that packages the site including documentation and optionally with the database , and then moves the package to a download area where it is ready for download and deployment on the clients site. It took a lot of time to create and test this system but it sure is nice to have. It currently only runs in a Linux bash shell but I am hoping to convert it to a web based interface down the road so that less techy folks in the company, even sales people, can create Moodle sites on demand. Best regards, Michael

That is valid. You can also use just 
```text
echo $OUTPUT->help_icon('stringid', 'plugintype_pluginname');
```

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Clamav with moodle 2.9 on Centos7 problem
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi Scott, I've just got this working as part of general investigations into moodle and Centos 7, specifically SELinux (see http://blog.mrverrall.co.uk/2015/10/moodle-on-centos-and-red-hat-7.html ). The Steps for clamav amount to.... Install the clam daemon and tools (you've obviously already done this) 
```text
yum install -y clamav-scanner-systemd clamav clamav-update
```
 Edit /etc/clam.d/scan.conf to delete line 'Example' near the top 
```text
sed -i '/^Example/d' /etc/clamd.d/scan.conf
```
 Uncomment the following line from /etc/clamd.d/scan.conf '# LocalSocket /var/run/clamd.scan/clamd.sock' 
```text
sed -i 's#^
\(.*\)
\(LocalSocket /var/run/clamd\.scan/clamd\.sock\)
#\2#' /etc/clamd.d/scan.conf
```
 Allow httpd to access the clamav socket by changing the group on /var/run/clamd.scan as per instruction at: /usr/share/doc/clamav- server -0.98.7/README (or you could add apache to the clamscan group) 
```text
chgrp apache /var/run/clamd.scan
```
 link scan.conf to /etc/cland.conf so command line tools 'just work' 
```text
ln -s /etc/clamd.d/scan.conf /etc/clamd.conf
```
 SELinux - Allow Clamd to work 
```text
setsebool -P antivirus_can_scan_system 1
```
 Start our Clamav service, NB: The service name is not clamd.service as you mention in your post.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle edit form not working
ResponsesInList.Text: If you're looking for sample code for using a Moodle form, then a quick search for 'extends moodleform' in the code should find a huge number of examples. A few things to start with - if you want to make sure that the $USER object is valid, then please put 'require_login()' after $PAGE->set_url(), instead of doing lots of tests to see if $USER is null. Also, if you want to restrict access to certain users, then define a capability in your plugin's db/access.php file and then call 'require_capability('your new capability', context_system::instance())', instead of testing for specific userids. The form file should contain just the definition of the form - remove all the stuff before the start of the class, but put a 'defined('MOODLE_INTERNAL') || die(); ' line at the start. require_once your form file from the other file. Nowhere in the file do you appear to call $form->display() (or the equivalent echo $form->render()), which is needed to display the form you have defined. Also, you should do your form processing (including the redirects) before you call 'echo $OUTPUT->header();'

It seems that there is no way in the API to specify the table prefix for the users table (although that is possible in some other similar Moodle APIs.) Just let me wrap that query to make it a bit more readable. 
```text
SELECT 
DISTINCT u.id, u.firstnamephonetic,u.lastnamephonetic,u.middlename,

    u.alternatename,u.firstname,u.lastname, u.username, d.dateissued, d.uniquehash,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) AS nctransfers

        FROM mdl_badge_certificate_trasnfers AS bcf
        WHERE bcf.userid = u.id AND bcf.badgecertificateid = c.id
            AND bcf.transfereruserid = u.id
        ORDER BY created DESC LIMIT 1
    ) AS ndatelasttransfer

FROM mdl_badge_issued AS d
JOIN mdl_badge AS b ON d.badgeid = b.id
JOIN mdl_user AS u ON d.userid = u.id
JOIN mdl_badge_certificate AS c ON b.certid = c.id
JOIN mdl_quizgrading_results AS qr ON qr.userid = u.id

WHERE b.certid = ? AND c.quizgradingid = ? AND firstname LIKE ? ESCAPE '\\'
```

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Filtering by first and last name in table_sql
ResponsesInList.Text: Moodle does not add a firstname column to your query. It adds an AND firstname LIKE 'a%' bit to the WHERE clause of your query, but that does not increase the number of columns present, whcih may or may not be ambiguous. As I already said, there is no way to add a prefix to that field (if you can patch Moodle core to allow this, then that would be good). In the mean time, you need a work-around, and as I said, the first step is to determine which other table in your query, other than mdl_user, has a firstname column.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Events 2.0, Descriptions, and Event Names
ResponsesInList.Text: I also encountered this, but got it working. The get_name function requires that the returned string is defined in the language string and must have a proper key. It's easier to explain by code. Event File: plugin_folder \classes\event\ something_happened.php class something_happened extends \core\event\base { ... public static function get_name() { return get_string('event somethinghappened ', ' plugin_name '); //<-- the language string key is very important. Note that it should start with the word 'event' followed by the event name without the underscore. } ... } Language File: plugin_folder\lang\en\ plugin_name .php $string[' event somethinghappened ' ] = 'Something has happened'; I hope this will help.

ResponsesInList.Title: Dynamic Cohorts
ResponsesInList.Text: We have some funding to extend the current cohorts functionality to include 'dynamic' cohorts (see below for a summary). Are there were any plans to extend cohorts in this direction, and if so, would you be interested in this implementation for core? We'd be happy to contribute the code and are keen on collaborating to ensure it aligns well with any existing or future plans in this direction. Any feedback is also welcome on the implementation below or any problems that this change might introduce. --- Existing cohorts would be given a 'type' with a choice between static or dynamic. Existing functionality would remain the same with existing cohorts being labelled as 'static'. Dynamic cohorts would be defined by a set of rules, for example: Users with an email matching '@ example.com ' Users who have logged on in the last 3 months Users with a user custom profile field set to 'instructor' etc. There would be a wide range of 'rules' and rules would be class-based to allow more to be added easily. Groups of rules could be combined into rulesets, and applied with AND/OR logic so you could build up complex rulesets: Users who have logged on in the last 3 months AND have their city set to 'New York' Users who's language is set to 'es' OR Users who's language is set to 'fr' On the back end, the cohort would still be defined as a list of userids in the cohort_members table. Event handlers would be added to check for changes that could affect cohort membership. An additional cron task would be included to catch any cases missed by the event handlers (for example, if a third party module modified a table directly). Any events triggered by changes to cohort membership would also need to be retriggered when a cohort membership changes.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Dynamic Cohorts
ResponsesInList.Text: Did this project ever happen?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Dynamic Cohorts
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Aaron, Simon works for totara and, I suppose, they have implemented it there. I want to point out here that it is very possible in moodle. What you need to do is to create a custom plugin (for example "admin tool"), listen to the necessary events and automatically create cohorts and modify their members when you need to. Cohorts in moodle have "component" property that can be set by plugins. If set, only the plugin will be responsible for editing cohort and it's members. These cohorts will be properly shown in Site administration>Users>Cohorts but without editing options. Everywhere where you can use normal cohorts (such as enrolments) you will be able to use the dynamic cohorts too.

ResponsesInList.Title: Displaying a simple "update successful!" message
ResponsesInList.Text: If I want my plugin to do $SUBJECT upon successfully saving form input, do I need to use messaging to set up a popup-only provider specific to my plugin, or is there a simpler way to just flash a brief message on the screen?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Displaying a simple "update successful!" message
ResponsesInList.Text: Normally, most Moodle forms accept HTTP POST data, process them (store in the database typically) and then redirect to a page that displays the success message with a continue button (continuing automatically after several seconds usually). Typical example is posting to a forum. I know this is quite out-fashioned these days. There is no "on-next-screen notification API" I am aware of. However, if you are redirecting the user back to a page served by your plugin, you can easily implement such support yourself. I used something like that in the workshopallocation_random plugin.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Displaying a simple "update successful!" message
ResponsesInList.Text: One option is to call `redirect(url, message)` using the optional second `message` parameter. That causes a simple page to display briefly (3 seconds, by default) with the message, then redirecting automatically to the given URL .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Displaying a simple "update successful!" message
ResponsesInList.Text: If you don't like redirects (because you are allowed to ;) , you can store your messages on $SESSION or $USER and use $OUTPUT->notification() to print notifications using bootstrap classes. Altough it is on the (much) older docs ( https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Output_Components#notification ) it seems to work pretty well.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Displaying a simple "update successful!" message
ResponsesInList.Text: `$OUTPUT->notification()` is nice. I'm going to start using that. (With redirects ).

ResponsesInList.Title: AJAX, Mustache and Moodleform
ResponsesInList.Text: I've got a heavily AJAX /Mustache driven plugin in development right now. (Aside: how awesome is Mustache. omg.) In it there is, of course, a settings form, because it wouldn't be a moodle plugin if it didn't have a settings form. Right now it's just a bog standard HTML form whose input values are collected via JQuery and then funnelled through the core/ajax utility to a webservice. It works, but it's ugly, it's non-standard, and I want to use some of the fancier widgets in Moodleform, like the date/time picker. My question: Is there a standard way right now for (a) displaying Moodleforms with Javascript (b) integrating Moodleforms into Mustache and (c) submitting form values via AJAX? My current plan is probably to just render the form as HTML, stick it in a context variable, and then render it with the {{{triple brackets}}}. That doesn't exactly solve (c), although I could figure out some Javascript to do that well. But with all this fancy new stuff, I was wondering if there is some cool, super easy way to do it that I have overlooked.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: AJAX, Mustache and Moodleform
ResponsesInList.Text: I am ready to stand corrected on this, but I think the simple answer is 'no'. At the moment, Mustache rendering and Moodle forms rendering are two completely separate things and there is no standard way to integrate a Moodle form inside a Mustache template. As Moodle forms are entirely implemented in PHP and Mustache templates are renderable by javascript or PHP, I find it hard to imagine there ever being a simple integration between the two. I suspect that your proposed solution is probably the best you are going to achieve for the moment. You might want to look at using a combination of the jquery .serialize() and $.ajax() functions in order to prepare and send your form for processing (I suspect, but haven't tested, that the server -side part could then just instantiate the form and call $form->get_data() to retrieve the values).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: AJAX, Mustache and Moodleform
ResponsesInList.Text: I've done the display and handling of forms via AJAX before, I've got a write-up on the wiki: https://docs.moodle.org/dev/User:Mark_Johnson/Mforms_and_AJAX This was pre-moustache through so I don't know how/if it would integrate.  Also note that that guide is based on YUI's io-form module, as Davo says you'll want to use the jQuery equivalents to serialise the form data and do the AJAX calls.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: AJAX, Mustache and Moodleform
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks Mark, I'll have a read.

ResponsesInList.Title: Code freeze 3.0 starts Mon 5 October
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi, all. This message is to provide notice to developers about the impending code-freeze starting on Monday 5 October. The code freeze is a point after which no new code (only fixes to
existing code) is accepted until beyond the release. This stabilisation
allows for QA testing and means developers are able to respond rapidly
to bugs found. For more information see... http://docs.moodle.org/dev/Process#Events_during_cycle Thanks to all the contributors to Moodle 3.0. We are waiting until all
new features land in product and will prepare the release notes page
from this list of issues .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Code freeze 3.0 starts Mon 5 October
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi, starting from today we are "freezing" new feature development for 3.0. During this week (and probably the next one as well) intgrators will go through the big list of issues submitted in the last moment. Saying that, the issues that were sent for peer review before today, and maybe even some that will be sent later, may still be considered for inclusion in 3.0. Moodle tries to fill the release with as many new features as possible but at the same time we want to run QA cycle with all the major changes already integrated so we can deliver the good value product to you. If you are a plugin author, it is probably best to wait until at least
next week before starting to check your plugin for 3.0 compatibility as
this will be a busy week of changes in the codebase.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Fatal Error in filterlib.php
ResponsesInList.Text: This error has been looked at previously however I know the post is old but I think still relevant https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=119598 .  This is a limit which is set on your max_execution_time in the PHP.ini file by increasing this you may resolve the issue if not you may have a loop which is not ending or an error in the code causing the time out but I would test the max_execution_time by setting this high initially to maybe 200 or 300 to see if this resolves the error and if not then look at the code more closely. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Fatal Error in filterlib.php
ResponsesInList.Text: Changing settings in php.ini require restart of apache service to be seen/used in Moodle. The hint you've given (via hosts cpanel) could indicate your implementation is on a shared system.   On shared systems customers share the resources of a single server .  Hosting providers sell 'packages' which limit ... things like amount of HD space that can be used, etc.   That also includes preventing customers on such server from using up more than their fair share of resources ... thus a cap on PHP settings - how long a script can run, how much memory can be allocated to run a script, etc.    So if your server is on a shared system, you could contact the host helpdesk and inquire about your limits and/or a way to increase the time.   IF on a shared system, the hosting provider may only offer a more expensive package ... or a VPS where you don't have to 'share' those types of resources. The link your Moodle has to Server PHP info should disclose such information for you. Timing out might only be one issue.   Suggest turning on debugging and see what Moodle reports.  There could be other issues related to php settings not in your control. 'spirit of sharing', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No company info on the Moodle contributions page
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Petr. That is not quite true. It was not Martin. It was me who removed that column from the report. And I did it for what I believe are good reasons. Contributor's institution, stored in their profile field, is a subject of change in such a dynamic environment as IT is. Moodle contributors may have the institution filled in their profile, yet they contribute in their free time as a hobby. Some folks were contributing to Moodle while working for various universities, schools or companies over the time. Some became part of the HQ team. Or they were part of the HQ team and then left. Or mix of all above. We are not able to have all these changes easily tracked and presented in a simple report now. And the displayed data were confusing. So I decided to simply drop that column from the report. There was no public discussion about that decision, in same way as there had been no public discussion about it when I was implementing this credits report. Also, we are not displaying the institution at other credit pages like https://lang.moodle.org/local/amos/credits.php or https://docs.moodle.org/en/Special:ListUsers As in any open source project, it is individual's reputation and respect within the community that counts at the end of the day. If contributors' current occupation is important for someone, they can easily find it in the contributor's user profile. And contributors themselves are free and encouraged to describe their professional history in the description field there, too. Said that, I am indeed open for further improvements in these reports. Should there be a real demand in the dev community for it, our meta-data can be extended to store contributor's institution in certain time periods (similarly to how Mahara does it, for example). Such data would then be more accurate for our credits report. But I also think we have more important issues, bugs and features in Moodle itself to work on. Hope this clarifies a bit.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: The future of YUI in core.
ResponsesInList.Text: This is a question that could be on the topics list for this months developer meeting My guess is that from MDL 2.9 and onwards it is preferred to use jQuery when updating plugins. There quite a lot of YUI code in core and I think it does not make any sense to rewrite it to jQuery. The YUI code has been proven to work and new code could just add new issues. Focussing on creating new and improved code is so much more rewarding than rewriting old code. I know creating custom course formats can be a pain when trying to support core course JavaScript . The problem with custom course formats is having to use css classes to find DOM elements in your course output to make stuff like hiding / showing sections work. There is no documentation for this and in my experience much of it comes down to debugging the Javascript and trying to find the required DOM elements. I would vote for a roadmap that focusses on creating new Moodle UI's like the course formats based on simple and clean mustache templates for course page layouts and documentation in the mustache templates on the important DOM elements to make all of the JavaScript work, and perhaps while doing so move the YUI for course formats to AMD modules. ResponsesInList.Title: $CFG->themerev
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi. I would like to know what kind of theme modifications that var stores. Thx

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: $CFG->themerev
ResponsesInList.Text: It doesn't hold any modifications to the theme. It is a unique number, that is changed whenever the theme is changed. It is used in the URL for all the theme-related stuff (e.g. CSS ) so they can be served with caching headers to say "keep this for a long time, it won't change". If the contents of that stuff does change then you need to change the URL so that the browsers download the new CSS.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: $CFG->themerev
ResponsesInList.Text: This number also changes when you do a 'Purge all caches'.  When 'theme designer mode' is on it is set to '-1' such that there is no caching.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is there any way to close database connection after fetch data
ResponsesInList.Text: you haven't really given much context to go on, but the connection should be closed automatically once the PHP request is finished. It sounds like you really should be looking at caching the result ( https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Cache_API ), rather than doing the DB query multiple times (although 25 DB queries per second sounds well within the capabilities of any reasonable DB server - that's only a couple of page loads for a typical Moodle page). Whilst you're at it, you should remove the $_REQUEST line and use the Moodle 'optional_param' or 'required_param' function instead. Also, the code would be a lot more readable if you used $DB->get_records instead of $DB->get_records_sql. What are you trying to achieve with this - the code appears to be gathering a single question from the course and then converting it into a harder to read format (by converting an object with helpful value names to an array with all the value names stripped out).

ResponsesInList.Text: Try: $DB->dispose()

I'm not convinced that it is a major problem if the internal name of a plugin doesn't encompass the full range of different meanings that the plugin supports - that name is only seen (occasionally) by site admins. I would assume it is a bigger issue in creating a suitable human-readable name in the language files. However, even then, organisations can still override the official name (via language customisation) to give a name that is more appropriate in the local context .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Naming convention for Third Party Moduls
ResponsesInList.Text: I also think English names should be preferred! ResponsesInList.Title: Settling and stabilising environmental requirements earlier in the development cycle
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, since some years ago and until now, we always have created/cloned the "environmental requirements" issues ( MDL-50182 , MDL-48145 , MDL-45504 ...) for a given Moodle major release when the previous one was released. And the goal has been, always, to have such requirements decided and implemented as soon as possible. But lately, in practice, see 2.9 ( MDL-48145 ), 3.0 still unresolved ( MDL-50182 ), we have failed to achieve that goal on time so, effectively, "master" (3.0) has been using previous release (2.9) requirements instead of its own ones, making it harder to change anything so late (6 weeks for 3.0 release right now). We, integrators, did detect this behavior some months ago and agreed to introduce some simple changes in the handling of those "environmental requirements" issues in order to: get them prospected, agreed and implemented earlier, still giving developers full time to include all sort of comments, opinions. make them stable over the (master) 6 months development cycle so they won't change in the middle. While originally (May 2015) we had planned to already implement the changes for 3.0, I forgot about this completely, my fault! And just yesterday, when preparing some reports and reviewing some notes, I remembered it, so we'll start applying the new approach for 3.1 upwards. In summary these are the changes planned: After releasing a major version (X.Y), within the on-sync period , the requirements for next Moodle version (X.Y+1) will be decided and immediately implemented. Those requirements will be stable for the development cycle of X.Y+1 and modifications only will be allowed with justified reasons (error, unadvertised end of life...). Once X.Y+1 requirements have been decided (by the point 1. above), a new X.Y+2 issue will be created , so people can start discussing about it, along the whole development cycle of X.Y+1. Repeat 1 & 2 for next cycle. In practice, for next versions, that means: As commented above, we are already late with 3.0 requirements ( MDL-50182 ). It will be implemented this/next week and done. Exactly this is the type of problem that we want to avoid in the future. The issue for 3.1 ( MDL-51580 ) has been created already, with explicit due-date 3 weeks after 3.0 release. It will be implemented immediately after that date and will remain stable for the 3.1 development cycle. A new issue (still not existing) will be created for 3.2 once point 1. is decided, so everybody will be able to comment/contribute there for 6 months. Repeat 1 & 2 for next (3.2) development cycle. And that's it. Hope it leads to earlier and stabler requirement definitions. Of course, comments, questions, objections are welcome. Ciao

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Please help!! my cron stoped running
ResponsesInList.Text: Depending on which DB you are using, you could have one of several types of locks being used. Assuming you are on mysql , the lock type will be dbrow locking. This lock type has a built in timeout of 24 hours - so if you do nothing for 24 hours the lock will be cleaned up and things will start working again. I don't know why the lock is stuck - it could be because a php process was killed while the lock was open - but it is not a normal situation. If you want to release the lock sooner, you could shutdown your webserver (to make sure nothing is running that is holding a lock), and then delete all the records from the lock_db table.

ResponsesInList.Title: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: In another thread the topic of a Moodle Marketplace for the sale and purchase of themes and plugins is being not discussed. So I thought it might get discussed here. Right now there are almost no premium plugins for Moodle. Most plugin developers develop for themselves or their organisation, and quite often those are submitted to the Moodle plugins database . Some, like me, write plugins under contract and may or may not put them on the plugins database. There is no shortage of great plugins, and new ones arrive regularly. So it could be said that Moodle is doing just fine without premium plugins. But I am not so sure. So let me just make the case for premium. It pays for support and updates and upgrades of the plugin. Currently there is no revenue for these things for plugin developers. They just get done for the same reason the plugin was developed in the first place. ie the needs of the developer, or their organisation. Or out of the developer's generosity. So we get abandoned plugins, and plugins that don't make it past the first few versions. Also as many plugins as there are, there could be more and they could be better through iterations of development. Note the lack of good alternatives to Paypal enrolment and the enormous adoption of the Essential theme. Donations and crowdfunding are often mentioned in this context . And they are relevant, but donations simply don't pay the bills. And crowdfunding for updates, support and upgrades is a whole lot less effective than for the initial development. It might also be argued that Moodle is free, so plugins should be too. This is a pretty strong point. Nobody wants money to get in the way of education. But Moodle has a revenue system via Moodle Partners, and thats no small part of why Moodle is so fully featured and mature. Plugin developers don't share in this. And plugins that don't last long enough to get mature, or get abandoned don't help anyone. Of course plugin developers are free to put a price tag on their plugins if they wish. But individuals are loathe to install something thats not on the plugins database these days. And larger organizations are often hosted by partners who don't make access to 3rd part plugins available easily. But its still true that even given those impediments, you could sell your plugin off-Moodle.org. I have tried, albeit a bit half heartedly. But it would be a great if there was something like the plugins database on Moodle.org for premium themes and plugins. Because deep down, as a plugin developer, I want to make a bit of money and spend more time on the plugins I write. The list of my own plugins that I can't maintain due to time and commitments to contract work is now just embarassing. Perhaps I am an exception here. But I would like to know what others think about this, and if Moodle HQ will consider any initiatives in the direction of premium plugins.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Justin, By premium, I assume you mean paid for. How would that work? Plugins for Moodle, by their nature, i.e. dependent upon Moodle in order to work, must be covered by Moodle's licence (GPL). Additionally, with commercial restrictions on code come the issues with enforcement, claims over intellectual property, etc. What happens if someone buys a "premium" Moodle plugin and uploads it to Github, which they're full entitled and encouraged to do by the GPL? What's more, if developers and organisations benefit from the many 1000's of hours of development and expertise that have gone into creating Moodle, shouldn't they contribute their modifications and additions back? There are already 3rd party commercial organisations that are making money out of providing plugins, themes, and additional features that are not contributed back to Moodle. Their work-around is simply not to share their source code and provide their modifications and additions as a service. If a project gets abandoned by the original developer and it's still popular, there's nothing to stop someone from cloning it and taking it over. If a module is restrictively licensed or the source code is in some way unavailable, continuing development can become a lot more complicated (i.e. getting permission and access) and much less likely to happen. Perhaps what we need is a way of flagging when a plugin or theme has been abandoned, e.g. if the developer fails to respond or agrees to hand over access, and have some way of passing ownership/editing rights of the module in the Moodle repo to a new developer. Just some thoughts.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Perhaps what we need is a way of flagging when a plugin or theme has been abandoned, e.g. if the developer fails to respond or agrees to hand over access, and have some way of passing ownership/editing rights of the module in the Moodle repo to a new developer. *cough* Plugins adoption programme *cough*

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for the responses. It likes like I haven't hit a nerve though. So it goes, I guess. Matt, in answer to your question(s), "premium" as in you have to pay to get it. So that would cover free + in-app purchase style upgrades, as well as straight out purchases. They would be GPL. Nothing would prevent people downloading and uploading onto github and other such actions. (But who would do such a thing? ) The idea of giving back because of all the value you get for free with Moodle, is ok from one view point. But remember not everyone gets Moodle for free. Many organizations pay pretty good money for Moodle and associated services. Thats the revenue that funds development. I don't think it really cries ungrateful to try and find a funding model that works for plugins too. Especially since one that works within Moodle.org , would likely see a percentage or a listing fee go back to Moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: I love premium plugins, because it allows free-lance programmers to work full-time on Moodle instead of, well, not being able to do anything for Moodle. Most GPL, free plugins are made by people who already have a salary for teaching or for administering an institutional Moodle site.  But a few great programmers, like Justin, quit their jobs in order to work full-time for Moodle. I am the opposite.  I get a salary from my school, so I can contribute courseware to the Moodle community for free via community Hubs.  But I can't program, so I got my school to pay about US$500/year to a commercial Moodle development firm to maintain and upgrade the Sharing Cart (a popular block that 10,000 people download per year).  If the Sharing Cart did not have that 500 dollar funding each year, it would die, like so many other good plugins. That is where a different funding model comes in--premium, paid plugins.  It can keep those plugins going by having freelancers do it.  But it sounds like there is a lot of trust going on, in that it is possible to share these paid plugins without paying for them--which I hope no one ever does.  Thanks Justin for risking your family's well-being in order to build a business to help develop Moodle.  Forgive me for being slow to contribute, but I do want to get your pay-for Quizlet module later this year.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: The customer value for premium plugins often lies in support. Plenty of people share premium wordpress plugins but if you come to rely on those plugins without access to updates and their support desk then you are running a gauntlet. A few years back I saw people running Google adwords on search terms like "wordpress themes" offering zip files for $50 with every premium theme pack (Woo, Elegant, StudioPress etc). Their sales page made a point of saying it was legal under GPL. You don't see those ads any more, who would want to buy something you rely on from a fly by night particularly when you don't know what kind of "modifications" may have been made? A fairly infamous one cropped up on Joomla a few years back. Someone gave away a free jQuery slider plugin that made a call back to their server and brought back a simple author credit in the HTML source (invisible to the user). This plugin was distributed for a long time, perhaps six months. It was quite popular, thousands of sites installed it and were happy with it. Subsequently some SEO's noticed some shady sites shoot up to the top of Googles rankings where they began hoovering up sales commission on car insurance and other high value commercial products. When said SEO's analysed how they had accomplished this remarkable feat they found thousands of Joomla sites linking to it. The authors server had stopped serving a simple author credit and replaced it with hidden links anchored with terms like "car insurance" pointing at these websites. At that time anchored backlinks were pretty well all that mattered to Google and the whole plugin (there were actually a few permutations of it) had been nothing more than elaborate scheme to make a stack of money very quickly. There is something to be said for the premium model!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Just to point out Kamesh - In this instance 'premium' = paid for, in my experience of some of those externally sold themes in particular it does not necessarily mean better quality. Neither does it necessarily mean that any given institution would find exactly the functionality they want and would still mean people using moodle partners or free lancers to 'custom-fit' the plugin to their requirements - a premium plugin store in whatever form is not going to change that. External commercial plugins (of the type sold on some of those sites) do not go through the kind of approval that the plugins in the moodle.org database go through and do not always follow best practice or moodle standard ways of doing things (one example is the use of jquery not being implemented using standard methods). There have also been instances of a freely available theme having one or two lines of code altered and then being put up for commercial sale. My advice would be to search for the plugin that does the job you want it to do best - if that's free and in the moodle database that's ideal. If you end up paying for it from one of those external sites then be very careful as you may find you cannot actually test it on your site with your combination of plugins and settings until after you have paid for it. The frequent viewpoint of 'you get what you pay for' isn't always true! I've been involved recently with a project where someone further up the food chain than me opted to pay multiple 10s of thousands of pounds for a commercial solution that to my mind would not have been allowed into the free moodle plugins database in the state it was, but would have been sent back to make it stable and actually be properly functional. That is separate from the discussion about whether/how to provide some benefit to those independant developers. I think the contributions many people put in to Moodle from the community and freely available to the community are one of Moodle's major strong points. I have major doubts about the idea of an official 'premium' channel - although I do recognise the need for developers (particularly the independent ones) to get some benefit from the work they put in and also the benefits for users in having the confidence that some kind of quality checks have been done on the code in those plugins (as is already the case in the plugins database). However, I can immediately see issues with commercial contributors making their contributions paid for rather than potential contributions to core, a split in the service levels and the complications for the community forums that could entail, as well as the 'image' issue as already mentioned 'ah its a free licence for the core software but all the decent plugins you have to pay extra for' etc. As I said, I can see the benefits from a developer point of view, not sure about for the community as a whole, but I don't have a constructive alternative to actually add to that discussion, beyond the recommendation to any user to thoroughly test any plugin in their own situation - a task made harder if you have to justify buying the plugin before you can even test it.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: So in theory, there might be an official Premium Plugins directory, similar to the existing plugins directory, which works like this: In order to list, you pay a recurring fee (which goes to Moodle HQ, because they host the service). You submit your plugin to be listed, and it gets some kind of code review to make sure that it meets a minimum standard and isn't malicious. A bit like submitting apps to the Apple or Android store. This is the expensive bit, so the hosting fee would have to cover the position. You have to fill in some required fields and answer some questions about support and usage, i.e. Users get 1 year of free support, the support forum address is X and the public source repo is Y (for GPL compliance), and that the code is yours forever (you are paying for the support not the software). It supports Moodle X through Y under these terms. It's these specific fields that need to be nutted out. Submission would also mean that someone at Moodle HQ or a trusted peer review community system tries out your plugin pre-sales, and tries out your support for turnaround and validity. Not enough votes, the plugin submission is rejected. This isn't too far from the current plugin submission guidelines. Sales are handled through the premium store address only, and 10% is deducted from the final payment (somehow handling vat/gst/etc) which also goes back to Moodle HQ. The rest is deposited back to the developer through something like paypal. The end user who makes the purchase clicks on a disclaimer to purchase, along the lines of "Support is handled at X, and has no association with Moodle HQ, and is supported for term Y, source is available under GPL at URL . If the end user is using Moodle Z and the plugin only states that its supported up to Y, then there's no responsibility for either Moodle HQ or the developer to do anything about it (no "I bought it and it didn't work" argument, if they ticked some "I Agree" during the checkout); but then, there's nothing stopping another community member re-posting the same plugin that does support Moodle Z. Fragmentation of plugin sales may occur, but thats the risk selling GPL'd software.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Firstly, I really want to help support plugin developers and to do anything we can towards this. Secondly, I really want to keep administration minimal. However, I'm not convinced an "app store" approach is going to work for our environment of GPL software.  There's just too many ways to circumvent it or ignore it.   There are other models out there - one I like is patreon.com I had a different idea just now, so I thought I'd throw it in here for discussion.  It may be doomed from the start, who knows, have a think. Let's call it a Premium Subscription Model A: We have a switch in moodle.org/plugins that developers can switch a plugin to Premium.  When they do this they must give us a Paypal ID to receive money. If  user wants to access ANY of these premium plugins they need to start a Premium subscription (this could be monthly regular payments, straight into Paypal to Moodle HQ).  This gives them access to ALL premium plugins (for one Moodle site based on fixed IP) without further hassles, so it's a pretty sweet deal. The money collects in an account all month.  Subscription stats will be public. At the end of the month, Moodle HQ takes 10% for our expenses, leaving 90%.  If Premium Devs want Moodle HQ to do extra reviewing etc then it could be a bit more. We have a public algorithm that works out the proportion of this money that each developer should get, based on things that indicate worthiness, such as: Whether the plugin was updated in this month and by how much. Number of installs Number of updates from unique URLs Number/type of ratings Once we know how much each developer gets, we split up the booty and automate a bunch of payments to every premium developer. Of course the main question is what would the algorithm be to be fair and resist gaming of the system?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Its great to get some positive and creative input into this, and its an interesting proposal Martin. The app store idea has drawbacks in the GPL context, though I am ok with them. But the premium community has problems too. While the algorythm is still undefined, the problems are less apparent. But some scenarios that I see as problematic are: i) no. of updates. Personally I try not to introduce updates to the plugins database in between minor releases of Moodle. Unless its really necessary, ie a bug fix that can't be ignored. Several reasons for this, but the point here is that release frequency might not be something that people agree on the value of. ii) a buggy plugin with enthusiastic sincere support. How high do we value this? Who makes these judgements iii) a wildly popular plugin that needs no support. Again how to value this? iv) diminishing returns Eventually developers will be fighting it out for a share of a finite pool. A fantastic new contribution will either diminish everyone else's return or not reap a fantastic return. And this will depend on the algorythm. This is actually quite important. Because the incentive to innovate or provide more and more functionality , better support etc is greater when an equivalent reward can be anticipated. But if the reward is not determined by the developers actions as much as by the algorythm, I think it won't be as effective in encouraging developers to provide value. In true Adam Smith style free market thinking, these decisions are best left up to the market aren't they? The clearest and most automatic way of establishing a value for a plugin in my opinion, is by charging for it. People will vote intelligently with their dollars if we give them the information they need. Can we reconcile this somehow with the premium community model? Having said all the above, I do like the premium community idea. Its simple and great value for subscribers. Its boots and all, in or out and kind of Moodle'y. It just needs very careful thought.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks Justin for keeping this topic alive, and thanks everybody for good comments here. I've been watching this discussion since the start but I intentionally did not want to step in earlier. When ideas are being brainstormed, it is better to keep the objections behind the doors for a while. I've been thinking (and talking, as my wife can second) about this a lot and I am going to join this thread now to play devil's advocate role a bit. Some disclaimer first. The Old Gods and the New know that it would make me only happy to see more folks being able to contribute to Moodle and be paid for doing so. The thing is, I have no idea how to achieve that. And I am very sceptical when it comes to Martin's proposal. Yet, I have no constructive proposal myself so I won't be very helpful here. I am sorry in advance. The truth is simple. People don't want to pay for software if they don't have to (many of them started with Moodle because of that). That is why donations don't work well enough, that is why crowd-funding does not work well enough for us. Let us not pretend there are masses of users waiting impatiently with their PayPal open for us to open the Prominent Plugins Social Club they could subscribe to. If they really want to financially support their favourite plugins, they already can. I am not fan of the model where HQ would redistribute the collected money on any criteria. Firstly, HQ is a software company, not an elected political government. Secondly, no such criteria can ever be fair and objective. I can't really see how things like the number of releases or diff stats could help us to fairly compare two different plugins. The plugin maintenance is a complex thing. Some plugins are simple and stable, and do not need software updates at all. Some maintainers prefer discussing things and providing support in forums, some in comments, some in Github tracker, some in e-mails. Some do not communicate with users at all, yet are able to develop top quality software. Any criteria based on technicalities are just easy to be cheated. What would stop people from releasing versions frequently for no real reason once they realize how The Algorithm works? And no, I don't think the button "report this to David so he can investigate and decide whether or not this plugin receives money this month" would work. Or let us have such button and volunteer yourself to do this kind of work. My karma suffers enough from approval reviews already. Also, I am afraid this could easily open Pandora's box in the whole Moodle community. Could any contributor put their plugin into the Premium plugins programme? If so, what will stop most of them doing so? If not, what criteria will be there? Are we preparing a solid basement for "some plugins are more equal than others" atmosphere here? Once plugin developers start receiving money for their work, why should our language pack maintainers and contributors continue translating for free? Should the wiki documentation contributors get their part of the cake, too? And what about bug reporters and QA testers - are not they contributing to Moodle , too? Are we ready to implement similar programmes for these good people? Premium English language pack? Premium user documentation? Premium tested Moodle version? What are we actually looking for? What kind of plugins do we want to see supported? Is it the technical coding quality (solid patterns, clean coding style, following coding guidelines, attaching behaviour and unit tests)? Is it modern and attractive user interface? Is it actual usefulness in pedagogical scenarios? Is it just anything as long as it is regularly updated? And what do we understand by "updated" at the end? I am seeing many different types of plugins submitted into the plugins directory and it would be personally very difficult for me to judge and compare them. How would Premium plugins be integrated into the whole plugins machinery that integrates AMOS , available updates notifications, automatic upgrades etc. Would there be support for free/community version of the plugin vs premium version of the plugin? If so, will these two share the same component ( frankenstyle ) name? Or will it be conceptually different plugin? What information about the premium plugins will be available publicly? I am running into details now as I have learnt that answering details early helps to avoid design flaws later. If something like this should happen, I really believe it should be people (subscribers, those who pay) who decide where money, or at least most of the money, goes. Say something like 60% to the plugin of my choice, do whatever you think is the best with the rest. Still, making people actually want to send us money is the essential issue here. These gatherings are only successful when they come with well designed and attractive marketing campaigns, social media virals and that stuff. Nothing easy. Nothing cheap. Good luck. We will need it.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text:
I agree with Derek that officially introducing paid for plugins and the kinds of enforcement that would require and the possible effects that could have on contributors and contributions overall needs deeper reflection and discussion. How will introducing restrictions, pay walls, and presumably prosecuting infractions affect the Moodle community and people's perceptions of it more broadly speaking. What are the philosophical contradictions between Moodle's FOSS foundation and proprietary, restrictive software and how can they co-exist? Perhaps it would be useful at this point to look back on the discussion about 3rd party Moodle service providers/vendors (one in particular) and the reaction their behaviour got from the Moodle community: Is TotaraLMS closed source? : https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=171235 And MoodleHQ's reaction and Totara's reaction to that: "This is a clone of the Totara source code (which is based on Moodle) as of November 29th 2013. It's not being updated because our access to the original repository was terminated shortly after distributing this clone." Source: https://github.com/moodlehq/totara Yes, we need to hear more from the "silent majority" on this issue. We also need to continue to explore what the possible options would mean in the broader context rather than just trying to imagine a narrow, limited range of use-case scenarios to support one side or the other of an argument. In other words, do we really know what we're arguing for or against? As a developer, I've made a commitment to Moodle and its FOSS foundation. I've contributed and maintained plugins free of charge. I haven't been directly paid for any of those contributions. However, it has brought me work indirectly, e.g. making modifications/customisations to my and other modules for clients as well as other indirect paid work. Being a Moodle contributor with a track record can also greatly improve your employment prospects. I guess what I'm trying to say is that there are other ways in which contributing to Moodle can pay off. And, at a time when even the big proprietary stalwarts and governments are increasingly taking the FOSS route, why would Moodle make itself less attractive to those potential new users? e.g. The European Union is in the process of drafting a directive that gives preference to FOSS over proprietary, restrictive options and most member countries are already implementing their own policies to that effect. What would happen if people start asking about how much of Moodle is actually FOSS? Could you imagine what Blackboard, Desire2Learn, etc. would do with this? At the end of this I think the question should be, "How would this help
or hinder Moodle and its community of developers, designers, and users?"
How much would we end up serving an outspoken minority to the detriment
of the quieter majority? Just some thoughts.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Re: "donations don't work," - What have we tried so far? Why didn't those strategies work? What makes a Moodle user decide to donate or not donate? Other, more successful approaches to seeking donations The following examples are for different types of communities and activities (independent news and media) but I think they may have some applicable ideas. Democracy Now! https://www.democracynow.org/donate The Real News: http://therealnews.com/t2/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=1021 Both sites frequently use email campaigns. They use social media not only to raise awareness of who they are and what they do, but also to encourage support. They sometimes use JS nag-ware to donate that you have to click through to access the site. They schedule fund-raiser campaigns with leader-boards and other techniques to encourage people to donate. They both encourage subscription-based donations on a regular monthly or yearly basis. They explicitly explain how their funding models work and why people should donate, i.e. what benefit it is to their communities. MoodleHQ has its own funding model and strategies, so the 3rd party plugins model would probably be better perceived at separate and distinct from that, i.e. donors understand that their donations are exclusively going to support 3rd party plugins. If users want to donate to MoodleHQ as well, they can. Would that mean competition between the two? If so, would that be healthy or unhealthy for Moodle in general? Allocating donations Perhaps some form of voting system to divide donated funds could be worth looking into, e.g. vote for your favourite plugins when you donate? In models like this, I think it'd be important for donors to see a donation history so that they can see how many people have donated how much to whom, i.e. open and transparent, and let them decide which plugins to favour on that basis. This would do away with complex, easy to manipulate and gain algorithmic approaches, i.e. let the donors make intelligent, well-informed decisions rather than leave it to stupid machines.

To plug my current portfolio: https://moodle.org/plugins/browse.php?list=contributor&id=442195 - some of my plugins have had a long life and are purely mine, like Collapsed Topics, others I have taken over like Grid format and Essential.  The later in terms of recognition though, I have spent a considerable amount of time on. With core commits, I currently only have 77 ( https://moodle.org/dev/contributions.php ) but I am on the first page and hopefully will increase soon with MDL-50869 .  Though I doubt I'll ever overtake K-9. Is this a measure of a good Moodle developer?  Maybe.  But I am very critical of my own skills.  Behat etc. still evades my understanding almost in a mental block way, despite being happy with such concepts as JUnit for testing.  So just what makes a good Moodle developer, I think a combination of, but certainly not any in isolation: PHP. Appreciation of JavaScript and YUI / jQuery frameworks. LESS / CSS . Command line. An understanding of the structure, form, modularity of the core code. An attitude and willingness to adapt, change, support and not believe you know everything. Just a thought. Gareth
