You also say: " Probably the best way to go about trying to make some money from any developments you do, is simply to offer paid support." Yes, Agreed.  How do you propose this be set up? ------ I've asked twice on this matter, hypothesising a kind of  a give-a-little to coders: https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=314916#p1263153 https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=314916#p1276566 Still waiting to hear back from Martin or David. I know from where Martin stands there may be worries.  (Will it siphon off money from MoodleHQ? - but from Guildo's post, they don't seem to want this - and other issues maybe??) From where David stands there may be an admin overhead? Shannon and Martin (and whoever else is involved) may also we worried this could impact on the activities of the Association. maybe. Maybe Moodle Partners could be concerned? ------ My view of such a setup is very simple: if person X has a plugin on Moodle.org database, we can give to that person via Moodle.org. If person X ALSO works for a company, then it is decided if this is in their own time (so they get the money) or company time (and company gets the money - or a split) Plus?? Minor details: Minimum disbursements.  (ie less than $Z then hold over until amount grows) PR to make it account-wise attractive to any institution Plus?? Scenarios: Out of appreciation, because we use a plugin we give a little.  Maybe if it is an institution, once a year a budget time. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Overhead is the key worry for me. Apart from all our core work on Moodle and with Partners we're all very busy here setting up Moodle Association and MoodleCloud at the moment, which are designed to give us stable revenue to hire more people to work on Moodle core. We don't have spare time to be managing small development contracts with large amounts of people or brokering tiny transactions with 3rd party developers.  Any moodle.org system involving plugin-based payments needs to be quite simple to set up and have almost no maintenance costs (which is why I suggested the subscription-based system above). There are also the long-term effects of any changes on the community around this open source project that need to be considered well.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm not sure we are talking about the same thing here Martin.  Some clarifications follow. I'm suggesting a Give a Little style arrangement where we can give to developers who manage plugins in the database. Enable gifts to come to developers who are listed in the plugin directory. Setup as a simple credit card payment (or whatever)  You probably already have this.  I have done a little research on this, and it is not complex. Then once a month, do a tally.  If the income for developer X is above a certain amount, this is transferred into their account.  If it is not above a certain amount, then it is carried over to the next month. I know you are working on cloud and association.  But this arrangement should not be a big, complex or time consuming arrangement to set up. You (ie MoodleHQ) would not "managing small developer contracts".  I've read the thread, and cannot see what this refers to. You say " Any moodle.org system involving plugin-based payments needs to be quite simple to set up and have almost no maintenance costs" I think this will fill the boll. I'm not sure that numbers will be large.  If you are concerned to make this fiscally neutral as far as HQ admin goes, then just take a cut. As others have said, it is better to have this inside MoodleHQ rather than something like Moodle Garage or some other entity.  This will make it easier with no extra effort to attract funding from entities that may need some extra audit trail. You say:  " There are also the long-term effects of any changes on the community around this open source project that need to be considered well"  I'm not sure what this means. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Premium Plugins and Themes
ResponsesInList.Text: Conn, you say: " Donations I can't really see working that well to make any real money in this context, as it's not individuals using your systems, 99% of the time it's institutions, so it would be more awkward to simply donate because they like it and want to support it" What's your evidence for this? Just based on what I have found working in a college over the past few years. Budgets are very tight, and it can be hard to get things through finance without them being well backed up. I can imagine a lot of places would find it very hard to justify any kind of real outlay on donating to the developer of a moodle plugin, especially as i'm sure most places use a lot of plugins, from a range of people. This is of course much easier for individuals, as they can do whatever they want with their money. Maybe I'm wrong though, but it seems to me like it would be difficult. You also say: " Probably the best way to go about trying to make some money from any developments you do, is simply to offer paid support." Yes, Agreed.  How do you propose this be set up? That would probably depend on the person/institution who are supporting the plugin, as they will be able to offer different things. Though I suppose a framework could be setup on moodle.org which could be used by any developer who wanted to. For example maybe you could setup different levels of support, defining what guarantees you offer at different levels (e.g. installation, upgrades, 24 hour response times, etc...), price (monthly, one-time, etc...), and then payment is done through moodle.org (I think it has paypal support doesn't it?) I've never done paid support myself, as all our stuff we do here is free and we do free support, so perhaps it would be an idea to do a few case studies of where this is being done well, if anyone wanted to explore it further.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Select Atto instance
ResponsesInList.Text: As something similar was needed by a client, the workaround I found was to create an Atto plugin, which did not add any button to the UI. Within this plugin initialiser I saved the instance (this) into a place I could get at it (I knew the id of the editor I wanted in this case, so I only needed to save one instance - you could always save the instances in an object, indexed by the id). I then defined the functions I needed within the plugin and then wrote some wrapper functions that accessed those functions via the saved instance. Not a replacement for the proposed editor manager, but a reasonable workaround for a project that is needed now. The use case for this client was a set of commenting/annotation tools that sit alongside the text editor, but not part of the editor UI.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Assign Theme to user or at login
ResponsesInList.Text: No it wouldn't, it allows the user to choose the theme in a setting on their profile page - but there are options: you could set the theme in the database directly using a script and then use css to hide the option to change it from the user profile page. OR You could use the user profile fields to add the user's company/institution e.g. in the Optional fields, Institution. You could then detect that $USER variable, add it to the body classes and then use it to adjust any of the css you want to - including adding an institutional logo. You could then just have the single theme and if new companies get involved you can add the adjustments through the customcss setting, rather than creating a new child theme.

In a few places (that shall not be named), after the CTO had said that they were a pure Oracle shop and had left the meeting... the Oracle DBAs would confess that actually they were running quite a few installs of Pg but hadn't told anyone. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Databases: Who uses Oracle?
ResponsesInList.Text:
Do you think the not-good performance means
that the code needs to be optimized more I had several discussions with Eloy about performance with Ora and MSSQL and what we could do to support them better. If I remember right, the perf problems with MSSQL and Oracle are: The lack a complete and fast limit/offset implementation. That means that paginating through the list of users is horrid. Eloy may have implemented a double-nested subselect to workaround this, or perhaps we just advance the cursor over the rows we want to offset over. Either workaround is slow, grep for offset in lib/dmllib.php . CLOB/Text inserts need to be done in 2 stages (INSERT a null, and then UPDATE with the actual data). I think that Ora10 doesn't have this limitation, but I'm not sure what Moodle/AdoDB are doing with this. Limited/slow Oracle extension in PHP - For each database backend, the PHP engine has a library/extension that acts a bit like a driver. The extension for Ora has have 2 limitations that have a huge impact on performance: When dealing with selects with many rows the Ora driver pulls all the rows into memory, rather than iterating over them. If that's true, it's a memory hog. When going to a specific row in the result (like trying to advance the cursor to emulate offset) it cannot skip to the row. Instead, it moves the cursor through all the rows. I may be accusing Ora of sins committed by MSSQL -- we were trying to solve portability issues for both and it's all mixed up in my head right now. I'm hoping Eloy can chime in with some authority here... Note that none of these are showstoppers for small/medium sites. For a large installation, I'd consider putting some pressure on Oracle to get a fix to the issues above At least plan for a bit of a load test with real-sized datasets. You can hedge your bets keeping Pg as an alternative...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Databases: Who uses Oracle?
ResponsesInList.Text: " What can we expect from a Oracle and Moodle integration?" You can expect things to be a bit slower. There are two main problems: 1) Oracle cannot tell the differences between the empty string "" and NULL. Moodle, however, uses both values and the difference is important. Therefore Moodle has to check all data going to and from the database, and replace empty string with another value. That slows down every interaction with the database. 2) Moodle handles a lot of textual content (CLOB columns in the database). The Oracle protocol for communicating between the database and the application server deals with CLOBS in a really inefficient way, which also slows things down. There is a third problem not related to performance: 3) Since very few people use Oracle with Moodle, then if there are database-specific bugs (which are rare) then things are more likely to break on Oracle than on MySQL or Postgres. Also, if a community plugin fails to work on some databases, it is more likely that the one that fails is Oracle. Therefore, you should only use Oracle if you really have no other choice.

ResponsesInList.Title: Generating Moodle API Documentation
ResponsesInList.Text:
Overview I am starting to write some Moodle code and looked all over for (i) a location that I could see the actual API documented and/or (ii) instructions on how to officially generate such. Unfortunately, I could find neither --all links, etc. mentioned (e.g., xref.moodle.org, phpdocs.moodle.org) are non-existent. There doesn't seem to be any current API documentation online at all. Some posts (e.g., this forum) suggest using grep to look through the docs as a solution. Since I am unfamiliar with the APIs, this is not a realistic solution, so I thought I would build the documentation myself. This post is to share my experience doing this as there are other posts in these forums and elsewhere on the Internet asking about how to get API documentation --and those answers IMHO are unsatisfactory especially when compared to the instructions that appear below. A Comment About Current Online Developer Documentation The online documentation is tutorial and/or overview oriented. While this is wonderful, in several places Moodle developer pages say rather than dive into the minutiae of the API, examples will be presented. Unfortunately, these examples are not complete with respect to the API (and there are no additional examples to make it more complete), and, many of the examples are out-of-date with respect to current stable Moodle. Some even cause deprecation warnings to be emitted. (I am not complaining --just mentioning what one experiences if one is starting to do plugin development today rather than some years ago.) For what I am coding, I really need an API reference --and there doesn't appear to be one online. Nicely the PHP code does have comments with markup. Unfortunately, such is scattered across some ~7800 files. While I do realize that only a small number of files really matter, there is still more than a handful of files: such really deserves to be generated into suitable documentation generated by individual programmers. Unfortunately, there are no instructions I could find for this. PHPDocumentor I first started with PHPDocumentor. For Moodle v2.9 it has been running for more than 24 hours and it is still not finished! So I cannot comment on its results yet except to say that PHPDocumentor is extremely slow to process Moodle's PHP. For this reason, I would argue PHPDocumentor is an unacceptable solution unless it was run by someone and then posted online for all to use. (PHPDocumentor also emits an ENORMOUS number of warnings. Whether or not these are important, I don't know yet.) Doxygen Personally I like Doxygen and use that myself with, for example, C++ code. Since Doxygen works with PHP, I tried it with Moodle v2.9 stable. Unfortunately, it only output class information when I first tried it. I investigated why and realized that Moodle's PHP files don't have this markup line in them: 
```text
/** @file */
```
 This line causes doxygen to generate the documentation for the functions, etc. in the file that are not in a class. So I added this to each PHP file and then generated the Doxygen documentation, e.g., 
```text
# Insert /** @file */ as the second line of every PHP file...


$ find . -type f -name '*.php' -exec sed -i '2s|^|/** @file */\n|' \{\} \;


# Generate a default Doxygen configuration file (if needed)...


$ doxygen -g
```
 NOTE: The removal of /** @file */ is not a delete-the-second line just in case there was an error adding such to a file. The above removal line will revert a git repository back to pristine state (i.e., git status will not show any of the /** @file */ modified files). If you are paranoid and are using git, one can easily use git stash instead similar to this: 
```text
# Save your current repository...


$ git stash push


# Insert /** @file */...


$ find . -type f -name '*.php' -exec sed -i '2s|^|/** @file */\n|' \{\} \;


# Run Doxygen...


$ doxygen /path/to/Doxyfile


# Revert back to a pristine repo...


$ git stash push


# Throw away the /** @file */ changes...


$ git stash drop


# Bring back your stash...


$ git stash pop
```
 Unlike PHPDocumentor, Doxygen runs quickly. I have attached the Doxyfile I used which does not generate LaTeX, caller graphs, or callee graphs. The result with Moodle v2.9 is about 1.3 GiB. I also tried creating caller and callee graphs. Obviously Doxygen will take significantly longer but it is still acceptable if one wants such information --as it only has to be generated once. The result is about 3.9 GiB. Closing Comments While I can appreciate hosting and bandwidth reasons for not having API documentation online in a convenient format, I would argue that there should be instructions on how programmers can generate such when it is desired. Given the dreadfully and unacceptably slow speed of PHPDocumentor, I don't see such as a realistic and practical solution. Doxygen appears to work well with the aforementioned /** @file */ fix. As this fix is easy to implement (e.g., using the above find command), may I suggest the Moodle team should add such to all PHP files to facilitate Doxygen-generated documentation. If that is not possible, then the Moodle Developer documentation should document how programmers can generate the API documentation in convenient HTML with Doxygen (e.g., using the steps I outlined above). I've posted this as I hope this helps others do the same.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Generating Moodle API Documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Paul, we've been looking multiple times on generating phpdocs for moodle using phpdocumentor, doxygen and some other tools. We have developed guildelines to prepare the code for it and also local_moodlecheck plugin to check the code for compliance (it is also used by cibot). The guildelines are not 100% compliant with either of documentor tools but we have scripts that automatically correct phpdocs blocks and tokens to make code ready for one or another. The problem, however, is that generated phpdocs are completely unusable. Moodle code was being written over 16 years, it started before OOP existed and at the moment is a big mixture of very different coding styles. When we generate phpdocs the doxygen/phpdocumentor starts classifying by namespaces and classes and therefore highlights the areas where we use classes such as third party libraries, events or renderers (which are not an important part of API). At the same time functions in the files like lib/moodlelib.php, lib/accesslib.php, etc. are very hard to find. And it is hard to teach documentors about core/plugins/3rdparty difference, they pile everything together. We've even been considering writing our own documentor and add non-standard @category token to the functions/classes/files to identify areas. Never really got enough time for it, sorry. Here is the issue in tracker to follow: MDLSITE-1603

ResponsesInList.Text:

ResponsesInList.Title: Contribute back moodle enhancements to open source projects
ResponsesInList.Text: As a general principle of open source software it's considered good manners to contribute any changes or enhancements you make back to the open source project. Moodle has taken a lot of open source projects - from the forms lib to bootstrap and mustache - without contributing alterations/enhancements made back to the main project and this seems a bit rude. If you are going to fork a project and make enhancements, the whole community of people using that open source product should be able to benefit from your enhancements. If moodle is not doing this then not only is it not giving back, but also forking into a dead end that can never update - something moodle as an open source product in itself would never support or suggest - that would be just be double standards. Ideally i'd like to see this enshrined in Moodles development philosophy. Thoughts, as always, most welcome.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Contribute back moodle enhancements to open source projects
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Stuart, Thank you for your words of wisdom. It's interesting, and slightly disappointing, to hear these views. Hopefully we can improve your opinion. I agree, it is generally good manners to contribute any changes, or enhancements made back to an open source project. It's something that I've personally believed for many years, and is something that I am passionate about. I myself have contributed to many projects, including Moodle, Mahara (I was one of the first non-Catalyst developers with access to the project), Request Tracker, Debian, ADOdb, YUI, TinyMCE, and countless others. It's something I've also found my previous employers willing to work with too - that's how several core Moodle features came about (e.g. Activity chooser, short forms, form change checker, course JS rewrite, in-progress new AntiVirus systems, ...). Yes, Moodle has taken a lot from other Open Source projects, and yes, the list does include our forms library (The PEAR Quickforms library), Bootstrap, Mustache, and others. It also includes things like PHPMailer, Typo3, HTMLPurifier, TinyMCE, FlowPlayer, MathJax, numerous other PEAR libraries, AdoDB, YUI, jQuery, AMD, PHPUnit, Behat, HTML2Text, and many, many more. Most of these are just presented in their official state, or have just had the components that we do not require removed (e.g. the src files, examples, etc.). Without going through every readme_moodle.txt, I couldn't tell you what other modifications we have made. Where we have made other modifications, these are often very Moodle-specific (e.g. retro-fitting our own textlib handling, or language string provision). I disagree that we have not contributed our alterations and enhancements back. There is countless evidence of where we have done this, both of old, and recently: I myself was one of the first non-Yahoo YUI developers, and that was largely because of the contributions that Moodle put back into the Project. On Moodle's behalf, I've also contributed to Composer, Various YUI-related projects (Shifter, Yeti, YUIDoc, Aand friends), syn (used by Selenium for synthesised mouse movement and clicks), bigbluebutton, TinyMCE (that irritating iOS bug when you opened the keyboard), and others. Damyon Wiese has recently had a pull request accepted onto one of the projects you have shamed us for ( https://github.com/bobthecow/mustache.php/pull/265 ) and has another pull request ready to go once the change in the specification has been ratified ( https://github.com/janl/mustache.js/pull/473 ). He has been working with developers on those projects. Both John Okely, and I have been contributing to development of ADOdb recently ( https://github.com/ADOdb/ADOdb/pull/142 and in various issues); Eloy Lafuente contributed the ADOdb UTF-8 MSSQL driver (ms sql _n); Bugfixes for libraries we use such as Typo3, PHPMailer, HTML2Text, and others; I don't have a list of them all, but I'm pretty sure that there are countless other examples from HQ developers both past and present. For some projects, it is very hard for us to contribute back, or it does not make sense to contribute our changes back. This may be because the project has been retired or replaced (this is the case of our forms library - it has long since been retired, and replaced by it's official developer, and I believe that we did attempt to contribute at various times in its history). The new version of the library is so vastly different, that it would be difficult for us to contribute our changes to it. In the case of Bootstrap, I'm not aware of any real changes that we have made to the library. In any case we are, again, using an old version of the library which is out of official support. The changes that I am aware of are pretty Moodle-specific or changes which would not be accepted anyway (e.g. fixing to work with lessc compiler, which they state is not supported). I should also point out that, at many times, we have contributed in numerous other ways. We cannot always contribute with code changes, but sometimes we contribute with our advice, feedback, bug reports, and in other ways. These ways are (usually) appreciated by those projects. There is certainly no rule to not push back, and it is something which I generally feel encouraged to do as a developer here at HQ. Perhaps you have some examples of where we actually have not, and should have contributed so that we can start to rectify these where appropriate? I'd also be interested to know what influenced you to open this discussion? Best wishes, Andrew

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Contribute back moodle enhancements to open source projects
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Andrew, its great to see Damyon contributing to mustache, and that this is being taken seriously. I really hope this continues so moodle can keep up to date with mustache. I’m sure we both agree it would be a shame to see mustache or anything else get into the same state as bootstrap or the forms lib, where moodle is now trapped in a dead end of unsupported legacy code full of Moodle-specific enhancements. Do you know if there are any plans to take this more future friendly approach with bootstrap or the forms lib? As always, no shaming intended and it’s great to see contributions to projects.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Contribute back moodle enhancements to open source projects
ResponsesInList.Text: Formslib was discussed in length at the hackfest in 2012: https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Perth_Hackfest_October_2012/Forms_API That lists a smaller group of people in a break-out group but was covered in great length with a large number of developers. The original Formslib dev even offered some advice and engaged within the moodle forums. From my vague re-collection the decision was made that it would be a lot of work to replace, faster to fix the existing issues we have with it and at the time it was hard to justify spending a significant amount of HQ staff time to re-develop/replace something without clear reasons that it would improve the user-interface. Is it worth spending say 6 months of a developers time on rewriting formslib (and potentially breaking 3rd party plugins) or spending that time on something like site-wide reporting or outcomes. Of course that decision may change in future - We also talked a lot about YUI vs Jquery at the hackfest in 2012 choosing not to use both YUI and JQuery at that stage, but have more recently decided to move away from YUI. Personally my experience has been that Moodle HQ (and other core contributors) have always strived to pass any enhancements/fixes back upstream to open source projects as this makes it easier to maintain within Moodle in the long-term. There are many examples of this and Andrew has listed only a small subset of those. Another example - Iñaki Arenaza wrote a patch for PHP back in 2007 to enable pagination support in ldap but it took something like 5 years before it was integrated. What does happen is that organisations modify Moodle code or write plugins that they do not share back with the community. Of course it is perfectly acceptable according to the GPL licence and I probably wouldn't personally call them "rude" but it certainly would be nice if they contributed to the community.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Contribute back moodle enhancements to open source projects
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Stuart, I'm not quite sure what you mean by "the same state as bootstrap". Just to be clear, the bootstrapbase theme has a `less/bootstrap` directory within it. This directory contains a near-virgin copy of the Bootstrap code, downloaded from http://getbootstrap.com/2.3.0/ . We have made the following changes to the code: stripped out everything except for the .less files; Apply MDL-42195 - this is a backport change from Bootstrap 3; Apply MDL-46470 - actually, this looks like a bug on our part. It probably should have been applied to the moodle directory and not the bootstrap code. I have created MDL-51207 to address this mistake; Apply MDL-48328 - this allows us to compile using lessc as well as recess (lessc has better debugging during development). The upstream maintainers have stated that they only support compiling with recess and will not fix this issue in Bootstrap itself . As you can see, there isn't much more that we can do to contribute back in the case of Bootstrap. We have technically forked it, but only in the sense that we have back-ported changes from the latest version to ours, and addressed issues which they have said they will not fix in the version we use. The reason that we are currently 'stuck' with Bootstrap 2.3.0 is not because we are `trapped in a dead end of unsupported legacy code full of Moodle-specific enhancements`, but because half of the markup and classes used have changed with version 3 of Bootstrap, and they are almost certain to be different again in Bootstrap 4 - if nothing else, the compiler is because BS4 uses sass instead of less. Again, this is something we're working to improve with renderer and template improvements. I should point out that `formslib` is actually a Moodle library, not an upstream library. It uses the HTML_QuickForm library extensively, but the moodleform class does not extend anything. As I mentioned in my previous reply, we have attempted to contribute back to HTML_QuickForm with some of our changes, but the code is deprecated, and no longer maintained by it's author. We need to move to a new version, but that has nothing to do with our contributions to either the original project, or any other related projects. We are stuck with a lot of legacy code here, but much of that code is many years old - we are aware of it and we are trying to improve the entire situation. I was brainstorming with Damyon only last week about how we can get past that issue. Unlike most plugin developers and other groups who do not release their changes back, we have to think very carefully about changes which will break backwards compatibility. This tends to make things slow, and to make us very cautious. I believe that our plans are generally to contribute back where appropriate (not every project accepts changes, agrees with our changes, or is actively maintained). Over the past few years, with changes in development processes, we're trying to avoid those future issues - the move from CVS to Git , Integration processes, improve testing, official deprecation and backport processes, thirdpartylibs. xml checking and enforcing, and more along those lines has really helped that. I hope that clarifies things for you, Andrew

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Contribute back moodle enhancements to open source projects
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Andrew, i’m very excited to know “ I was brainstorming with Damyon only last week about how we can get past that issue. “ As you're undoubtedly aware poor usability is not something that benefits learners, educators, developers or admin in moodle. Being stuck on moodle’s custom unupdatable forms lib is something i’m sure we would all like to avoid with any other open source lib you guys pick for moodle - including yui, bootstrap, jquery or mustache. From my personal perspective as a developer who has used bootstrap, jquery, underscore with mustache in moodle, and has always been able to keep their moodle up to date with the latest version of these open source projects, i’d be sad to see moodle’s use of these projects fall into the same ‘moodle specific patches’  as bootstrap or jquery has, and forms lib did. Be very interested to see your plans for these issues if possible?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Remote authentication for Zendesk via Moodle
ResponsesInList.Text: Open the zendesk_auth.php file in a text editor. Enter the path to your Moodle config. (Usually something like /home/user/public_html/config.php) Log into your Zendesk as an administrator. Go to Settings -> Channels -> API Enable token access Generate a new access token and copy it Go back to your text editor and paste it into the $sToken variable ($sTocken = "3483s9sdf0482g3984fs092") then SAVE the file Upload the file to your Moodle server in the root moodle directory (Usually something like /home/user/public_html/) Go to Settings -> Security -> Authentication Enable Single Sign On Enter the remote login url (Something like http://yourdomain.com/zendesk_auth.php) Enter the remote logout url which is your regular moodle logout (Something like http://yourdomain.com/login/logout.php ) Check allow update of external ID's So what is really going on here? User goes to zendesk. Zendesk runs the zendesk_auth.php to handle login. zendesk_auth.php checks if the user is logged in and if true sends the username, email and user id to zendesk and because we are using the token it logs them in. If they are not logged in then they must log in to moodle then they are redirected to zendesk. Hopefully this rushed instructions makes sense and gets you started.. I would love to complete my Zendesk block but I have a large 1.9 to 2+ conversion to do first.

ResponsesInList.Title: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text: Is Moodle using semantic versioning ( http://semver.org /)? It looks like it is, but when you look closer it seems this isn't the case. I read this but I'm really not sure: https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Moodle_versions Semantic versioning has three parts: MAJOR version when you make incompatible API changes MINOR version when you add functionality in a backwards-compatible manner PATCH version when you make backwards-compatible bug fixes It seems to me that Moodle uses only two of these despite having a three-part version number. It seems to me that in practice the first two numbers are the same thing. Can someone shed some light to this and correct me if I'm wrong?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, the first 2 are the major version. E.g. 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, 2.7, etc... are all major versions, as opposed to "2" being the major version the 3rd part is the minor version of that major version

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text: Not really. After 2.9 will come 3.0, but that is not any different from the change from 2.8 to 2,9. In Moodle terms 2.x -> 2.y (or 2.9 to 3.0) is a major version, and may have API changes (which are normally documented in the release notes.) 2.9.z is a minor version. We don't number patches, but every week there is a 2.9.z+ weekly release. All patches are, of course, available from the git repo.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text: Ok, thanks for clarifying it! I must say that I in my opinion Moodle should also adopt Semver for versioning. I would like to know that if I make a plugin for 3.0.0 it will still work without changes during the whole lifetime of version 3.x.x no matter how many minor releases (e.g. 3.12.x) were made. As a plugin developer, I find the current way misleading.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text: I personally like Tom Preston-Werner's semantic versioning, too. Especially for the node.js packages and similar repositories. But I am not sure about actual benefits being worth of a change for the Moodle core. The main motivation for the semantic versioning, as I understood it, was to make the format unified and standardized so that package dependency managers (such as npm in node.js) can rely on it. That is not our case in 99%, I believe. Moodle's development model has become date-driven years ago and it seems to work very well since then (definitely better than feature-driven model used before). If there was a need for a change in the versioning scheme (and again, I don't think there is), it would be more natural to follow Mahara and switch to the Ubuntu-like date based version numbers, such as Moodle 15.05 (for the version released in May 2015). if I make a plugin for 3.0.0 it will still work without changes during the whole lifetime of version 3.x.x No. If you submit a plugin to the plugins directory, you will declare it supports Moodle 3.0. Moodle does not make any API and significant UI changes on stable branches so your plugin should work without changes for all 3.0.0, 3.0.1, 3.0.2, ... 3.0.x Moodle versions. Moodle 3.1.0 will be next major release (with API and UI changes expected) and you as the maintainer are supposed to check it works well there. You can still think in terms of semantic versioning in Moodle, as Tim exaplains. Given Moodle version X.Y.Z, you just need to consider X.Y as the major version and Z as the minor version.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text:
```text
Moodle's development model has become date-driven years ago and it seems to work very well
```
 Using Semver does not prevent you from continuing the date-driven releases. You can for example make: Major version once a year Minor version once a month Patch version every week 
```text
it would be more natural to follow [...] Ubuntu-like date based version numbers, such as Moodle 15.05 (for the version released in May 2015).
```
 Semver doesn't prevent this either! Let's continue with examples using the release schedule I mentioned above. Using the date-driven approach the major (non-BC) versions from different years would then take the form of: 15.5.1 (Released in 2015 on May 1st) 16.3.8 (Released in 2016 on March 8th) For the version from 2015 the minor versions (BC-compatible API changes) could be for example: 15. 1 .1 (Released 1st of January) 15. 2 .1 (Released 1st of February) 15. 3 .1 (Released 1st of March) etc. And respectively the patch releases (bug and security fixes) could be: 15.5. 1 (Released 1st of May) 15.5. 8 (Released 8th of May) 15.5. 15 (Released 15th of May) etc. 
```text
You can still think in terms of semantic versioning in Moodle, as Tim exaplains.
```
 This is not true. "There will be changes to API or UI" is not enough information for a plugin developer. There's a clear difference between changes that : Have been made in a BC-way Have not been made in a BC-way This is the idea behind Semver; It is able to communicate to the developer whether the API/UI changes have been made in a backwards compatible way or not. Moodle's current versioning fails to do this. And this causes extra work for plugin devs, as we currently need to manually check whether our plugins work in each X.Y release.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text: is not enough information for a plugin developer I don't think the version number itself can provide such information - be it semver or not. When we increase the major version number in Moodle (such as from 3.0 to 3.1), we simply reserve right to make non-bc changes (in the API, database structure or UI). On contrary, all changes should be considered as backwards-compatible on minor releases (such as from 2.9.1 to 2.9.2). I can't really see "clear difference" between what Moodle does and what semver does, unless I am missing something,

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text:
```text
all changes should be considered as backwards-compatible on minor releases (such as from 2.9.1 to 2.9.2).
```
 Yes, but isn't this just because the changes do not contain new features in the first place? At least according to the docs they don't: 
```text
Minor versions are released every two months, including both bugs and security issues fixed.
```
 So currently Moodle releases are either: Bug/security fixes New features (that can be BC or non-BC) What Semver does is that it uses three levels instead of just two: Bug/security fixes (version n.n. X ) New features that are BC (version n. X .n) New features that aren't BC (version X .n.n) If Moodle started using the three-level system, it would allow Moodle sites to get all the latest and greatest features (note: not just bug and security issues) from the newest n. X .n version without having to worry whether some of the installed plugins would get broken because of the upgrade. So that's what the goal would be; The ability to get new features without having to worry at all about backwards compatibility. This naturally does not get fixed just by changing the way how version number is incremented. (Maybe I was unclear about this earlier). Instead it would require Moodle to have separate git branches for each version (major, minor, patch). When producing new code, developer would choose the correct branch depending on whether the change is a fix, new BC feature or a new non-BC feature. I hope I'm making sense.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?
ResponsesInList.Text: The problem is that it makes a branch hell for devs, and makes documentation harder. You now have 3 levels of branches that have to be maintained: X-1.Y.z X-1.Y-1.z X-1.Y-2.z X.Y X.Y-1.z X+1.Y Plus, in the Moodle community particularly, this is probably of limited value. Most larger Moodle installs don't want mid-stream new features. Not only do they still have to test everything, but they have to update documentation, and training, etc. The marginal cost to test all their plugins to make sure they are still working in minimum when they only plan on updating once or twice a year anyways. The other thing this does is it makes it harder to jump to the X+1 release. Right now we move in small, steady jumps. Very few things break between each release, so the work is minimal. What would almost certainly happen is that people would never leave the X release to the X+1 because it will just be too much work. We saw that with 1.9, and you see it in other projects. The current system does a better job at keeping sites more current. The thing is, current Moodle numbering system already tells you that, when Y changes, they can't garantee that your plugins will continue to work, you have to test them, because there are almost always API changes in those releases. The only thing that really added confusion to the mix was the choice to go to 3.0 instead of 2.10. Because there are no plans for a major rework in the pipeline, it was decided that it was less cumbersome to let it roll forward to 3.0, and I agree. There is another way to look at it - The next major version is so different from 2.0, that it deserves it be a new major release, even though we have gotten there via evolution. While I get the benefits of semantic versioning, as both a plugin dev and a large site admin, I think it would just add workload and confusion with very little upside.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is Moodle using semantic versioning?

I like the idea of Moodle using semantic versioning too, but also think it's really difficult to view the whole of Moodle as a single API! What might be an interesting idea would be to use semver for the APIs that comprise Moodle individually. To give an example, I run a pretty large Moodle installation which currently has 80 non-core plugins. When we upgrade to a new version of Moodle each year, I spend pretty much an entire working month puzzling over upgrade.txt files, grepping for uses of functions that have changed or been deprecated, updating the code to the new API etc. It would be fantastic to be able to declare what API versions a plugin was written against and have Moodle indicate which had changed to a non-backwards-compatible version, and which might have new backwards-compatible functionality I might want to consider using. For example: 
```text
$plugin->dependencies = array (


    'core_block' => '2.3.5',  // Block API


    'core_cache' => '1.1.2',  // 
Cache
 API


    'core_dml'   => '1.0.0', // DML API


    'core_file'  => '1.0.1',  // File API


    'local_strathuserselect' => 2015052000,

);
```
 I realise this might be a fair amount of work to implement and keep up-to-date, so may not practically be worth doing, but it would be a useful feature for plugin developers. It certainly seems a more workable way of using semantic versioning in Moodle than trying to use it for the product as a whole.

ResponsesInList.Title: How to customize the signup form
ResponsesInList.Text: It took me awhile to find this, so I thought I would post how I customized the sign up/registration form. I already had a custom authentication plugin I created, but if you do do not have one you need to create one (I usually start with a copy of the email auth), and then set your site to use that authentication.  See https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Authentication_plugins Now, add a new function to override the default signup form.  I added mine under the can signup function function can_signup() { return true; } Add the new function by copying and pasting this under the can signup function: /*Override signup form*/ function signup_form() { global $CFG; require_once($CFG-> dirroot .'/auth/'.$this->authtype.'/signup_form.php'); return new login_signup_form(null, null, 'post', '', array('autocomplete'=>'on')); } Next, copy the signup_form.php file from the login folder into you new authentication folder and make any changes you want to there.

ResponsesInList.Title: Error code: storedfilecannotread
ResponsesInList.Text: I did something silly and wanted to share the fix in case someone else did the same thing. When you upload a file (e.g a scorm package) in Moodle through the UI it uses the Moodle file api to store it in moodledata/filedir and point to it in the moodle database table mdl_files. What I did was accidentally delete half of the filedir directory. The person who is responsible for backups realized after I did this that they had no backups. So when you clicked on a scorm activity link, for example, in the course you would see the following error: More information about this error Debug info: [ dataroot ]/filedir/ff/d9/ffd980468bb9a9d42e24991891182efb973eba94 Error code: storedfilecannotread Stack trace: line 454 of /lib/filestorage/stored_file.php: file_exception thrown line 2127 of /lib/filelib.php: call to stored_file->readfile() line 2491 of /lib/filelib.php: call to readfile_accel() line 1005 of /mod/scorm/lib.php: call to send_stored_file() line 4601 of /lib/filelib.php: call to scorm_pluginfile() line 37 of /pluginfile.php: call to file_pluginfile() We had the scorm files though. And so to fix this problem you should access the Moodle database and issue the following command (this sql is just for the scorm file fix): delete from mdl_files where contextid=(SELECT id FROM `mdl_context` WHERE instanceid=(SELECT id FROM `mdl_course_modules` where course=20 and module=18 and instance = (select id from mdl_scorm where name='[name of scorm activity]'))) just subsitute "name of scorm activity" with whatever that activity is named in teh course or database . . . "Module 1" for example. This deletes all the previously associated files in the file system associated with that scorm activity/contextid. Then you just turn on editing in the Moodle UI and re-upload the scorm package for the given activity. Then the link will work again. So this is how i rebuilt the filedir. Of course as I said above this is just for the scorms we had. If you uploaded anything else throught he Moodle UI it would be in the filedir too and therefore be broken.

ResponsesInList.Title: course backup and restore user data only
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, I have to do course backup on one site and restore it on another site. Due to size of course contents, we just wanted to do the backup of user data excluding the course contents. how we can do that using code. currently i am using the back_controller class such as $controller = new restore_controller($folder, $course_id, backup::INTERACTIVE_NO, backup::MODE_GENERAL, $userdoingrestore, backup::TARGET_NEW_COURSE); This includes the course contents as well, we want to do only user data course backup. Regards,

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: course backup and restore user data only
ResponsesInList.Text: You cannot do that, as Moodle would not know which activities the user data related to - for example the 3rd activity in the course might be a forum with id 5 on one site, but with id 238 on the other site. In theory, Moodle could try and guess based on activity order, activity type or activity name (all of which could change). In practice that would be very unreliable and Moodle has no support for doing so. If you really wanted to do this, then you'd need to write your own restore system from scratch  (there might be a few bits you could reuse, but all the activities assume that they will either restore just structure, or structure + user data).

ResponsesInList.Title: Reasons not to use database locking for cron?
ResponsesInList.Text:
Are there any good reasons to avoid db_record_lock_factory in favour of
file_lock_factory for cron job locking? (I'm having trouble working this
out from the documentation.) I'd assume that the performance will be a
lot worse, but the lock API documentation explicitly says "locking is not meant to be fast", so presumably this doesn't matter too much. The reason I'm asking is that we're (very occasionally) seeing cron jobs running twice at the same time and are concerned it might be something to do with file locking. As far as we can see, file locking is generally sound on our setup, but we might prefer to use database locking as it seems simpler and potentially more stable than relying on file locking across a cluster.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Reasons not to use database locking for cron?
ResponsesInList.Text: That really depends on your setup. The rule of thumb would be - if you have just one server instance for web and another for database setup cron on your web node. If you have multiple web servers behind load balancer for one moodle instance than add another server that will not be accessible from outside and will host cron process. That way you are sure that one and only one cron instance is run for particular setup.

ResponsesInList.Title: How to crash MS Edge in one easy step
ResponsesInList.Text: Last week, I received a somewhat puzzling report from a user who claimed that he couldn't open files from Moodle in Microsoft Edge.  Upon further investigation, I was able to determine that the trouble was with PDF files displaying embedded in the page: when you open one, Edge stops responding to user input.  You can scroll the page (but not the PDF) - but nothing else; no UI element within Edge will work, and clicking on links does nothing (except occasionally highlight the link).  If you have multiple tabs open and still have it set to warn when closing multiple tabs, attempting to close it via right-click on the taskbar button will pop up that confirmation box - but you can't interact with that, either!  The quickest way to kill Edge when it's in this state seems to be to drag the titlebar down to the bottom of the screen, though you can also use other methods such as ending the task in Task Manager. I was eventually able to track it down to Moodle's embed maximiser script (which resizes the embed to take up as much space as possible on the page).  That script sets the height and width of the embed to 0px briefly, so it can check the size of the page without it present; for some reason, this specific act puts Edge into the strange state where it refuses all input.  I've submitted a patch which instead uses display:none to make the embed take up no space while it calculates - MDL-51190 - which is currently awaiting peer review, but thought I'd post here in case anyone else has been scratching their heads over this issue.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to crash MS Edge in one easy step
ResponsesInList.Text: Did you also report this to Microsoft? (Mind you, I have no idea how you would do that.) It seems like a serious bug in Edge.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to crash MS Edge in one easy step
ResponsesInList.Text: I've been working on reducing it to a minimal case, so I can provide a demo with my report.  I've pretty much got it sorted, so I'll be reporting it to MS (somehow!) today.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to crash MS Edge in one easy step
ResponsesInList.Text: Edge falls over the edge in one easy step.

ResponsesInList.Title: How do I add a default timestamp in upgrade.php?
ResponsesInList.Text:
How can I add a default to a field that is a timestamp, so that if updates to the record don't include the column, it is automatically populated by the database engine? In mysql , the create for the column would be: 
```text
`time` timestamp NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP COMMENT 'event timestamp'
```
 In the install. xml file, timestamp isn't an allowed type so it uses datetime . 
```text
<FIELD NAME="time" TYPE="datetime" NOTNULL="true" DEFAULT="CURRENT_TIMESTAMP" SEQUENCE="false"/>
```
 XMLDB editor warns about this if the type is set to timestamp , even though lib/xmldb/xmldb_field.php seems to show knowledge of the  XMLDB_TYPE_TIMESTAMP field type. I used xmldb editor to generate the php. This generates the column as type "datetime", with the default set at "current_timestamp". Obviously it's getting this from the install.xml file. 
```text
  $table->add_field('time', XMLDB_TYPE_DATETIME, null, null, XMLDB_NOTNULL, null, 'CURRENT_TIMESTAMP');
```
 When upgrade.php is executed, it throws an error: 
```text
Debug info: Invalid default value for 'time'


time DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
```
 I'm having to create it without a default, then go in and alter the table by hand. Surely there's an official way?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How do I add a default timestamp in upgrade.php?
ResponsesInList.Text: You don't. ResponsesInList.Title: Should missing file exceptions just return 404s?
ResponsesInList.Text:
When I'm doing development with client code, and I don't have an up to date copy of their sitedata, I often run into missing file exceptions. Rsyncing 30GB+ isn't always practical. This can be quite annoying. Examples are editing course module settings when images in the description aren't present. Of course it shouldn't happen on actual production site because playing with sitedata is bad! I can get around the error by hacking the filelib temporarily. I'd like peoples opinions: Should this be a fatal exception? Or should filelib just return a 404 for missing files? 
```text
Can not read file, either file does not exist or there are 
permission
 problems

More information about this error
Debug info: [
dataroot
]/filedir/96/65/96656d3179a228823322761c3de1dad9b0a5a338
Error code: storedfilecannotread
Stack trace:

    line 187 of /lib/filestorage/stored_file.php: file_exception thrown
    line 881 of /lib/filestorage/stored_file.php: call to stored_file->update()
    line 424 of /lib/filelib.php: call to stored_file->set_source()
    line 178 of /course/modedit.php: call to file_prepare_draft_area()
```

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Should missing file exceptions just return 404s?
ResponsesInList.Text: Surely if you are working on a clone of the client's site, if you clone the database and the dataroot at the same time, that shouldn't happen (put it into maintenance mode before you make the clone so its not changing). If you clone the site code and the database, but not the data folder itself (or use an out of date copy of the data folder), then this issue is almost inevitable.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Should missing file exceptions just return 404s?
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, it is inevitable in the case of missing sitedata. But does it seem right that a web page breaks completely if a non essential file is missing, rather than just returning a 404 and showing a missing file icon in the page?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Should missing file exceptions just return 404s?
ResponsesInList.Text: Personally, I'd say the error message coming up provides far more information than a simple 404 page and may be important if the same error cropped up for someone with their site set up correctly, so taking that information away and providing just a 404 error page could lead to people who do have the correct sitedata folder (or at least, aim to have) not getting debug information to help solve an issue. Out of interest, what shows for a 'normal user' without debugging enabled? - I would say there is potentially a case to have some kind of 404 page without the debug stack trace for users who do not have debugging enabled, if the alternative is a plain white screen crash as sometimes happens with these 'fatal errors' For developers, I'd say the debug info is the right way to go, and not a simple 404 page.

ResponsesInList.Title: How can we improve the peer review process?
ResponsesInList.Text:
One of issues which came out of the really interesting discussion about code freeze was the problems of getting peer reviews completed. Having seen how that discussion evolved, I thought it was worth starting another. To start off with... we are definitely improving! In 2011/12 we did 769 peer reviews, 2012/13 1539 and in the last 12 months 2200 peer reviews have been completed. Much more important than that is that the quality of reviews is improving (at least from my perspective as an integrator). Twelve months ago we were still integrating code which had not been peer reviewed on a regular basis; today it's a rarity. Moodle code has never been as throughly reviewed as it does today. That said, we continue to have a massive backlog of issues waiting for peer review and we have an even more gigantic pile of patched issues which have not ever been looked at.
This is bad, i'm sure you know, but to reiterate: The longer an issue is delayed before integration, the bigger the chance it won't be relevant or conflict Contributors tend to be much more able to respond to review comments when initially submitting code You can get a new contributor 'hooked' by reacting quickly to their patch (it worked for me!) Here are some of the causes of this problem, as I see it: There is an incredible amount of code being created by the Moodle community and it's not as fun to review code as to write it! In Moodle HQ, we don't quite have the right processs/balance/prioritisation for managing peer reviews (in contrast to Integration Review, where we have a full-time team dedicated to the task). I don't think it is necessary/appropiate for the community to discuss this! I'm just acknowledging I don't think it is a perfect situation. There is a degree of expectation that Moodle HQ should be resonsible for all peer reviews. Developers don't feel knowledgeable enough about a code area to peer review many issues, so they ignore it. Some issues are so big/fundamental/controversial they get ignored because the peer reviewer wouldn't know the next step. Some issues are so in the wrong direction/quality they get ignored because it is quite difficult to give bad feedback. Some thoughts of mine: It could be beneficial to have a way of seperating the big/controversial/hard issues away from smaller ones. With the goal of processing the smaller ones as fast as possible (and getting a small number waiting in the queue). Ideally we'd also tell the developer of the issue that their issue is a trickier one to review and that they would expect delays. My argument against this is that I'm not sure if this triaging would just be moving the problem around. Somehow I would like to empower you to peer review something you are uncomfortable with, especially if the issue has been waiting for a while. There are many areas of Moodle which are not well understood by many people and by leaving the issue to someone else we don't help solve that. It's better the assignee gets some feedback, even if you are not a domain expert. (Note: this is kind of what the Integration team have to do on some issues on a weekly basis ) What are your thoughts?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can we improve the peer review process?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Dan, First thanks for the efforts of three people (Damyon, Dan, and Marina) in Moodle HQ reviewing my large change for 2.7! Second, I agree with the 'small change vs large change' and also 'not in my area' vs 'not that complicated anyway' issue. I wonder if there should even be different states or labels, like 'Waiting for peer review (anyone)' or 'Waiting for peer review (HQ)' (or 'Component maintainer' or something not necessarily HQ). Tim and I often review each others' small changes, hopefully this is useful, but for large changes it can be inappropriate especially as we obviously come from the same institution so are more likely to have the same take on things. In general while it would be great to have community contributions in peer review it seems harder to achieve especially for those of us who are doing this as part of our regular job. Say there is a simple issue waiting peer review, I could probably do the review, but unless it happens to be related to something my employer wants done, I can't really justify it. Even on a volunteer level the same thing probably applies - if I use glossary a lot and there's a minor bug I really want to fix, I'll submit a fix for the bug, but let's suppose there is something waiting in peer review about forum, I wouldn't have any interest or expertise in reviewing it (supposing I even see it). Evil thought: You could have some way that when you mark an issue waiting for peer review, if you then yourself peer-review some other issue (while waiting), your waiting issue gets a priority peer review tag or something... --sam

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can we improve the peer review process?
ResponsesInList.Text: Of course, when you say "There is a degree of expectation that Moodle HQ should be resonsible for all peer reviews." you forget about components like quiz/question where there is an active component maintainer. I manage to review 90+% of patches very quickly. However, once an issue has got stuck in limbo, it can sit there for a very long time. I think that is just me. I completely agree that quick turn-around on reviews is important for encoraging contributors. Working out any given change involes creating a certian amount of metal state to understand the code, and it is much easier to make any requested changes while you still remember all that. Similarly, if peer review something, and point out that changes are needed, it is easiest if those changes come back quickly for re-peer-review, while you still remember how the patch worked. So, quick turn arounds are important on both sides. It is certainly worth hilighing small changes. I have a proposal for that: CiBiT should not just add comments to issues. For an issue that gets reworked many times, it just adds lots of clutter. Instead I think we should have specific custom fields like: CiBoT status: [blank / all good / problems] CiBoT last results: [link to the smurf.html file] CiBoT commit checked: [commit hash of what was checked, as a link to github] CiBoT diff size: [ git diff --short-stat output] That last filed makes it easy to search for small changes. The other fields make it easy to see at a glance what the CiBoT status is, and avoid cluttering the comment history with this. If you ever need to see all the versions that were checked, the tracker keeps a full history of all fields.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can we improve the peer review process?
ResponsesInList.Text: I forgot one thing I wanted to say. Regarding " Some issues are so big/fundamental/controversial they get ignored because the peer reviewer wouldn't know the next step. " Any issue like that should not be up for peer review. Before any code was written there should have been a thread in a forum, that should have reached some sort of consensus. To put it another way, if I am responsible for peer reviewing something controversial, and the developer disagrees with me, then I don't want to have a two-person argument with the developer. I want to developer to start a forum thread to canvas more opinions. Hopefully, with enough eyes, a good solution can be found, or at least the least bad compromise.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can we improve the peer review process?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can we improve the peer review process?
ResponsesInList.Text: I think you could encourage more peer review by: Making it a bit more obvious that it is something you want developers to do Making it clear how to do it Providing easy access to a list of what needs reviewing. To be honest it never really occurred to me that I could be peer reviewing things - I guess the phrase comes with a certain weight of responsibility. This is linked to your point 3 but is more "am I qualified to do it" rather than "I'm not expected to do it". For my point 1 I just did some searching to find out how to peer review and found this: "The component lead should peer-review the change. If there is no component lead for an affected component, any other recognised developer may complete the peer review." From http://docs.moodle.org/dev/Process#Peer_review Which make it seem more like an exceptional event rather than something that is actively encouraged. For 2, the how to peer review checklist is good. For 3, I just went looking for tickets that needed peer reviewing. Although I could create my own filter in JIRA for tickets with status of Peer Review I eventually also found the Peer Review Dashboard , which is much more helpful. It was tucked away though (Under Tools > Find Dashboards > Search for "Peer Review"). I think it would be good to make it much more prominent. Simon

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can we improve the peer review process?
ResponsesInList.Text: I definitely agree that timeliness is critical to encourage engagement. It's discouraging as a dev to write up patches and features for Moodle and see them sit around for weeks or months (and then get bumped back to the next 6mo release cycle). It makes it harder to stay engaged. Part of the problem that I personally see if that it's not clear that me doing a peer review is actually helpful overall. Yes, it might catch things, but it doesn't really move the issue forward in the process. If I do a peer review, I can only either leave it in 'Waiting for peer review' status, or send it back to dev in progress. Since I don't have powers to send it to integration, it still has to sit around waiting for someone with the power to do so to mark it for integration. Maybe another ticket state, or a label, to indicate that peer review has been done, and it needs a less in-depth review by someone with power for submission. Basically, the bottle neck is sending for integration, as that is the part that has the fewest people who can contribute, but the process as it is laid out now tangles the peer review and the sending for integration into one apparent step. They should be disentangled (or the number of devs trusted to mark for integration should be expanded, especially since there is a more robust integration review process in place anyways).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can we improve the peer review process?
ResponsesInList.Text: Spot on, Eric - without a (standard) way to differentiate peer-reviewed tickets from ones which are still awaiting peer review (other than sending to integration, which as you say is a permission that not many people have), it doesn't seem as though it'd really help much.  In practice, it might be that once you post a comment with your peer review results, somebody from HQ / with permission to put it up for integration is more likely to see those results and push it along - but it'd be much more likely for that to happen if we could either update the ticket state (probably the preferable option) or add an agreed-upon tag in order to flag it as having been reviewed, as otherwise it'd rely on somebody with the power already being at least a watcher on the ticket (which isn't always the case). (Sorry if this is a bit of a jumbled mess - it's a quick brain dump before flying out the door well past usual home time!)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can we improve the peer review process?
ResponsesInList.Text: Yeah, I agree. I also think that the peer reviewer having a track record of saying 'this is ready for integration' at the right time would be a good way of determining if the peer reviewer has proven to know when something is ready and the ability to send for integration. In an ideal world everyone would be able to send for integration if they had been peer reviewed - the reason the permission is controlled is just so that we don't have an incredibly huge list of issues sent for integration which are unsuitable, waste time and mean good quality issues don't get processed. (Or the same problem as we have in peer review in integration review!). I plan to raise this at our next Integration team meeting. Thanks to Fréd for finding it.) We really need to sort out peer review.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: An example of how badly we suck at peer review
ResponsesInList.Text: "Peer review" is another phrase that can be used as a substitute for "Quality Control". From a systems perspective, It does not really matter who checks what, as long as they are competent to do the checking. It does matter how many layers of "peer review" you want to put into place. The more "peer review" the better the end product, as long as the peers are competent. Being in this position for something completely different, I know it is sometimes a nerve-wrecking experience to be reviewed, but it is an essential one. After all, higher standards of quality control are the end result and it is never, never personal. A possible problem I think I am seeing is that the frequency of releases and updates are not helping maintain high levels of quality control. Please, do not misunderstand or misinterpret me, the product is good so far, but for how much longer? If standards inadvertently slip, as Tim seems to be indicating, then small errors accumulate, and large errors result.  I am sure the testers, the Devs are all doing the best they can, but increasingly we are seeing complex systems collapse because of accumulated errors, even with high quality control standards. I suspect Moodle is no different. I would offer that the release schedule could be cut in half and the freed up time could be devoted to quality control of upcoming releases.  The community would not mind, I suspect, no-one is breaking their neck to have a buggy product. They would much rather a slower release of a healthy, tested and a fully integrated product.

ResponsesInList.Title: Develop Moodle 1.9 theme in 2.9
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello, I need to build a brand new custom moodle 1.9 theme. I have failed to create a moodle 1.9 website that functions. Should I choose to develop a new theme in the latest version of moodle, will it be compatible with moodle 1.9? Alternatively, can someone suggest how I might easily create a moodle 1.9 environment?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Develop Moodle 1.9 theme in 2.9
ResponsesInList.Text: Moodle 2.9 themes are not at all compatible with Moodle 1.9. You probably don't have much control over the situation, but Moodle 1.9 is now completely unsupported - no bug fixes, no security fixes and (in pretty much all cases) no fixes from 3rd-part plugin developers to support it. The first thing that should happen is for the site you are working with to upgrade to Moodle 2.9 (via Moodle 2.2). As for setting up Moodle 1.9, it should be more or less the same as setting up a Moodle 2.9 site. As a quick experiment, I just tried an install based on some M1.9 code I had lying around and it worked fine, apart from a few debugging warnings, on the same dev box I've got all my other Moodle sites on (in case it helps: Debian Linux + Apache webserver + PHP 5.6 + MySQL 5.5.44).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Develop Moodle 1.9 theme in 2.9
ResponsesInList.Text: Not only did themes change entirely between Moodle1.9 and Moodle2.0 but they have been constantly developing and improving with every version since then. So no, as Davo says, you cannot create a 1.9 theme on Moodle2.x You can set up 1.9 in the same way as 2.x on a local computer to develop a theme. You may then be able to find some useful themes in the OLD themes list https://moodle.org/mod/data/view.php?id=6552 and old 1.9 themes documentation at https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Themes_1.9 However, please bear in mind that both Moodle1.9 and its themes are unsupported and the best solution to your issue, as Davo suggests, would be to get the site upgraded - both for the sake of the features, the support and also the security fixes that have gone on over the last few years.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Can't get scheduled tasks to work in plugin.
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi I think it is bug in Moodle, scheduled tasks implemented in local plugins are not performed by cron job core\plugininfo\local does not overwrite get_enabled_plugins method, it returns NULL for all local plugins get_next_scheduled_task method checks if plugin is enabled, if ($plugininfo) { if (!$task->get_run_if_component_disabled() && !$plugininfo->is_enabled()) { $lock->release(); continue; } } is_enabled() returns NULL for all local plugins so task is not performed

ResponsesInList.Title: Common Field mdl_logstore_standard_log and mdl_resource
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi there, I need to create query that can get data from mdl_logstore_standard_log and mdl_resource to build a new table. But I couldn't find common field between those tables. Does anyone know about this? Or do you have some references about the scheme? Your answer will be very helpful for me. Thank you.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Common Field mdl_logstore_standard_log and mdl_resource
ResponsesInList.Text: If your code is within Moodle, make sure you read up on using the API to access logs ( https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Logging_2#Reading_API ). In mdl_logstore_standard, there are two fields contextlevel and contextinstanceid - if the contextlevel is 50, then this represents a course module, so the contextinstanceid will be the id of the table mdl_course_modules. In mdl_course_modules, the 'module' field refers to an id in the table mdl_modules - this tells you the type of module this refers to. In mdl_course_modules, the 'instance' field refers to an id in the table mdl_NAMEOFMODULE - where NAMEOFMODULE is the name of the module you discovered by looking in mdl_modules. e.g. if 'module' refers to 'resource', then 'instance' is the id in the table 'mdl_resource'. That should be enough information to do what you were asking.

Re: JS reference error regarding external library with 2.9
ResponsesInList.Text: I had similar problems with Generico and VideoEasy and PoodLL in Moodle 2.9. So I suspect that you are experiencing what I did. The thing is that in Moodle 2.9 require.js is available to load modules via AMD. If your modules are not AMD modules that is fine. However many third party libraries actually check if this is an AMD environment or not. I experienced this with literally canvas,  jquery ui and a few other libraries. If they detect the availability of require.js they switch to using an anonymous define when they start. Require.js needs scripts that use anonymous defines, to be loaded via AMD, ie by require.js. Otherwise it conflicts. So you need to switch from YUI to AMD if you want to use those libraries. Or hack the library so that it doesn't put itself into AMD /anonymous define mode. (I played with that but thought better of it.)

ResponsesInList.Title: Odp: Re: JS reference error regarding external library with 2.9
ResponsesInList.Text: Thank you very much for helping me out. Indeed, c3's discovery of AMD mode turned out to be the source of the problem. For now, I used the latter solution, i.e. disarming AMD checking in c3 and everything works again. Of course it's just a temporary workaround before I rewrite my plugin's js scripts according to the new guidelines for Moodle 2.9+.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backup and restore including files
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Anthony, the "unknown_context_mapping" error happens when, on restore, the mapping between the original context of the module (in the backup file) and the new one (belonging to the created new module by restore) cannot be found. And that's one strange problem, as far as contexts are handled automatically (without developer's action) by backup & restore. So I'd start doing something like this: 1) Try the restore without files. Just comment the add_related_files() and restore. Does it work? Any other error? 2) Examine the backup code of the module and the results generated within the .mbz file. It should help to clarify if something is wrong @ source (your module/backup implementation or backup core stuff doing something wrongly). 3) Examine/debug the restore code and its execution, to see if the (automatic) points where the contexts are created are working or no and why you module misses the mapping commented above. If you want / can, feel free to create one CONTRIB or MDL issue about it, with all the info, ideally also with the module's code (or send it to me by email) and one backup example file. That's all I can say based in the error given, surely with more info... we'll be able to advance. Hope it helps, ciao
