ResponsesInList.Title: Why client side developing should get more attention
ResponsesInList.Text: I'll start with the obvious by declaring this is my own opinion and I'll be happy for every feedback regarding any mistake on my part. I have been developing for Moodle for the past couple of years. I started writing component for our version at the time (1.9) and moved on through the migration procedure into 2.5 and now 2.7. Throughout this it became very obvious that while plenty of work has been made on the server side, the client side received - at least most of the times - a little more than the minimal attention just to make it work the way it should. The result was (and in some placed still is) a somewhat rigid and a heavy looking interface. Now, the immediate response would be that this is a system dedicated for learning and not playing and I agree, I have no intention to imply we should redesign everything according to the latest fad, I simply believe that good UX can go a long way. For example I can bring the implementation of bootstrap that made a big impact. Just compare it to the pre-bootstrap Moodle and see for yourself the benefits of a more flexible display. However, this is still a use of a third-party code, the state of mind appears to remain almost the same as in 1.9. For example, I can bring the discussion about the end of YUI here , where some of the opinions were to just use the most basic JS and nothing more. This alone showed me that JS is regarded as nothing more than a tool for enabling and disabling some fields. I'm currently working on a component that relies heavily on client side code for AJAX , displaying and general usability . It's a little bit more complicated than server side coding in the matter of cross platform compatibility and security, but the results are quite worth it. Not only does it save some server processing time by moving it to the browser, the workflow can become simpler and sometimes faster and yes, more appealing for the eye. One of the major benefits of replacing YUI with JQuery - according to latest discussions - is that it will bring more developers with client side orientation that will only do good for the user experience. So this is my opinion in a nutshell, I'll be happy for your response if only to know if I'm on the right track here.

ResponsesInList.Text: i would imagine you will see more focus on client side, when html5 gets finalized for a database installed inside the browser, that websites can use to store info into easily and retrieve it easily.  and in that being to upload entire site template to the user browser database, and using ajax calls for various variables. others words almost treating entire site like a live video conference with text chat, audio and video, and screen sharing.  and only needing to update stuff for variables vs needing to push/pull entire html code. the exception being... quizes or like, were user is not suppose to see certain things. do you want them to have an open book quiz? or trying to force students to answer directly without access to anything. do you want anyone to see options for site admin menu? most likely not. so were do you want stuff split up and how should it be broken up? the other issue is complying with disability act's,  and folks using screen readers. ""needing pure html that is pushed to the browser"" vs being able to use javascript . there is also issue with different languages... and moodle has kept "buttons" down to a very min. and uses text'ed links vs a button like graphic. due to one word in one language maybe "yes"  could be "asdfjasdfla" long in another. and with buttons being created on the fly. does cause some extra "processing power" if made on the client computer. i would imagine there be plenty of schools / library running older slower computers. ajax is not all that is cracked up to be. if entire site template is downloaded to client computer. and everything is done with ajax. one little bug. could cause entire site to go down.  not to mention, ya just gotta love them web browsers and there garbage collection *big frown*. and the need to refresh entire page, and pull all back from sever. to clear out any bugs / issues. ============ moodle provides a long list of "pre-built form elements" with ajax and everything mixed in. ============ how many "client sides" is wanted? pure html push to browser, screen readers. smart phones touch screen for laptops and lcd screens full ajax with mix'ed in pure push html for certain things (say quizzes, and site admin menu). pure html push to browser, with some ajax for certain things to reduce server load, and bandwidth load. server just pushes min amount of html, and client is required to have its own "software" per say. to interpret what is coming from the server?  (more like a multi player game) large initial client side download , and then just min amount of info passed between client/server. (variables, role/ context info, question/answer info) vs (charter just shot gun, character just moved x,y from xx,yy) ================ for distance learning... folks still use dial up!!!! i would love a full ajax or game client environment. vs twiddling my thumbs as i wait for a page load. one set down, waiting for i don't 4 to 20 minutes... and ready set go... only issue is javascript, and easily hacking it... and if page is SSL... ya in for some more trouble.. :/ then again could be a bonus pending on how ya look at it. the only issue with full ajax / game client like front end. is duplicating a good amount of all the back end functions, that sets on the server, on the client side. being an open source, seems like a lot of extra work. when trying to add features is higher up on the todo list. vs client side. more so when considering the lowest common denominators.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why client side developing should get more attention
ResponsesInList.Text: Actually I didn't mean to go as far as to suggest a full HTML5 / AJAX interface. What I meant is, we should make more use of what our JS library (YUI for now) has to offer us that we hardly use. For example: Add AJAX-dedicated elements in a form. Add more advanced form display rules, like 'hideIf' to toggle display of different sections when checking options. Like above, set 'expandIf' for header elements. Add more dynamic displays. Lightbox gallery is the most "dynamic" component I've encountered so far. And so on... These are just examples from the top of my head, it's less about adapting to a new technology and more about accepting and using what is already here.

ResponsesInList.Title: Password generation and password policy
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi! I noticed that moodle (2.7.1+) generates passwords for new users not quite in accordance to site password policy. Example policy is: minpasswordlength 8 minpassworddigits 1 minpasswordlower 1 minpasswordupper 1 minpasswordnonalphanum 0 But moodle generates 10 symbols length password with some non-alpha symbols. I think this is due to generate_password function logic (which is called by setnew_password_and_mail function). $password = str_shuffle (substr(str_shuffle ($passwordlower), 0, $lower) . substr(str_shuffle ($passwordupper), 0, $upper) . substr(str_shuffle ($passworddigits), 0, $digits) . substr(str_shuffle ($passwordnonalphanum), 0 , $nonalphanum) . substr(str_shuffle ($passwordlower . $passwordupper . $passworddigits . $passwordnonalphanum), 0 , $additional)); $additional is calculated as $maxlen - $total. $maxlen is defaults to 10, $total is sum of minpassworddigits+minpasswordlower+minpasswordupper+minpasswordnonalphanum. So in our case $additional is 7. Thus we have additional shuffled symbols with possibility of non-alpha inside. I understand that logically min* parameters does not means strict numbers of symbols, but how we can exclude, for example, non-alpha symbols from password generation? Thank you in advance.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Password generation and password policy
ResponsesInList.Text: As you said, the minimums given do not put any upper limit on the number of characters of a particular type being in the generated password (0 means 'does not have to contain', rather than 'should not contain'). Without changing the code, there is no way to exclude non-alpha symbols from the generator. If you are willing to change the code, then you could add the following, just before the line you have indicated: if (!$nonalphanum) { $passwordnonalphanum = ''; } This reduces the pool of available non-alphanum characters for password generation to nothing, if there are none required in the password. This might be something to consider adding to future versions of Moodle (as you wouldn't be the first person to find this a problem).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Wny are there enrolment plugins instead of a function for enrolment and a function for unenrolment?
ResponsesInList.Text: Q. Why are there enrolment plugins? A. Like so many aspects of Moodle, the plugins allow the functionality to be extended - if a particular organisation wants a new method of enroling/unenroling users from courses, then they can write one, instead of having to modify core code to get what they want. A single function call with a parameter would be fine, if you could somehow come up with a definitive list of every possible way that every possible organisation could possibly ever want to manage the enrolment / unenrolment of users on their courses. Q. How can I find out which plugin should be doing the unenrolment? A. If your web service is the main way of managing enrolment in your organisation's courses, then you should already know which enrolment method you are using (probably 'manual'). If, for some reason, you do not know what method a user is using and want to force them to be unenroled from the course regardless, then you can look up which method was used (and bear in mind, some methods, such as LDAP might automatically re-enrol them on the next updated, or a user might get upset if a course allowed PayPal enrolment, they've paid for the course and then the webservice has removed them). To help you along the way of finding out which plugin has been used, look in the DB tables mdl_user_enrolments and mdl_enrol. mdl_enrol will tell you the enrolment methods available for the course you are looking at (courseid), the name of the plugin (enrol) and the id of that instance of the enrolment plugin (id) (plus lots of other details). Looking in mdl_user_enrolments you can find a combination of the userid you are looking for and the enrolid you looked up in mdl_enrol. That will tell you what method was used to enrol the user, so you now know which method to call to unenrol the user. You may even find some helpful functions to do a lot of this for you, if you look in enrol/locallib.php.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Getting student count
ResponsesInList.Text:
you have to use this sql query 
```text
SELECT COUNT(*)

FROM mdl_course AS course 
JOIN mdl_enrol AS en ON en.courseid = course.id
JOIN mdl_user_enrolments AS ue ON ue.enrolid = en.id
JOIN mdl_user AS user2 ON ue.userid = user2.id
```

ResponsesInList.Title: should 'save and return' return to ID?
ResponsesInList.Text:
if you edit a mod and select 'save and return to course' you are returned to view.php with a first parameter of the course id and the second parameter of the section ID containing the mod you edited, like this: 
```text
/course/view.php?id=239&section=1
```
 In a course with more than a few items in a section if you're editing a lower listed mod (scrolled down the page) then you have to scroll to return to that item, potentially a minor inconvenience if you want to see the results of your edit (on a label) or edit the next resource in the page cascade. Every mod on the page is given a unique ID which seems to be based on its unique id in the Moodle system, meaning that it's well-formed semantic HTML and we should be able to use that ID selector for in-page scrolling.  I suggest that we should append the ID selector to the return URL like this: 
```text
http://vle.tiseagles.com/course/view.php?id=239&section=1#module-27191
```
 It is safe and valid to pass the hash in the URL even if the id is unknown, meaning that this: 
```text
http://vle.tiseagles.com/course/view.php?id=239&section=1#
```
 is still valid.  It seems trivial to add this to the return url of /course/modedit.php by adding to the $data object something like $data->idr = '#module=' . $cm->id; in the $update == true section and then adding $data->idr to the return URL when constructed and I propose that we should do that. However, I haven't investigated this fully, but it looks like the function course_url() might need to have a modid added to the $options array optional parameter added to direct to a specific module and that might affect course formats and even moodle_url() (I haven't investigated fully). I still advocate that this would be a good thing.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: should 'save and return' return to ID?
ResponsesInList.Text:
It is not quite as simple as you're suggesting because the course
format can be in single-page view in which case currently the section is
done using a # anchor so that would need to be replaced. No reason the logic can't be done, just to note. Possible argument against, again when using single-page view: # anchors scroll so that the anchor is exactly at the top of the screen. Assuming that sections have a reasonable length (< 1 screen) which should be true in most cases, it would be desirable to view the entire section so as to show the resource in context . In other words if you have a section like this: Week 3 - Read something - Write in a forum - Do this quiz then it pretty much makes sense for a return link for the last 'Do this quiz' line to also show the entire contents of week 3. I don't necessarily follow that argument, but it's something to consider. On the other hand, I think 'save and return' directly to the module link would have a slight accessibility benefit as well as being useful in the case of giant sections. --sam

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: should 'save and return' return to ID?
ResponsesInList.Text: Have a look in the quiz/question code. Specifically look in question/qengine.js at M.core_scroll_manager. We use that when a student is interacting with a question in the middle of a long page of a quiz, to take them back to exactly where they were when the page reloads. That works nicely. Consider moving that code out of question/ and into lib/yui, and reusing it.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: should 'save and return' return to ID?
ResponsesInList.Text: On the other hand. If you have sections that long that you need this, you may also want to re-think the overall layout and the design of the content structure in the course. ResponsesInList.Title: Help me understand inheritance and overriding in plugins
ResponsesInList.Text: I've realised that I don't understand inheritance and overriding in plugins, and I hope someone can help. Let's suppose that there's an existing Moodle plugin which I want to use, but need to change the behaviour of very slightly. As an example, assume it's the email-based self-registration plugin ( https://docs.moodle.org/28/en/Email-based_self-registration ). Now, I know from looking at the source that this is implemented by class auth_emailadmin . And I know that it's got various methods: can_signup, user_signup, user_update_password, and so on. And assume I'm entirely happy with how those work, but I want to rewrite the user_authenticated_hook method so that it sends authorisation information to a server on my domain . It seems to me that a bad way to do this would be for me to copy all the code from auth_emailadmin into my own plugin and then modify its user_authenticated_hook method. It's bad because if the Moodle developers ever update auth_emailadmin, my plugin won't get those updates. It seems that a better way for me to write my plugin would be for me to define a new class auth_jocelyns_plugin that extends auth_emailadmin and that defines just one method: user_authenticated_hook with my own code in it. Is that the recommended means? I can't find any guidance in the documents about how to write plugins. One possible problem is that my Moodle would need to have the code for both auth_jocelyns_plugin and auth_emailadmin. But it would somehow have to be told never to execute the second except as part of the first. The question occurred to me when I was thinking about Felipe Carasso 's Login/Logout user redirect plugin, and how it works. I need to write a plugin that does something rather similar, but I don't understand how Moodle works with subclasses of plugins.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Help me understand inheritance and overriding in plugins
ResponsesInList.Text: Two things. Firstly, in order to implement your functionality "to contact an authorisation server elsewhere on our system whenever a user successfully logs in" you may better want to implement a local plugin that adds event observer for the `\core\event\user_loggedin` event. See API docs for details. Regarding the ability to subclass existing plugins, it's generally not that easy. Generally, Moodle plugins can't be simply subclassed and expected to work as-is. In certain cases (and auth plugins are probably that case) you can subclass an existing plugin. Or better, make your own plugin to re-use some parent's plugin functionality. But given how plugins store their settings, how individual instances are enabled/disabled etc., it requires quite a deep research of how the communication between the core and the given plugin type actually works.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: $DB->get_records() returns only 1 row
ResponsesInList.Text: Moodle expects the first column returned to be a unique ID; if your view is returning the same value for the first column in each row, this is why - as the first column is treated as the key of the array when building the resultset internally.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: $DB->get_records() returns only 1 row
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Perry, Perhaps you could paste the code that you've tried here so that we can have a look and point you in the right direction? You say you're trying to match all rows in the table with the ID specified. Typically IDs are unique so I assume that you're not matching the ID field but another field. If you are matching on IDs, and you have multiple rows which have the same value in the 'id' field, then this is your problem. Because of the way in which recordsets are converted into records by $DB->get_records(), the first field (typically id) is used as the array key in you list of records. If all of the results have the same id, then they will all be placed into the same key and keep getting overwritten. I would recommend increasing your debugging level as this will tell you about some common problems. If you really do need to return multiple records with the same first field value, there are a couple of options to you: 1) use recordsets instead (don't forget to close the recordset when you're done with it). These are iterators rather than an array so you can arrange them into your own datastructure but you cannot treat the in quite the same way; 2) use get_records_ sql and have the first field return a concatenation of the unique data items. E.g. 'id || "_" || userid' Hope this helps, Andrew

If you do have a unique first column (which is almost always the case in Moodle, since every table has a primary key that is a single integer) then it is very nice that get_records returns you an array where the array keys are that primary key. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No settings option in local plugin
ResponsesInList.Text:
Your `$settings` variable holds a newly created settings page. You still have to attach that page as a node in the admin settings tree. Try to add something like 
```text
$ADMIN->add('localplugins', $settings);
```
 to make your settings page appear at Site administration / Plugins / Local plugins. As far as I know, local plugins are queried as the last ones when populating the admin tree so they can attach their settings to any other existing node. IIRC there should be no need to bump the plugin version.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why is dangerous add columns to core tables?
ResponsesInList.Text: Ok, I ask a more specific question... Can I rely on the immutability of core tables within a major version? If yes, why should I be afraid of making a *personal* and *not shared* extension? Another question, how can be changed tables in a major upgrade?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why is dangerous add columns to core tables?
ResponsesInList.Text: As a policy, Moodle core tables are not changed on stable branches. During the major version upgrade (i.e. from one stable branch to another, such as from 2.7.x to 2.8.y) the core tables can be eventually changed in any way, usually without explicit note in the release notes. However, I really think that keeping your data in an own plugin's scope is much cleaner and more maintainable solution for the future.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why is dangerous add columns to core tables?
ResponsesInList.Text: Please understand it's really difficult to answer such question. Who knows what would happen to core tables in the future? Even if tables like `mdl_user` are pretty stable, the cleaner solution is to keep data in their owner's scope. Your hack can work for years with no problems. But that does not make it a good solution. In programming, "it seems to work" is just not enough IMHO . It's your site and your responsibility. You can hardly expect core developers telling you it's OK and safe to modify core tables. p.s. look into `lib/db/upgrade.php` and search for methods like `drop_table()` to get an idea what's happening during major upgrades.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why is dangerous add columns to core tables?
ResponsesInList.Text: I have developed number of modules,blocks,plugins for moodle/totara. There are some rules we follow to make code scalable and easy to maintain. One of those rules is to never touch core tables. I have done some mistakes before when I was new to moodle coding and I directly edited core code or added fields to core tables. Have had issues while upgrading or testers found issues during System test/UAT and many times after we go live. It becomes difficult to fix and also while upgrading to later versions it could take lot of your time to make sure this change is not affecting anywhere else. I suggest if you need to make any hacks to core functionality it is easier to create a plugin within /local/, For eg-/local/<pluginname>_extension. Within the folder create a /db/ folder which can have install. xml (which is generated via xmldb-editor if you need to add some tables), upgrade.php etc scripts. You could also write some code for various customization related to core module within this local plugin. So, this would mean minimal core hacks, and doesn't involve any risk.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using Composer Dependencies
ResponsesInList.Text: Generally, composer in Moodle is only used to install Behat + PHPUnit for developers. Also the only automatic class loading built in to Moodle (that I am aware of) is that which uses the 'classes/' subdirectories within individual plugins. The usual way of handling requirements of 3rd-party libraries in Moodle is to include the library in a subdirectory of the plugin (I'm not arguing this is, necessarily, a good way to handle dependencies, but Moodle originally pre-dates composer by nearly 10 years and can currently be installed without needing to set up composer).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using Composer Dependencies
ResponsesInList.Text: There is a proposal to use Composer to install Moodle itself https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=275466

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using Composer Dependencies
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm not an expert in this area (read: I know nothing about it and I am just guessing) but I am afraid that the autoloading in Moodle has been implemented differently from what http://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-4/ says. Moodle autoloader expects that classes are provided either by the Moodle core itself (and are located in lib/classes/ of Moodle core) or by individual plugins (and can be found in the classes/ directory of that particular plugin). The first element is supposed to contain the component frankenstyle name, not the "vendor namespace".

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using Composer Dependencies
ResponsesInList.Text: Actually - this is not a bad way at all of including this library. Most libraries ship with their own solution for autoloading - either a separate autoloader, or a file containing a big list of includes. In the case of composer dependencies, composer itself generates the autoloader file - so including this file is all you need to do. Moodle relies on it's own custom autoloader, but it expects classes to exist in certain folders and have a certain naming convention, so it's unlikely to ever be able to load anything but Moodle classes. If you wanted to e.g. upload your plugin to the plugins DB - you would have to copy the composer dependencies into your plugin and update the paths etc - because you must keep all of your plugins code inside the plugin folder. Cheers - Damo

ResponsesInList.Title: Need Help Writing SQL Report with # of Teacher Posts
ResponsesInList.Text:
Greetings! I'm using the Dashboard in Moodle to run the SQL reports and have hit a snag.  I am searching for a report that returns the course name, discussion forum name, teacher name, and # of posts. I have a report that returns the course name, discussion forum name, # of posts but not specific to the teacher (role).  Can anyone help improve this SQL report. 
```text
SELECT c.shortname,f.name,
(SELECT COUNT(fp.id) FROM mdl_forum_discussions fd JOIN mdl_forum_posts AS fp ON fd.id = fp.discussion WHERE f.id = fd.forum) AS Posts

FROM mdl_forum AS f 
JOIN mdl_course AS c ON f.course = c.id

WHERE `type` != 'news'
AND name NOT LIKE '%question%'
AND name NOT LIKE '%introduction%'
AND category = 338
ORDER BY c.shortname
```

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Need Help Writing SQL Report with # of Teacher Posts
ResponsesInList.Text: Achieving this purely in single SQL query is not trivial. If you can afford some simplification, you could join the `role_assignments` table and check for users that have the given role explicitly assigned at the course context level. That is the most common case (user enrolled as a teacher to the course) but it does not take into account other eventual aspects (such as enrolment status or the role assigned at other context levels). Other approach could be to use `get_role_users()` for each course. But that does not scale nicely (it executes SQL query for each course in the loop) so it depends on how performance is important for you (i.e. how your dashboard is displayed and when/how often). You may want to cache the returned list of teachers in courses. The conceptually cleaner (yet less pragmatic) solution might be to use `get_enrolled_sql()` with the `$withcapability` parameter provided (probably UNION'ed across the courses). The code should never check against roles, only against capabilities.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: 2 moodle code in one server
ResponsesInList.Text: Vineeth, in the directory tree you should have something like moodle23 and moodle27. The code for each version goes into the respective directory. The database created for the moodle23 directory should be something like "moodle23" and for the moodle27 directory, it should be "moodle27". On installation, when it asks for the name of the database to be created, put in the name for the code version used. I suspect that what you have done is to use the more generic "moodle" database name for both of them. Do not assume that the installation will automatically look for the right database, you have to point it in the right direction. As Severin has said, make sure the config.php file is correctly identifying the right database and moodledata directory for that version. What he did not say was that you can manually edit the config.php file to point to the right database and moodledata directory. Just change the names in the file to look something like: In one config.php file, $CFG->dbname    = 'moodle27'; === === $CFG-> wwwroot = 'http://path/to/moodle27/moodle27'; $CFG-> dataroot = 'C:/path/to/server/moodledata27'; and in the other.... $CFG->dbname    = 'moodle23'; === === $CFG->wwwroot   = 'http://path/to/moodle23/moodle23'; $CFG->dataroot  = 'C:/path/to/server/moodledata23'; That should solve the immediate problem. The other problem you may find is that if you  log into one while the other is open, you get errors, and dumped out of the first one, make sure your cookies reflect the version of the Moodle you are using, so add the prefix of mdl23_ and mdl27_ respectively. This is how I set up v2.4, 2.7. 2.8. 2.81, Moodles on my private server, how I am practicing upgrading for the v2.4 Moodles I am administering. (It is getting a bit messy but the v2.4 is going in the new year, they are being replaced by the v2.81 I think it will be....maybe.)

ResponsesInList.Title: Cache data source aggregation - do we want it?
ResponsesInList.Text:
There is about a little known, largely undocumented cache code feature - data source aggregation.
Data sources can be used by cache code in Moodle to automatically generate missing data. Such that when something is requested from the cache but isn't in there if a data source is specified it will be initialised and the cache code will try to get the missing data from that.
Data source aggregation allows for multiple data sources to be created, and when initialising a cache a specific loader aggregate can be requested. MDL-47832 We have found that data source aggregate functionality has been broken for a long time, and appears to have never really worked well are there are two options before us: We fix it. We remove it. We have code for both, we just need to decide.
The preference at the moment is to remove it, we would do so without deprecating it as its broken and likely unused. It will also help to keep the cache code slim and in a very small way help performance.
Do you have an opinion on this, do you use this functionality in a cache you have written (or are trying to use it) and really if you would like to see this functionality remain we'd like to hear from you.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Cache data source aggregation - do we want it?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Sam. Thanks for raising this and letting us involved in this decision. Just noting there is a use case and more comments in the tracker that put this into the context .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Cache data source aggregation - do we want it?
ResponsesInList.Text: As already complemented in the tracker: this seems like an over-complicated feature that no-one acutally needs. Let's kill it and simplify that code. That can only improve performance. (It seems like a very clever feature, but probaby overengineered for what we need.)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Get all courses for a user
ResponsesInList.Text: You could write your own function to do it, just getting the data out of the database yourself. Example: SELECT c.* FROM {role_assignments} r INNER JOIN { context } x ON r.contextid = x.id INNER JOIN {course} c ON c.id = x.instanceid WHERE x.contextlevel = 50 AND r.userid = ? AND c.visible = 1 ORDER BY c.fullname ASC Passing in the id of the user as the parameter. You could then change the query slightly to get only courses where they are a Teacher or Student or Course Creator, etc... by adding in another where clause, e.g. AND r.roleid = 5 Would be only where they are a student on the course. You can lookup which ids correspond to which roles in the mdl_role table

ResponsesInList.Title: Multiple Agency Installation
ResponsesInList.Text: First off let me start by saying this isn't a duplicate of the numerous other posts floating around concerning multi-tenancy in moodle as this instance is slightly different. I have spent the past couple of weeks researching the different architecture paradigms that allow an individual to have multiple moodle sites running off of a single codebase (such as having multiple virtualhosts and config files, or using remote-learner's Elis plugin, etc), however I'm not certain these will work for this particular situation. What we are trying to accomplish is an "Enterprise" version of moodle(with Elis) that will allow for separation of agencies. For example if a user from agency1 logs in they will only have access to agency1's courses and users while being unaware that the system supports other agencies. If this was all we were seeking to accomplish, using multiple virtalhosts and config.php files would be sufficient, however there is another catch. While agency1 is unable to see agencies 2 - 4, they may wish to create a course that must be completed by ALL agencies. If we went with the multiple virtualhosts and config.php files we would still be running individual databases to store the information for each agency, therefore there would be no cross functionality for users. A user would need to be registered on each moodle installation to be able to take courses assigned by that particular agency. It sounds like what we are needing is a single installation that breaks the different agencies up into "UserSets" where there is a centralized database that all of the agencies are using. This is where Remote Learner's ELIS plugin is said to excel. It gives the administrator the ability to create multiple usersets and then lock specific users down to these usersets. Users within a userset then operate unaware that there are other agencies using the same system. From what I can gather Elis should work to solve this case if we included a "global" userset that every agency would have access to to push out global classes to all of the users of the system while keeping their agency specific courses hidden. What concerns me however about Elis is the scalability. Once the system grows to several thousand users, I can see the single moodle database becoming so slow it would be almost unusable. Therefore I am leery about using Elis on a large scale. Would anyone have any ideas about how to handle this situation? Am I being paranoid about using Elis? At this point any feedback would be great, even if it's "OMG Don't do that!".

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Multiple Agency Installation
ResponsesInList.Text: I don't know much about ELIS itself, but it sounds from your comments as though you have done your research and that is the tool that will meet your requirements - your question then really seems to be about whether your database/infrastructure will manage the size of installation you want, rather than the ability to split it into 'agencies'. 'Several thousand users' - as in users enrolled on your Moodle site or are you expecting several thousand concurrent users? Moodle is used to support institutions which have multiple tens of thousands of users and higher, and its a case of getting that architecture right, so hopefully Tim or someone from the OU, or one of the other large scale users will be able to respond to you as to how they do it. You might even want to sepak directly to RL themselves to see if they have any information about scale or clients you can talk to about their experiences. Might this thread be of some use? https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=214680

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Making forms that aren't so vertical

ResponsesInList.Title: What would be an ideal Moodle hackfest for you?
ResponsesInList.Text: In recent years, it became quite common that there are so called Moodle hackfests (or developer days/sessions) happening typically as a part of Moodle moots or as stand-alone events. Hackfest is generally an open session for developers to meet face to face and brainstorm the future Moodle development. I was lucky to be able to attend some of them and I always felt big potential of them. These developer sessions can have various format and atmosphere, depending on many things. For those who are organising such an event, it might be useful to know what participants would actually like to see and do there. So I decided to open this discussion to collect recommendations and ideas on how to use the given time in an effective way that would be both useful (in terms of outputs) and entertaining for the participants. If you were attending a Moodle hackfest as a developer, what format would suit you the best? Should it be more like an (un)conference with plenary talks and mini-presentations? Or rather a round table format for discussing things? Bit of both? Something else? Should it be one stream or rather divided into groups focused on particular topics? Would it be good to have time for actual prototype coding there? Or better use the limited time for discussions and leave the coding for later?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What would be an ideal Moodle hackfest for you?
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for this post David We are considering including a Hackfest into the next Moodle Moot here in New Zealand - so I will be interested to see what people say here

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What would be an ideal Moodle hackfest for you?
ResponsesInList.Text: For anyone who has not been to a hackfest before, they normally involve more yacking than hacking. That is people talking to each other. That is not unreasonable, since you can write code any time, but talking to other Moodle developers face-to-face is something you can't do often. I also don't think there should be much, if any plenary talks or mini-presentations. Hackfests should be workshops where everyone participates, not one person at the front talking. I think the best-organised hack-fest I went to was the one in Edinburgh last year. It used an organised unconference structure: At the start we spent some time writing things we wanted to talk about on post-it notes. These were stuck on the wall grouped by theme. Then we were all given a certain number (4? 6?) sticky dots which we could stick on the topics we wanted to be part of discussing. Then Michael de Raadt spent some time analysing that, do decide the programme for the rest of the day. There were 40 participants, so we had about 4 groups of 10 for 4 sessions, so up to 16 topics. And, in fact, while Michael was doing that Martin Dougiamas said some general things to everyone, so I guess that counts as a plenary talk, but we can probably make an exception for Martin. Actually, in this hackfest, things ended up falling into about 12 sessions, so the the last of the 4 sessions was kept for any discussions that had not finished earlier. The other good thing was that there was a lot of encouragement for each group to write notes during their discussion, and link them to the wiki: https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Hackfest_UK_2014 And, indeed, to follow that up later by turning the notes into a proper spec. Also, though I said no mini-presentations, there was one, I suggested that sam marshall into did a demo of the process of fixing a bug in Moodle core, and enough people voted for that so that he did. But that was still a group of people sitting round a table, not a classic presentation. The structure was not strict. People were welcome to head off on their one as a small group to discuss something if they wanted. For example, towards the end I managed to grab Bas Brands and Stuart Lamour, and we had a good chat about the Quiz UI that lead to these ideas . (I wish I had had time to implement more of those by now.) As I say, I thought this was the most successful hackfest I had been to. What do other people who were there think?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What would be an ideal Moodle hackfest for you?
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes - I think the Edinburgh hackfest worked well. It was also helpful to generate a list of useful tools that all Moodle developers should be aware of. The only other thought I had was maybe there could be an opportunity for some side-by-side peer reviewing of either core patches or non-core plugins? A chance for less experienced/confident developers to learn how to do a peer review or maybe a chance for them to get some direct feedback on code they have already written? Doing this would require some organisation in advance (much like Tomasz's suggestion below). Another item that might be useful (which may need a little bit of advance preparation), would be a round-table session on writing behat tests, as they can seem a bit scary if you haven't done them before, but are really worth learning how to do.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What would be an ideal Moodle hackfest for you?
ResponsesInList.Text: The Edinburgh hackfest was very nice indeed. And I agree that the yacking part (people talking to eacher other) is probably the most important part. If we were to write actual code and get things done we would need more than one day in a conference room. That said, if the Edinburgh hackfest would have been organised the day before the actual conference the people attending would be able to get to know each other better and we could do a session on the hackfest outcome for all those attending the conference, get some input from the actual users. Then again, scheduling it on a Monday might result in fewer ppl showing up for the hackfest. The unconference setup was great, and having lots of HQ devs attend was part of it's success too, Michael took the lead and knows how to set mood for good collaboration. I hope to be able to create a working group of developers for this or next years hackfest to actualy try and work on some code together. Get inspired and create cool stuff. Maybee we could still work on the Quiz UI for next years moot and show off the results Looking forward to my next hackfest!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What would be an ideal Moodle hackfest for you?
ResponsesInList.Text: Here is what I'd try for at least one hackfest session/track: * keep the group small * keep it focused * decide on topic upfront, so people can research/read up/prepare upfront The idea would be to get people truly interested in the given topic and with some expertise (or give them a chance to research upfront). The topic would be decided on a forum days before the actual event. The actual format of the meeting could be flexible - e.g. round table discussion. Ideally some people would come in prepared with code examples/prototypes already done. Tomek

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What would be an ideal Moodle hackfest for you?
ResponsesInList.Text: I don't attended any Moodle hackfest, but I did some hackatons. For that one I like the most, I grap some interesting points, and some of them you suggested above: State the hackfest focus upfront. People attending will be really interesting on that or those hackfest themes. Make few quick presentations of 10-15 minutes of usefull things/aspects/technology/whatever, that will be really useful for later on when discussing. For instance, the general and official workflow for the new log api v2, if that is some of the topics of the hackfest. Throw ideas to deliberate on (like the case of Tim Hunt's success story). Group ideas into general topics and build workshops for each general topic, either simultaneously or just few at a time, so that people interested in severa topics may have the opportunity to participate. The point 1 is very important for the viewpoint of the organization to focus discussions on some topics. But point 3 is really important to get participants get virtually "the control" of the hackfest, since they are discussing the topics they promoted too. Have a nice day! Jordi

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What would be an ideal Moodle hackfest for you?
ResponsesInList.Text: Two points that are not really answers to David's questions, but worth mentioning. Having a mandate from users to focus on an area of development will increase success Users are critical when development results in things that don't benefit them in a tangible way. It is true that developers can be tempted to refactor API code because it falls below some perceived standard, when there is often more critical work needed. A plan for the upcoming UK Moot (and possibly others) is to have working groups early in the conference followed by a developer hackfest at the end, which would generate the mandate developers could then work to. Developers would, of course, be welcomed at the earlier sessions. Not all hackfest work needs to flow from such user input, but some/most should. The goal should be solid design s As people have suggested, there's more talk than coding at a hackfest. That's not a bad thing, in fact it's probably the best use of that time. The goal of the hackfest should therefore be solid designs, taking suggestions from users and transforming them into a form that can be implemented. If people are keen to contributed later by implementing that design in code, then that's a bonus, but not one that should be expected of everyone who attends.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: HTTPS Protocol
ResponsesInList.Text: Unless you are actually using Apache proxy, then remove that line you've added. You must first make sure your apache server will respond to an ssl request: https://yourserver:443 If that hits your Moodle the theme will appear to be messed up.   That's ok. See: http://docs.moodle.org/24/en/Apache#SSL Then decide ... one can have https (SSL for logins only) or see http://www.inmotionhosting.com/support/edu/moodle/moodle-site-security/forcing-ssl-sitewide for running SSL all the time. Think I've read in these forums that running SSL all the time messes with caching ... something not desired. 'spirit of sharing', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: HTTPS Protocol
ResponsesInList.Text: There can be lots of reasons for a blank page. Were you running moodle on https prior to moving servers? Apache logs would be a good starting point to start troubleshooting. On unix they would usually be in /var/log/httpd/ You could test if https is working correctly by placing a test.html file with something plaintext in it, like "TEST" or anything. Running SSL the whole time is a good idea, it safeguards you against session hijacking.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: HTTPS Protocol
ResponsesInList.Text: Ken you are right.  In the past we had run moodle on HTTPS (using the vhost to force https) and now we run https for login only.  As you mention a side-effect of HTTPS is that all caching is disabled.  This isn't a Moodle issue- it's an encryption issue.  There is a HUGE performance gain in not forcing HTTPS everywhere.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: HTTPS Protocol
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, The correct solution after confirming that your SSL is all in place correctly, it simply to update the wwwroot setting to use https instead of https. Others are right in saying that you do not need the sslproxy setting. However, contrary to other advice, I would not advise using the loginhttps (the setting to make SSL only for login). In fact, I would personally like to see it removed entirely but this is currently not feasible. We removed the equivalent setting from Mahara over two years ago. It is incredibly easy for someone to steal another user's login when you're dealing with unencrypted connections - even if you encrypt the login itself. There's even a FireFox extension to demonstrate just how easy it is - see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firesheep for a bit more information. Although there is a minor performance benefit from not having SSL, it is minor and modern servers can more than cope with that increase in load. When the setting was introduced many years ago (specifically the 19th June 2004 - https://github.com/moodle/moodle/commit/8a33e3717d19e1d2d650634e301d23a82438c136 ), the servers people used for production were much less capable. We didn't have the benefit of modern multi-core processors and instruction sets which were more suited to SSL encryption and decryption (at least, not at an affordable price). Again, at the time that this setting was introduced, network bandwidth was a completely different ball-game. Many people were still on slower connections (e.g. dialup) and mobile data was non-existent. Today we're in a very different world and the chance are that your mobile phone has a connection 400 times faster (56K modem vs. a conservative 20MB 4G). Yes, you do lose the ability to cache between browser restarts . Once you have a browser open, as I understand it, you do have browser caching, though you still cannot benefit from proxy server caching. That said, there are a number of thing which you can do to reduce the load on your server. One of the easiest to configure is the use of the X-SendFile header (and it's counterparts). I would probably advise this anyway if you are able to do so. See https://github.com/moodle/moodle/blob/master/config-dist.php#L206 for further information. This reduces the load massively for Moodle as it hands off the byte-shift serving of files to the web server, whose primary design is to serve files. Moodle serves a lot of files using byte-shifting (that's where it reads the files off disk, and then serves them rather than the web server serving the files directly) - it does to to prevent unauthorised access. The X-SendFile changes keep the authentication in place, but then add a new header (X-SendFile: /path/to/file/on/server) which the server then intercepts and uses to read the file - therefore keeping the authentication but moving the file serving back to the web server. Another thing you can do is to introduce caching between Moodle and the SSL encryption stage. This is pretty easy with things like Varnish, and there's some functionality built into most modern web servers (I know there is for Nginx, and I think that there is for Apache2). You have to be very careful with this one, but it's generally safe to cache all of the theme directory and not much else. This is less of a benefit than X-SendFile. There are other caveats to forcing HTTPS at all times (notably that using content from insecure sites will display warnings to this effect), but in my opinion the increased security is a better solution and educating staff as to what these warnings mean, and how they can write their content to be future-proof is something that will probably be required longer-term anyway. Moodle also does try and replace some of these links itself - e.g. if you are using SSL, I think I'm right in saying that pasting a non-SSL YouTube link it will replace it with the SSL equivalent by the Media filter. Although Moodle is only carrying your virtual learning content, for many institutions this will include grades and will consequentially degree implications, and for some (e.g. research-based Universities) an attack of this type could potentially reveal sensitive research data which is not yet public and/or subject to appropriate copyright (so is a major concern in terms of Intellectual Property). Of course, it's entirely up you and you must weigh up the various options but please do your research and consider your own requirements before making a decision. Note, the opinions above are my own, and other developers at HQ may disagree. Prior to working at HQ, I did work for a University and was responsible for the development, running, and security of various sytems - we felt that SSL was an important requirement for our Moodle implementation (and many of our other systems too). Best wishes, Andrew

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: HTTPS Protocol
ResponsesInList.Text: Andrew, thanks for the detailed write-up.  I couldn't agree more that https IS more secure.  One thing you said that I'd like to clarify: It is incredibly easy for someone to steal another user's login when you're dealing with unencrypted connections - even if you encrypt the login itself. If the login itself is encrypted then it is incredibly difficult ( mostly ) to steal another user's login credentials.  If you're dealing with unencrypted connections it is possible to have the current session hijacked, but not the credentials, though passwords can be reset after hijacking.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using PHP In PLace of Page Content
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for the replies. I didn't check back in this thread early enough before continuing on with my own implementation. It's messy but it works. Here's what I did: 1. Open /moodle/mod/page/view.php 2. Somewhere early in the page add this function: function safe_string_sanitize($str) { $clean = preg_replace("/[^a-zA-Z0-9\/_|+ -]/", '', $str); $clean = strtolower(trim($clean, '-')); $clean = preg_replace("/[\/_|+ -]+/", '-', $clean); return $clean; } 3. Find the line "echo $OUTPUT->box($content, "generalbox center clearfix");" 4. Replace with: $dyn_content = $CFG-> dirroot . '/dynamic/' . safe_string_sanitize($course->shortname) . '/' . safe_string_sanitize($page->name) . '.php'; if (file_exists($dyn_content)) { include($dyn_content); } else { echo $OUTPUT->box($content, "generalbox center clearfix"); } 5. Place the content for your page in "/moodle/dynamic/{course-shortname}/{course-name}.php" This is just my quick hackish method. Maybe in the future I'll take the time to write a legitimate plugin. ResponsesInList.Text: One way is documented in Blocks FAQ - see #4 , which mentions teachers but can be adapted for any role.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: how do I let only certain users to view a block
ResponsesInList.Text: Do you mean that everyone can see the block, once it has been added, or that everyone has the ability to add the block? The block/BLOCKNAME:addinstance capability controls who is allowed to add the block to a Moodle page. There is no standard Moodle capability that will automatically control who will see a particular block once it has been created - you will have to write some code in your block to do this yourself. Thankfully, it is really easy to do, just add the following to your block's 'get_content()' function: if (!has_capability('block/BLOCKNAME:view', $this-> context )) { return null; } (Note: this assumes that you replace 'BLOCKNAME' with the name of your block and that you have defined the block/BLOCKNAME:view capability in access.php and, if necessary, you have bumped up the version number to install this new capability).

ResponsesInList.Title: PaintWeb an image editor in TinyMCE
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello everyone! I have recently taken over the impressive work of Mihai Sucan in integrating the PaintWeb image editing application in moodle. I'm writing this post in order to give an idea of the work in progress and to coordinate with moodle developers in order to hopefully include this application in a future release of moodle. Try PaintWeb within TinyMCE and get a feeling of what could be offered to moodle! I have started testing this feature inside my own copy of moodle 2.2.2+ and I'm pretty close to having a fully functional image editor inside TinyMCE. See my results so far in the image below: The next step is to coordinate my work with moodle developers in order to include in a future release of moodle (2.4 would be awesome! ;). For this purpose, I am trying to revive the originally posted feature to gather some interest and attention upon my work. So, if you drop by and you'd like to see this happen in moodle 2.4, please add your vote! Work in progress - I'll post my progress to this forum, so you can keep track of what is happening. ResponsesInList.Title: Getting Started
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi all, I've been working with Moodle for years, designing courses, but I've just started dipping my toe in the water with development and PHP.  I wanted to start by trying to create some simple blocks. After searching around, I was steered toward Moodle 1.9 Extension Development by Moore and Churchward.  Likewise, some info on the net directed me to the Introduction to Moodle Development course but that's written for Moodle 1.8.  I played around with the code from these on my Moodle 2.6 installation to see if I could get it to work but started to think that was maybe more confusing than helpful because current versions of Moodle seem to be so different. I found my way to the Moodle Dev Docs on blocks and worked through some of the examples there, which was obviously much better as it's designed for Moodle 2.0, and actually works!  I've been looking in the code of some of the existing blocks as well, trying to understand how they work but it's hard for a newbie.  I've decided to set a goal for myself to try to build a little "teacher contact info" block to get started, that displays the teacher's profile photo, name, and a link to send them a message, just to start learning the ropes. So I kind of wanted to introduce myself and get start getting involved with this forum.  I guess my first question is: what next?  Is there anywhere else I can find relatively up-to-date information on developing Moodle blocks or just working with the PHP code in Moodle generally? Thanks for your help! Donald Robertson

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Getting Started
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Donald. And welcome on the DEV board Writing a small block is a good start, for sure. Looking at existing blocks in both standard Moodle and the plugins directory is wise. I am not aware of more recent tutorial on writing Moodle blocks. Just some quick notes. UTSL Really, learning to rely on the source code itself rather than any external documentation is something you can only profit from. Use some good IDE. It does not necessarily be some heavy environment but an essential feature you want is to be able to quickly jump to a place where a given function is defined, and back. So you read the code, put the cursor into a function call like `get_string()` or any other Moodle function, press some magic key and your IDE should take you to a place where is is defined. The inline phpDocs there should then give you a clear info on what params it accepts etc. Give Git a go. The sooner, the better. There are quite awesome tutorials on starting with it around. See more tips at Finding your way into the Moodle code Consider writing a small blog / journal to track your learning experience and progress. It can help yourself and others reading it later, too.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: A script for finding plugins with old-style cron

Thats correct - the 'legacy cron' functions are not going away any time soon and they are fully backwards compatible. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Where to put files in data directory?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Michael, I've written clients that sometimes generate files in a computer's memory, e.g. screencaptures and webcam photos, and then write them as files on the server . I've found the simplest way to store such generated files in Moodle is by enabling and using Moodle's File system feature: https://docs.moodle.org/27/en/File_system_repository The location of the files are in /moodledata/repository/[your-plugin-repository]/ Files saved there are then accessible to Moodle's file management system but only if the File system repository is enabled. Files are also be available to FTP and other file management systems. To retrieve files via a plugin, it may be necessary to write a custom proxy script like this one: https://github.com/matbury/SWF-Activity-Module2.5/blob/master/swf/content.php I hope this helps!

ResponsesInList.Title: Why I argued Moodle development should follow the market leaders of social media
ResponsesInList.Text: In a recent blog post I argued that Moodle should look to follow the market leaders of social media in order to draw inspiration for future developments. This got a lot of comment and some disagreement. Here I explain my point in more detail. It is a truism to say that in order to obtain a deep understanding of something (or to be truly knowledgeable about it) we need to engage in the subject material. We also know that students often do not truly engage with their studies. Even the students that do well often have only done enough to pass assessments. In such cases their knowledge is usually transient and useful only for the purpose of passing the assessment. Many of us in education feel this is a wasted opportunity and are trying to get students to engage at a deeper level with their studies. So how do we do this? Usually it involves breaking the educational mould which many of our successful students have grown comfortable with. We need to step outside the traditional models of teaching and assessment. It helps if we conceptualize teaching as a process of guidance, and assessment as a process we do in order to guide our students better. It helps if we bypass theories of learning which articulate it as a process of "acquiring knowledge” and follow theories of learning which articulate it as a practice of doing. I have seen inspiring teaching and assessment methods being deployed at my institution: tutors who are changing the educational rules, making space for social interaction and rewarding students for engaging in activities which require criticality, personality and resourcefulness. I am happy to talk to you about it some time. However, of importance to my argument here - education is not the only cultural field that are trying to get people to engage. Social media companies attempt to get its users to engage too. And they are very successful at it. When I walk around the computer labs at my university I am more likely to see the students having a Facebook page open than our learning system. Why? Because they find it engaging and they want to interact with it. It is worth noting, and I am sure you will agree, that learning is not confined to educational settings. We are always learning. We learn from whatever we engage with - whether play-fighting with our siblings, building electric cars or having a football match. We are also learning when we are engaging with social media; learning about current affairs, personal hobbies, and what our friends, and the wider world, find funny and interesting. "So what?", you may ask, "We aren't interested if our students learning this stuff - we want them to learn the course curriculum". No, but we can draw insights from it - "if only we could marry the two”. In the same blog post I argued that in blended learning scenarios a Moodle course is like a bespoke textbook for the curricula being taught. And we all know that education at times struggles to get students to engage with their curricula learning, particularly engagement with content buried in textbooks and online resources. Let me explain, I find the bespoke textbook a helpful metaphor when conceptualising the creation of a course/site, but it isn't as helpful metaphor when thinking about the students' experience of interacting with the learning environment. Think of Facebook. From the user's point of view they are updating their profile, but from their friends' point of view they are adding to the stream in their list of News items. Similarly from a course creators' point to view they adding resources and activities to their bespoke textbook, but consider this: what if from their students' point of view the content or activity being added was to a stream of curricula-related updates. Would this stream be more effective in drawing our students into the course sites (bespoke textbooks) and engaging further? Evidence drawn from social media would predict so. According to Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg: "Every new product that wants to build engagement bases its design on feeds”. I argue then our learning systems could benefit from being based on feeds too. A feed-based learning system could be a dynamic and an addictive interface which keeps students coming back and engaging in curricula-based content. Steven Levy in Wired magazine (Jun '14) says, "Ever since Twitter and Facebook debuted in 2006, the model of continually streaming updates has come to define how we consume information”. Consume information? Is that like learning? I don't know, but my point is that when designing the Moodle software we should look to social media to find patterns which can encourage our students to interact and engage with curricula learning and increase  its vibrancy and relevance. Comments welcome.

ResponsesInList.Text: @Dawn - hi. Moodle is an institutional tool to support traditional teaching and assessment structures. This is not a revolutionary piece of software - hence its success so far. What I envisage are tweaks to the system following cues from leaders in other related industries. Moodle still supports educational models where the curriculum is determined by the institution and its tutors. I am not talking about an e-portfolio or PLE as I understand them. So for clarification - we keep the course site. The bespoke textbook exists and can be accessed in its entirety: read like an online textbook; tasks and activities completed like those in an online textbook. That still exists. But we have a layer on top of that. A home page probably. A page which provides dynamic hooks into the courses. Hooks with curricula-related social interaction and relevant, timely content - contributed by tutors and peers. Secondly, many will argue that social media models are not relevant to higher level learning in highly academic subjects. I disagree. We can make curricula content interesting and relevant to our students. It almost certainly felt both interesting and relevant to them when they chose to study it. This is primarily the role of the teachers and their teaching and assessment practices. But it can also be aided by the design of our online learning systems. We can support the development of knowledge in our students through using interface patterns which promote engagement and interaction. If we can make Moodle an addictive, sticky interface - full of curricula content and activities - we are increasing the students' engagement with the curricula and the relevance.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why I argued Moodle development should follow the market leaders of social media
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Paolo, Thanks for starting this discussion. There's a lot of discussions about how to make Moodle more "social" and there seems to be a lot of demand for Facebook-like features. I like the way your framing it and hope it'll be productive. My take on the "making it more attractive to learners" is this: Advertising, PR, Marketing, and to a great extent are entertainment and, more often than not, fit the mantra, "Don't make me think!" Education, on the other hand, wants its participants to think critically (i.e. "deeper learning"). Typically, critical thinking is unpopular because it... requires and great deal of time and effort, causes discomfort and unhappiness, generates conflict and tension, poses risks to relationships, is relatively easy to avoid, and is strikingly rare in everyday life (Adapted from Tom Angelo, Seven Layers for Higher and Deeper Learning , 27th Annual Teaching & Learning Innovation Conference, Guelph, Canada, 2014). Another way to put it is, "Some people can't tell the difference between critical thinkers and haters." I posit that if you filled up a learner's Facebook "friends" list with critical thinkers; always questioning assumptions, asking for well-reasoned, evidence supported arguments, reflecting critically on every incident; and blocked their real "friends", they'd more than likely not return to Facebook in between study/work quite so often. That said, I think it does help enormously for learners and teaching and support staff to build their social presence* and for their chosen platform (i.e. Moodle) to support this as well as possible. Learners need to know what's recent, what's coming next, where their "stuff" is, and when and where to find their classmates, teachers, and support staff. Perhaps a productive approach would be to look at what strategies and curriculum designs help to establish, cultivate, and encourage social presence, see what can already be done in Moodle to this end, and where it needs improvement, rather than copying what Facebook does to entertain its users and sell stuff. *See: Rourke, L., Anderson, T. Garrison, D. R., & Archer, W. (2001). Assessing social presence in asynchronous, text-based computer conferencing . Journal of Distance Education , 14(3), 51-70. Here's a list, in no particular order of papers and articles on social presence in online learning environments: On The Nature And Development of Social Presence In Online Course Discussions: http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.102.5653&rep=rep1&type=pdf Social presence in distributed group environments: the role of social identity: http://www.itd.cnr.it/home/Manuela_Delfino/Paper/Delfino-Manca_CHB.pdf Using Computer-mediated Communication to Establish Social and Supportive Environments in Teacher Education: http://www.personal.psu.edu/slt13/589_s2007/08_Arnold%20et%20al.pdf The Power of Presence: Our quest for the right mix of social presence in online courses: http://patricklowenthal.com/publications/The_power_of_presence--our_quest_for_the_right_mix_of_social_presence_in_online_courses.pdf Encyclopedia of Distance and Online Learning: Social Presence: http://www.patricklowenthal.com/publications/socialpresenceEDOLpre-print.pdf Social presence in online learning communities: http://www.lancaster.ac.uk/fss/organisations/netlc/past/nlc2010/abstracts/PDFs/Kear.pdf The evolution and influence of social presence theory on online learning: http://www.patricklowenthal.com/publications/evolution_social_presence.pdf From Pixel on a Screen to Real Person in Your Students' Lives: Establishing Social Presence using Digital Storytelling: http://www.cehd.umn.edu/PsTL/Water/Resources/Documents/LowenthalDunlap2010.pdf Assessing Social Presence In Asynchronous Text-based Computer Conferencing: http://auspace.athabascau.ca/bitstream/2149/732/1/Assessing%20Social%20Presence%20In%20Asynchronous%20Text-based%20Computer%20Conferencing.pdf Fostering Presence in Online Discussions: http://rapidintellect.com/AEQweb/5284v3.pdf I hope this helps!

ResponsesInList.Title: Getting number of rows from
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi I have this line of code: $userlist = $DB->get_recordset_ sql ("$select $from $where $sort", $params, $table->get_page_start(), $table->get_page_size()); I would like to retrieve the number of rows this has given without doing anymore sql calls to database , because our database is overloaded as it is. how can that be done ? I have moodle 2.7

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Getting number of rows from
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Di. There are a few ways to do this. While iterating through the record set, iterate a counter as well. eg $count = 0; foreach ($record) { $count++; } echo $count; Use iterator_count http://php.net/manual/en/function.iterator-count.php - but this approach breaks the iterator state. Use get_records_sql instead of get_recordset_sql - this will use more memory, but you can do count($userlist); Add a subselect query to your DB query which does select(count(*) from ...) - no less load on your DB though. Fix your database ;)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Getting number of rows from
ResponsesInList.Text: Other places in Moodle that need to do this to it by executing a separate count statement. That does not take twice as long as executing the single statement, because the first query will pull the necessary data into the DBs caches, and then the second query will run mostly on cached data and be much faster.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Overriding file
ResponsesInList.Text: The first question is what are you trying to do that requires you to edit that file? In many cases there are better alternatives than modifying core files. If you are really convinced that you cannot proceed without making this core code change, then make sure you are familiar with using git to manage your upgrades. Within a Moodle version (e.g. Moodle 2.5.1 => 2.5.3), you should just be able to merge the MOODLE_xx_STABLE branch into your branch (and then resolve any conflicts that occur - hopefully not too many, if you're only editing a single file). For major version upgrades, (e.g. Moodle 2.5 => 2.6), follow Tim's instructions at: http://tjhunt.blogspot.co.uk/2014/01/moving-ou-moodle-code-to-moodle-261.html

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Custom auth + account creation
ResponsesInList.Text: Is it not possible to simply allow Moodle to work as intended? Moodle asks the authentication plugin to check to see if the user can be authenticated If authenticated, Moodle checks if there is an account already - if not it creates one. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Cannot update existing capability in a module
ResponsesInList.Text: After a capability has been created, the only way to change which roles it is assigned to (other than manually changing the database entries), is to edit the role definitions via the UI (site admin > users > permissions > define roles). This is exactly as it should be - once the code has setup the default capability assignments on a site, the end user should be in control of which roles have which capabilities (it would cause confusion if a capability overridden by the site admin suddenly reverted during a plugin upgrade).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Cannot update existing capability in a module
ResponsesInList.Text: If you need to perform subsequent update of existing capabilities you would have to use upgrade.php facility. Write the code that will run through all roles and update them accordingly. I suggest to look into role_change_permission API in accesslib.php.

ResponsesInList.Text: Note that Moodle sanitises HTML on output, not input, so you may well see suspicious things in the database, The reason for this is that HTML sanitisation is very complex, and so the code that does it could well have bugs. If we only sanitised on input, and buggy code let something dangerous through, then you are stuck. Since we sanitise everything on output, if a bug is found and fixed, all dangerous stuff in old input is rendered harmless in future.

ResponsesInList.Title: Occurrence of 'and', 'or' in the code. Beware!
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm working on 2.7 and sometimes I find conditions in the code that are written with "and / or" instead of " && / ||" And while this is not necessarily a major issue, it still can cause some unexpected results. For example: $first = true; $second = false; $third = $first and $second; $third will be true , because '=' has a higher precedence than 'and', while $third = $first && $second; Will result with false . This is just the simplest example. More complex conditions can cause more unexpected results.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Multiple Moodle sites, one DB
ResponsesInList.Text: You can apply different themes on a user basis, but not by role. The issue with using roles is that the way Moodle works a user could potentially be a student on one course while being a tutor on another (e.g. a PhD student supporting seminars in an undergraduate class). From the back end it would probably be possible to add the user themes direct into the database and then hide that option from the user profile pages so that individual users can't see it to change it again. IF you are using site-wide roles (see above!) you could also add some code into the top of the layout files which detect that role and then adds a different body class according to the role which can then be used to apply different css - personally I'd go for setting the user themes and then hiding the option to change it (in css) rather than get into site-wide roles and the complexities of having two different sets of css depending on the role.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is my code secure?
ResponsesInList.Text: A few quick suggestions: Run codechecker against it - https://moodle.org/plugins/view.php?plugin=local_codechecker (there is a lot of layout that differs from Moodle coding guidelines) Make sure you remove the closing '?>' from the end of the files where you've included it Don't write if (!$DB->get_record(...)) { echo "Error message"; die(); } - use the 'MUST_EXIST' param It's a good idea to define javascript functions within a 'M.mod_feedbackwall' object, otherwise they may clash with other javascript functions with the same name on the same page (even better, use shifter to compress the javascript and the YUI module support to load and initialise the correct javascript, as required).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: oh just some thoughts for the future...
ResponsesInList.Text: Oh dear.... If you want to make points for the user/learner and not the coder, then why post in the Developer's Forum? Like fine wines, Moodle needs to be developed - but like so many other products, it is also trapped by its legacy. v2.0 was a step away from v1.xxxx, a rather large step. I would think that v3 will be a similarly large step away from v2.xxxx in which many of the things discussed will make their first appearances. We also have to recognise that the changing technology has an impact, D'nD was not available in v1.xxx as it was only developed more recently. Changing technology will dictate a change in tastes. ResponsesInList.Title: Large scale moodle installations 30.000+ users - tips?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, I have been reading here and around the web, on which precautions to make when making a large scale moodle. We are counting on 30.000 - 60.000 users, and that will of cause take its toll on the server (s). But which measurements are we talking about? Do we need a cluster of servers to run the site and another to run the database ? Do we need one big monster machine to run the site and another to run the database. Do we need one Big monster only to minimize mysql hang-load time. There are many different suggestions, but i like to hear from those who has experience in such a large scale solution. What are the requirements, for the hardware? I hope you can help. Thanks, kind regards Henrik Sune Pedersen

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Large scale moodle installations 30.000+ users - tips?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hej Henrik, the total number of users is not necessarily an indication of how big your setup has to be, it is mainly about concurrency. I used to run an 85k users, 500 concurrent (as in simultaneous) off one server (48Gb memory 24 CPU threads). You will need to optimize everything, database, webserver, php, memcache to achieve the best performance. One big machine makes it easy to optimize and configure, however this can only scale up to a certain amount. A cluster scales (if done right) much further, but is much more complicated to optimize, and will give worse performance for the end user due to added latencies. For database there are essentially three hardware parameters that influence performance: Memory Disk IOPS CPU Good luck! David

ResponsesInList.Title: My Private Files who uses them
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Is there an easy way from the front end of Moodle 2.7 for an admin to find out who is using the My Private Files.? We thought we had My Private Files turned off, but turns out we missed the bit in capabilities. If not what am I looking for in a MySQL database ? Thank you Heather

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: My Private Files who uses them
ResponsesInList.Text:
The following should list you all private files used by your users. Just please do not simply remove those records from the table. 
```text
SELECT userid, filepath, filename
  FROM mdl_files
 WHERE component = 'user' AND filearea = 'private' AND filename <> '.';
```
 You will probably want to play with query a bit, such as have `SELECT DISTINCT userid` there only or so.
